#68038. Industry News: Never-Say-Die Climbers Will Try Everest Again This Weekend

Industry News: Never-Say-Die Climbers Will Try Everest Again This Weekend

📅 17 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 2 min read (323 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Explorersweb

⏱️ ~2 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Despite a forecast of high winds on November 21 and 22, Andrei Vasiliev, Sergey Kondrashkin, and Vitaly Shipilov have decided to begin a fresh attempt on the West Ridge of Everest on Sunday.
  • The three stubborn Russians will again proceed via the West Ridge without bottled oxygen, support, or any other living soul on the mountain.
  • Industry observers note that the forecasts warn of very high winds all weekend.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Despite a forecast of high winds on November 21 and 22, Andrei Vasiliev, Sergey Kondrashkin, and Vitaly Shipilov have decided to begin a fresh attempt on the West Ridge of Everest on Sunday.

The three stubborn Russians will again proceed via the West Ridge without bottled oxygen, support, or any other living soul on the mountain.

Industry observers note that the forecasts warn of very high winds all weekend. Nevertheless, they will start up on Sunday, November 22, although that is the day with the strongest winds forecast.

It has been revealed that “That day, we will remain low on the mountain and climb to our Camp 1 at 5,600m,” Sergey Kondrashkin wrote. “From there, we will push upward when the weather improves and the winds die down, aiming to descend around November 28.”.

This means the team does not intend to summit quite yet. The goal is to acclimatize by reaching 7,500m and then return to their headquarters in Lobuche.

“The question is, will we manage to complete the summit push within the time frame of our permit, which expires on December 15, and will the weather cooperate?” said Kondrashkin.

Sources indicate that the fall season on Everest usually lasts until the end of November, since December 1 marks the start of Nepal’s winter climbing season. However, the permit dates may have been extended for this team, which is climbing off the normal route.

Once winter settles in, it will be the turn of Jost Kobusch of Germany, who will attempt to solo Everest in winter along the same route the Russians are now attempting.

Recent findings suggest that on their third and latest trip up the mountain so far, the team only reached 6,700m before hurricane-force winds up to 130kph forced them down, according to former team member Natalyia Belyankina. Belyankina had to leave the expedition for health reasons but has stayed in touch with the others.

#68032. What If Money Wasn’t the Barrier to Your PCT Dream?

📅 20 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 4m • 📚 Deep Dive (803 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Thetrek ↗ Open Full Page

What If Money Wasn’t the Barrier to Your PCT Dream?

📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (803 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Thetrek

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • The Pacific Crest Trail is a dream for thousands of people.
  • It has been revealed that but getting to the trail takes more than a dream.
  • Recent findings suggest that through the Trail Angel Fund, the PCT Grant provides $5,000 annually to a Washingtonian (and so far this year, we have raised enough money to send off TWO hikers!) between the ages of 18 and 33 who dream of thru-hiking the Pacific Crest Trail.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The Pacific Crest Trail is a dream for thousands of people. Spanning 2,650 miles from Mexico to Canada, the trail offers the opportunity to step away from everyday life, immerse yourself in the outdoors, and experience something that can be difficult to put into words.

It has been revealed that but getting to the trail takes more than a dream. For many aspiring thru-hikers, the financial commitment is one of the biggest barriers. Between gear, food, transportation, and the ability to step away from work for several months, the cost of a thru-hike can put the experience out of reach before someone even takes their first step.

The PCT Grant was created to help change that.

Recent findings suggest that through the Trail Angel Fund, the PCT Grant provides $5,000 annually to a Washingtonian (and so far this year, we have raised enough money to send off TWO hikers!) between the ages of 18 and 33 who dream of thru-hiking the Pacific Crest Trail. Its mission is to make long-distance hiking more accessible by easing the financial burden and giving someone the opportunity to pursue an experience they might not otherwise be able to afford.

At its heart, the program is about expanding access to the outdoors and recognizing that the transformative experiences found on trail shouldn’t be limited to those who can afford them.

2026 was the first year the PCT Grant came to life and chose its first recipient to take on thru-hiking the Pacific Crest Trail. That person was me! The face behind the screen: Cappy. Post trail, I have joined the PCT Grant Committee to spread some magic with hopes of creating that same opportunity for others.

Industry observers note that receiving the grant was a lifeline. It wasn’t just financial support; it was the difference between being able to pursue this dream and having to put it on hold. It gave me room to take a chance on myself and say yes to an experience that changed the way I see what’s possible in life.

As this year’s recipient, I experienced firsthand what this kind of support can make possible. The trail taught me a lot about the power of choice and trust. The power of choosing something before knowing exactly how it will unfold, doing it scared, and learning to become comfortable with the uncomfortable.

Spending five months on trail offered so much more than the physical accomplishment of a thru-hike. I discovered how much we are capable of when we give ourselves the opportunity to find out. This trail changed my life, and it will continue to do so.

As the program enters its second year, the focus is on growing awareness, strengthening community support, and building a foundation for future recipients.

It has been revealed that presently, the grant is funded to support one hiker annually, with a longer-term vision of expanding its reach and helping more aspiring thru-hikers access the trail. From our fundraising efforts (a post trail Q&A with Cappy and other media platforms helping to spread the word) we have raised enough money to fund a second hiker this coming year.

Donations play an vital role in making that possible. Every contribution helps sustain the program and move it closer to supporting additional hikers in the years ahead. We want to continue to grow this program so that even more hikers can set foot on the trail.

Recent findings suggest that applications for the 2027 PCT Grant are open through January 31, 2027. If you’re a Washingtonian between 18 and 33 with a dream of hiking the PCT, this could be an opportunity to make it happen.

And for those who have already experienced the magic of the trail, consider helping someone else get there.

Help make the next journey possible.

#68030. Jost Kobusch to Train For Everest on Difficult, Dangerous Lhotse Shar

📅 17 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 3m • 📚 Deep Dive (601 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Explorersweb ↗ Open Full Page

Jost Kobusch to Train For Everest on Difficult, Dangerous Lhotse Shar

📅 17 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (601 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Explorersweb

⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • According to recent reports, jost Kobusch of Germany has moved to the Khumbu Valley to finish his acclimatization before attempting to solo winter Everest, beginning on December 22.
  • In a recent development, kobusch is now in Chukhung village, from which he climbed 6,165m Island Peak (Imja Tse) yesterday.
  • Kobusch’s climb on Island Peak as shown in his tracker today.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, jost Kobusch of Germany has moved to the Khumbu Valley to finish his acclimatization before attempting to solo winter Everest, beginning on December 22. His preparations include reaching 8,000m on a different peak.

In a recent development, kobusch is now in Chukhung village, from which he climbed 6,165m Island Peak (Imja Tse) yesterday. He spent the night at 6,000m, topped out again today, and went back down, as shown in his live tracker. He told ExplorersWeb that he will now rest for a few days in Lukla and then hike up the valley again to inspect conditions on his next acclimatization goal: the difficult Lhotse Shar (8,383m).

Kobusch’s climb on Island Peak as shown in his tracker today.

“My plan is not to summit but to tag 8,000m up its flank, before heading for Everest,” he said.

Sources indicate that lhotse Shar is one of the main points of the Lhotse ridge, and it is climbed from south side of the mountain, with Chukhung as the starting point. The main options are to climb the southeastern flank of the Shar itself or try a direct line up the formidable south face of Lhotse.

Neither of them is easy, and the upper sections are statistically dangerous. According to Wikipedia, Lhotse Shar has the highest fatality rate of all principal or secondary 8,000m peaks. For every two climbers who summit, one person dies attempting to.

Lhotse and its various points, as seen from the south. Graphic by Gorskie Mapy.

Sources indicate that the Austrian expedition that first reached the summit of Lhotse Shar (from the Southeast Ridge) in 1970 set four altitude camps, the uppermost at 7,600m. They used supplemental oxygen on their summit push. “Almost the whole of the route from below Camp 1 to Camp 3 was fixed with rope, as climbing was very difficult,” they reported in the AAJ.

In a recent development, kobusch will not have to deal with the nearly vertical terrain and cornices near the summit, but will have to face difficult mixed terrain and uncertain conditions if he wants to venture up to 8,000m. He will not use bottled oxygen, and as far as we know, he will climb on his own.

Kobusch intends to reach the base of Everest on December 22 and solo the mountain in winter without oxygen, via the West Ridge — the same line currently being attempted by a Russian team.

This is Kobusch’s fourth attempt, and he is willing to try to reach the summit this time. However, when asked about it, he admits he does not know if such a feat is actually possible. “Every expedition, every training session, every difficult decision has been part of preparing myself for what I know will be the biggest challenge of my life,” he admits.

Kobusch’s is not the only confirmed climb this winter. Denis Urubko of Russia is reportedly preparing to climb Broad Peak in winter, possibly starting at the end of this year and continuing through January and February. On social media, Urubko mentioned he will be climbing with Vitaliy Skel. However, details of his route have not been confirmed.

Simone Moro of Italy has not decided whether to try Manaslu again this winter. He told ExplorersWeb he is still considering his plans while observing the “crazy weather this season.” Moro attempted Manaslu in fall to acclimatize and become familiar with the terrain. However, like every other team, he had to call off the attempt due to dangerous conditions following extremely heavy snowfall. Moro wants to climb the peak in alpine style.

Latest Update: The Paradox of Seeking First Ascents in Western Nepal

📅 18 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1231 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Explorersweb

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • In a recent development, western Nepal has plenty of unclimbed 6,000m peaks, and Fredrik Strang of Sweden and Sindre Kolbjornsgard of Norway went there planning to climb one.
  • In a recent development, what I remember most clearly about that narrow summit is not the grade, the exposure, or the possibility of being first.
  • Sindre Kolbjornsgard, left, and Fredrik Strang.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, western Nepal has plenty of unclimbed 6,000m peaks, and Fredrik Strang of Sweden and Sindre Kolbjornsgard of Norway went there planning to climb one. In the end, they settled for a slightly lower but equally memorable experience. It revealed again that adventure goes beyond first ascents.

In a recent development, what I remember most clearly about that narrow summit is not the grade, the exposure, or the possibility of being first. It is the silence. No helicopters. No voices from a fixed-rope queue. No machinery, no aircraft, no distant sound of a settlement. Only the two of us, a serrated horizon, and an unfamiliar feeling that the mountain had asked a question rather than supplied an answer.

Sindre Kolbjornsgard, left, and Fredrik Strang. Photo: Fredrik Strang.

After 18 expeditions to 8,000’ers and witnessing the evolution (or devolution) of climbing on these peaks’ normal routes, Strang and his partner knew they wanted something different. Quoting Ed Viesturs, Strang mentioned: “The point is to climb, not just to summit.” With that in mind, the climbers set four criteria for their objectives:.

Several route options face the climbers’ base camp tent. Photo: Fredrik Strang.

Sources indicate that strang noted that there are many unclimbed peaks left in Nepal, but they were looking for a compelling climb, not just a dull summit for the record. They finally found one that satisfied their criteria, but then, as with so many other teams in Nepal this fall, harsh weather put their original objective out of reach. Not to mention that traveling Western Nepal is anything but simple.

“Our intended destination was in the Nyalu Lek area north of Simikot,” Strang revealed. “We planned to cross Nyalu La, a pass around 5,000m, with a support party that included porters and pack animals.

“Getting from Surkhet to Simikot took two rough days by road, with landslides having damaged or obliterated sections of the route. At Simikot, we learned that Nyalu La was probably impassable. Even reaching the place where we planned to start trekking had been uncertain.”.

Recent findings suggest that when they did reach the area, they confirmed that their planned peak was not an option. Hiking further down the valley, they pitched their tent at Phendol Kermi Camp. Snow had covered the trails beyond, but they simply had no time or money to move to some other region in Nepal. Instead, they decided to explore whatever was close to their camp.

Sources indicate that during their stay, they encountered Mick Fowler and Victor Saunders of the UK. Bad weather had likewise spoiled the British pair’s plan to attempt an unclimbed 6,000m peak farther east, known only as Peak 6010, according to Mount Everest Foundation.. This would have been their second attempt on that peak. Ironically, dry conditions spoiled their 2025 attempt. This time, too much snow forced them back. Read more on the British climbers’ adventure here:.

Industry observers note that on October 6, Strang and Kolbjornsgard made their first acclimatization climb on a 5,177m peak at 30°20′49.82″N, 82°03′54.82″E. They found no records of any previous ascent.

Industry observers note that “From base camp, the mountain looked straightforward, and lower down, it largely was,” Strang recalls. “Steep grass, mud, and broken rock led toward the upper slopes. But at about 4,500m, the route disappeared beneath knee-deep snow, then waist-deep snow, and every step became a small excavation.”.

Sources indicate that in the following days, they scouted and flew their drone down side valleys, looking for possibilities. Their second peak was 5,227m in altitude, located at 30°07′50.86″N, 81°41′56.58″E. Again, there were no records of previous ascents. Parts of it were far from fun.

“Below 4,500m, progress was tolerable, but above that, we were back to forcing our way through knee-deep, sometimes chest-deep snow,” Strang wrote. “A tremendous amount of work for very little enjoyment.”.

Luckily, the climb improved once they reached the summit ridge, on relatively easy mixed rock and ice, which they assessed at PD+.

“Fowler and Saunders climbed the mountain several days later and found an easier way to descend and reascend the step on its western side,” Strang noted. “Their solution was a reminder that the first line a team takes is not necessarily the best one.”.

Still, the peak that most drew the climbers’ attention was a remarkable 5,337m tooth of rock above Yangchya Lake at approximately 30°07′09.36″N, 81°41′21.15″E.

“We began calling it Daara Peak — a name inspired by the Nepali word for a projecting tooth or fang and by the mountain’s striking shape,” Strang noted. He notes that the name is provisional while they await a response from the authorities about their suggestion.

Strang describes the peak as “a saber-toothed tiger’s canine protruding from a mass of rock. The terminal pinnacle was about eight meters high, overhanging and sharply defined against the sky.”.

The climbers about to reach what they called Daara Peak. Drone photo: Brizendra Bhattarai.

According to recent reports, the problem was approaching the peak in deep, heavy snow from Yangchya Lake. They failed on their first attempt to tackle its northeast headwall. After waiting out another snowy spell, the climbers returned for a second attempt on October 17-18.

The climbers dealt with 250m of rather poor rock, a complex approach to the headwall across a bergschrund with soft snow, and the uncertainty of moving on unfamiliar terrain. They had no idea of the difficulties ahead or whether they could protect the passages ahead on their way to the summit. The route included vertical granite walls, with cracks adequate for cams, some mixed terrain with the crux at M6, a steep couloir, and then the summit ridge: a granite edge with some 30cm of snow on top.

Climbing terrain on Daara Peak. Photo: Fredrik Strang.

Sources indicate that rather than technical difficulty, the section was delicate due to exposure and a lack of comfortable belay stations. Yet, the climbers reached the summit on October 18, including the top of the final pinnacle, thanks to a crack in the rock.

Strang admits that the climbing details suggest a rather straightforward ascent: a 5,337m summit via its northeast side in five pitches with difficulties up to M6. However, Strang judges the climb on a different scale. “The technical crux was behind us, but it was the part I remember most vividly,” he explained. “It was the silence.”.

According to recent reports, strang and Kolbjornsgard’s route up Daara Peak. Photo: Fredrik Strang.

It has been revealed that on many of the 8,000m peaks I have climbed, the human presence has become part of the landscape: camps, radio calls, fixed ropes, queues, and the distant sound of aircraft. Up here, none of that reached us. Mountains extended in every direction. There was no audience, no ceremony, no one to confirm that we had accomplished anything at all.

Strang also reflects on the paradox: They enjoyed the wild terrain but, if every climber chases solitude by visiting these last remote valleys, the character of these places will inevitably change. For Strang, the question is not to ban access. However, he says:.

Perhaps some summits should remain untouched — not because we lack the skill or courage to reach them, but because future generations deserve to inherit mountains that have not all been reduced to objectives.

Recent findings suggest that the climb from the ridge. Photo: Fredrik Strang.

Day 37: The Last Slice of Pizza

📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (937 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Thetrek

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • I slept like a baby in my curtained-off bunk.
  • Feeling charged up for the day, I set out into the dawn, ready for whatever the day held.
  • Sources indicate that as I walked, I stumbled upon a few Italians I knew.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

I slept like a baby in my curtained-off bunk. At least 9 hours, too, which was way more than I had been getting.

Feeling charged up for the day, I set out into the dawn, ready for whatever the day held.

Sources indicate that as I walked, I stumbled upon a few Italians I knew. The girl was my age, and we discussed the Camino ending and what our lives would be like once we returned home. She was studying to be an actress and wanted to do so for the passion of it and to help people, not for the money or to be famous. She held many side jobs as a way to pay for her education and dream, one of them being teaching theater to children in a church. She spoke of the importance of giving young people a spiritual outlet, in whatever way felt best to them.

The conversation then turned to my job and coaching. After telling her I help people find holistic balance in their life, she curiously asked me:.

“How do you find balance in your life?”.

This started a beautiful conversation about how we each live our lives, the things we prioritize, and our outlook on happiness and peace. A girl I’d met only a few days prior suddenly felt so familiar.

But then up ahead, I saw the brothers.

I yelled to them, and they waited for me to approach. With hugs and excitement, we all decided to go to a local restaurant, A Garnacha, for traditional Galician pulpo (octopus).

According to recent reports, with three orders of pulpo in front of us, we dove into the tentacles with the toothpicks we were given as utensils. Not many words were said as we devoured our plates. The boys asked if I liked it, and the best I could say was,.

“No es mi favorita, pero me gusta.”.

Sources indicate that for the first time in the whole Camino, the three of us walked together. Of course the Italian brother walked ahead, but we were still in close proximity.

The three of us dropped our packs at a pilgrim rest area, and ended up spending over an hour there.

We sang for the pilgrims that passed.

We laughed while we rested all together.

Industry observers note that my Argentinian brother and I were shocked by the fact that our Italian brother sat for that long. Having just bought his plane ticket home, he was feeling the weight of the Camino ending and wanted to slow down over the next few days.

He compared it to the last piece of pizza, and how you want to savor every single bite.

We were all savoring each moment together like it was the last piece of pizza.

It has been revealed that the last part of the walk we did independently. I came up to a stream with a beautiful stone bridge over top. I took the moment to stop and be still, watching the ripples of the water reflect on the bridge. I pulled acorns out of the cold water and made a game of throwing them at a rock.

It has been revealed that simplicity. That’s what I love about this lifestyle, and something I will greatly miss.

When I arrived in the town of Arzúa and made it to the municipal albergue, Xunta de Galicia Arzúa Pilgrims Hostel, I showered and collapsed on my bunk.

In a recent development, my Italian brother came and got me once our Argentinian brother arrived, and we all walked to a restaurant in search of Galician barbecue. They were out of the barbecue we were looking for, so we ordered almost the entire menu instead.

Homemade croquettes, pimientos de Padrón (peppers), mixed salad, raxo, and milanesa de pollo.

Recent findings suggest that there was not a crumb left. We got cheesecake and flan to top it off while the boys talked about the intersection of futbol and politics. I completely zoned out and started to see just how tired we all were.

That became quite evident in the street as we walked to find gelato. There was so much giggling and play, especially because we were delusional with exhaustion. But at one point, I walked behind the two of them as they were carrying on and thought,.

“I love these two so damn much.”.

And with a generous cone of gelato before bed, we all crashed for our last massive day.

She fell in love with long walks in nature during her Appalachian Trail 2022 thruhike where she dove into finding herself through the space that the trail provided. Since completing her flip-flop at Springer Mountain, she has crafted her lifestyle to travel full-time and serve others within her passion of holistic health. This walk is another step into the unknown to embark on "A Saunter of Spirit" as she raises awareness for mental health through raising money for Hike For Mental Health. #68019. Latest Update: A Climbing Expedition to 'Central Asia's Patagonia'

📅 18 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 10m • 📚 Deep Dive (1970 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Explorersweb ↗ Open Full Page

Latest Update: A Climbing Expedition to 'Central Asia's Patagonia'

📅 18 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 10 min read (1970 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Explorersweb

⏱️ ~10 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • In a recent development, A mix of nine young and veteran Croatian climbers spent the month of August in one of the world’s great big-wall destinations — Kyrgyzstan’s Karavshin Range in the Pamir-Alay Mountains.
  • The two leaders, Sinisa Skalec and Lukas Grbac Lackovic, spoke to ExplorersWeb about the place and their expedition.
  • Though suffering from stomach issues for most of the month (more on this later), the team repeated several granite classics, did a upcoming route on 4,430m Pik Breeze, and attempted another new line.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, A mix of nine young and veteran Croatian climbers spent the month of August in one of the world’s great big-wall destinations — Kyrgyzstan’s Karavshin Range in the Pamir-Alay Mountains. Reaching up to 5,509m, the once-unknown granite cliffs now draw dozens of international climbers each summer. The two core valleys, Ak-Su and Kara-Su, have become known as Central Asia’s Patagonia.

The two leaders, Sinisa Skalec and Lukas Grbac Lackovic, spoke to ExplorersWeb about the place and their expedition. First, a summary of their four weeks.

Though suffering from stomach issues for most of the month (more on this later), the team repeated several granite classics, did a upcoming route on 4,430m Pik Breeze, and attempted another new line.

It has been revealed that three climbers — Bruno Crljenic, Eva Pejic, and Lackovic — identified a potential new line below Pik Breeze’s west ridge. They knew of only one previous route on the mountain, done by Russians Marina Popova and Denis Prokofiev.

Crossing a scree slope on Pik Breeze.

Beginning at 5am, the three crossed a broad scree slope, then began climbing a couloir below Pik Breeze’s west ridge. They negotiated loose rock, briefly followed an existing line, then moved left into crack systems.

Canned Horse, 6c A0, top. Below, previous attempts and possible other lines on the face.

Recent findings suggest that they climbed until 9pm, when they bivouacked on a tiny ledge with space for only two people sitting and one lying down. Resuming at 8:30am, they reached a col after three pitches and continued directly up slabs and cracks. They finished on easier IV/V terrain and followed a 200m ridge to the summit.

Recent findings suggest that they called their latest line Canned Horse, 930m, 23 pitches, 6c A0. It took them a further eight hours to get back to base camp. During the climb, they found pitons on two pitches. They believe these belonged to another route on the west ridge, but the history of that line, and whether it was finished, is uncertain.

Pejic, Grbac Lackovic, and Crljenic on top of Pik Breeze.

Later in the month, one of those climbers, Eva Pejic, became quite ill and couldn’t leave base camp on her own. Five teammates helped evacuate her, carrying her for 11km, with assistance from other climbers in the area. She later recuperated in the Kyrgyz city of Osh.

On the first crux of ‘Perestroika Crack.’.

Three small teams of Croatian climbers also repeated Perestroika Crack, one of the best-known long granite routes in Central Asia. It rises about 900m up the north face of 4,240m Pik Slesova and is graded 7a. Three members reportedly free-climbed the route. One pair, Sinisa Skalec and Ivan Vitez, completed the line in a single marathon day, beginning at 5:45am, summiting at 5:40pm, and returning to base camp at 11pm.

Skalec and Vitez also repeated the French Ridge of 4,510m Kyrkchilta, 2,000m, 6b to 6b+. They needed one bivouac. Toward the end of August, this same pair attempted a first ascent on the Central Pyramid of Ortotyubek, overlooking base camp. Their attempted route mounted slabs and cracks to the left of the established Take It Easy line, which other Croatians had repeated during that month. The pair gave up their attempt on August 26 because of illness.

Base camp with Ortotyubek and Slesova in the background.

Here is our interview with Lukas Grbac Lackovic and Sinisa Skalec about Kyrgyzstan and the Ak-Su Valley.

Lukas Grbac Lackovic repeats the Central Route on a peak called Small Russian Tower.

Was Eva Pejic’s health problem related to altitude or something else? What was the illness you experienced on Ortotyubek?

Eva’s health problem was unrelated to altitude exposure or the expedition environment. However, most of us experienced gastrointestinal infections, with symptoms including diarrhea, bloating, fever, and general malaise.

It has been revealed that this significantly hindered our climbing, as everyone in the team got sick at least once, and some even twice. Recovery was slow and never quite complete –- we felt weak for most of the trip.

Sources indicate that one thing that helped us recover was having plain rice with some of our meals, which we could get from the cook if we asked nicely. If we were to go again, we would definitely bring our own food and cooking equipment. This can be inconvenient, but it could potentially save you at least a week of being sick and unable to climb.

Another view of base camp and peaks Ortotyubek and Slesova.

According to recent reports, can you describe the Karavshin Valley? How large is it? Are there many side valleys?

The two main valleys are Ak-Su and Kara-Su. Adjacent to them is the Jaupaya Valley, which provides a descent route from Pik Breeze and is home to several peaks around 5,000m high. The rock quality there appears poor, and we are not aware of any established rock routes in the valley.

Another interesting area, west of Kara Su, is the Orto-Chashma Gorge. An Italian team made a first ascent there during our visit.

Here in the West, we first heard about the area following the kidnapping of four American climbers in Kara-Su in 2000. Since then, it seems to have calmed down and become a popular climbing destination. Is the area considered safe nowadays, or are there still things climbers should be aware of?

At the moment, the security situation in the valley is good. There is always the possibility of tensions, of course, as the valleys lie close to the border with Tajikistan. However, in recent years, the number of climbers visiting the area has increased exponentially, reaching around 100 climbers this year.

Sources indicate that how many other climbing teams were in Ak-Su and neighboring Kara-Su while you were there? Where were they generally from?

Recent findings suggest that during the three weeks we spent in the valley, up to 50 climbers were in BC at the same time. Climbers came from all over the world — Chile, U.S., Spain, Slovakia, Poland, Belgium, Slovenia, France, Italy, Germany, Japan, Russia….

Why did your group decide to go there?

We had originally planned a different expedition, but had to change our destination just a few months before departure. Some friends from Croatia and Slovenia recommended the area because of its straightforward logistics and relatively good security, while still offering impressive big walls and proper crack climbing. It didn’t take much to convince us!

Are there any military checkpoints? Do you need special permission to enter the valleys?

Yes, you have to pass through a military checkpoint when entering the area. However, the outfitter handles the application for the necessary permits and ensures everything goes smoothly.

Sources indicate that some call the Karavshin Valley the Patagonia of Central Asia because of its aesthetic granite walls. Do you think that’s a fair description?

Sources indicate that patagonia is definitely more spectacular, but you pay the price with poor weather. If your goal is to climb almost every day, then the Karavshin Valley is a better choice.

Recent findings suggest that climbing in Patagonia requires much more logistical planning and preparation, and the approaches themselves are a whole different story. In the Karavshin Valley, on the other hand, there is no snow or ice during the season we visited (August), at least on the walls we climbed. Some of the walls are just a 15-minute walk from BC, and you can reach them all in approach shoes.

Perestroika Crack and some of the classic routes in the Karavshin region are arguably just as good as the best rock routes in Patagonia.

How does the granite compare to Yosemite and Patagonia?

The granite is more similar in texture to that found in Patagonia; it is not as smooth as in Yosemite. The overall rock quality is generally good, although, as everywhere, some sections are of poorer quality. One downside of the mild climate in the Karavshin Valley is the dirt and grass that accumulate in the cracks, which can sometimes detract from the aesthetic appeal of the routes. The more popular and frequently climbed routes have already been cleaned and are pleasant to climb.

You climbed 4-1/2 pitches of the route on Ortotyubek. How much did you have left to complete it?

Sources indicate that there were still two-and-a-half pitches left to complete the route up to the junction with Take It Easy. We envisioned the second half of the fifth pitch following the line up to a point just below the overhang that runs diagonally to the left.

It has been revealed that from there, the sixth pitch follows a thin crack, from which you need to traverse left and move into another system of thin cracks that runs across the roof and joins the Take It Easy belay (seventh pitch). The last pitch of Take It Easy offers a logical exit, and we don’t think there is any need to come up with an alternative.

It has been revealed that at the point where we stopped (first half of the fifth pitch), we left two pitons that we used as a temporary rappel anchor. Repeating parties are welcome to remove them, as they were only left for temporary use. We think a few bolts may be needed in the second half of the fifth pitch, but that obviously depends on the abilities of those planning to complete the route.

According to recent reports, all belays are equipped (the first and fourth belays have two 8mm bolts each, while the second and third have two pitons each). In addition, we left two or three pitons in the first pitch and two in the second pitch.

Industry observers note that as in the rest of the valley, some sections of the route are filled with dirt and grass. We made an effort to clean the cracks in the first four pitches, but there is still plenty of work to be done, especially on the sixth pitch, which we didn’t climb, where a thin crack is completely filled with dirt.

According to recent reports, how much unclimbed rock remains? Are the obvious lines already established, or are there still many promising routes?

Recent findings suggest that the most obvious and accessible lines may have already been climbed, but there is still plenty of potential. Anyone willing to put in the effort can establish a newly introduced route. The area is vast, and there is still plenty of room for new routes.

Industry observers note that your website mentions that there are guidebooks to certain routes in that area. Where are these available?

According to recent reports, most of the guidebooks we used are available online. We received some Russian guidebooks from climbing friends, although we didn’t use them very much. We’re not sure how easily they can be found online. Climbers from all over the world bring various materials to the camp, so most route topos and information can be obtained there.

What was the most unexpected experience on your expedition — something that might surprise climbers familiar with other big-wall areas?

In a recent development, we were pleasantly surprised by the kindness and honesty of the Kyrgyz people. When traveling to remote parts of the world, many of us tend to expect that someone will try to rip us off and that we will have to haggle over everything, but that was not the case here.

Although some things took longer than expected, everything we had agreed on in advance was respected, and all the logistics for transportation and accommodation worked very well.

As we mentioned earlier, our only complaint concerns the food and hygiene conditions at the camp, which were most likely responsible for the digestive problems experienced by virtually all the climbers staying there.

#68014. Avalanche Fatality Warns About Early Ski Conditions In The Alps

📅 19 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 4m • 📚 Deep Dive (803 w)

Avalanche Fatality Warns About Early Ski Conditions In The Alps

📅 19 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (803 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Explorersweb

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Recent findings suggest that little snow on the mountains doesn’t mean safe conditions.
  • With the ski season barely underway, this is Europe’s first avalanche victim this season.
  • Most victims perished in the Alps: 40 in Italy, 35 in France, 33 in Austria, and 18 in Switzerland.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that little snow on the mountains doesn’t mean safe conditions. An American off-piste skier died in the Austrian Alps last weekend after he triggered a small slab avalanche. It was far too small to bury him, but it carried him into an open crevasse below.

With the ski season barely underway, this is Europe’s first avalanche victim this season. Last year, 151 people died in avalanches in Europe between October 2025 and June 2026, according to the European Avalanche Warning Service (EAWS), a shockingly high number.

Most victims perished in the Alps: 40 in Italy, 35 in France, 33 in Austria, and 18 in Switzerland. It was the 13th most deadly year in the Alps since record-keeping began. It was also the highest tally ever since the “Winter of Terror” of 1951. Avalanche prevention standards have improved a lot since then, but the number of leisure skiers, climbers, and hikers in the mountains has multiplied as well. (Most of those 1951 victims lived in villages along avalanche paths.).

According to recent reports, last weekend’s accident took place at the Stubai Glacier ski resort. The glacier sections of the Alps typically open for skiing weeks earlier than other mountain resorts, thanks to their higher altitudes and glacial ice, which can provide good October skiing with just a thin layer of fresh snow on top. Stubai’s ski resort opened on October 9 this year.

In a recent development, A map of Stubai Glacier ski resort with the area where the accident happened circled in red. Photo: Stubaier Gletscher website.

Recent findings suggest that the skier was on his own, descending in an out-of-bounds area below East Daunkogel Peak at around 11:30am. His tracks on the snow show he eventually abandoned the snow-covered glacier and ventured onto a steeper, rocky area. At some point, he broke a small slab of crusty snow which dragged him some 50 meters into an open bergschrund, where he fatally fell 20 meters down, according to the Lawinen Report.

The accident site, with the skier’s tracks visible,  and the movement of the snow slab — 50m long and 25m wide — marked in pink. Photo: Lawinen Report.

Industry observers note that other skiers in the area saw the accident and raised the alarm, but the skier had died by the time they extracted him from the crevasse. The police stated the slab was only 10cm to 30cm thick, and the slide was just 25 meters wide. The crevasse was 50 meters below the fracture point.

Avalanche risks are obvious on heavily loaded slopes, but the accident shows that even a thin layer of unstable snow can cause a fatal fall. In this case, the snow had fallen recently on the verglass ice over glacier-polished smooth rocks, and had no time to settle. This is a typical early-season condition in mountain ranges around the world.

It has been revealed that the accident occurred at nearly 3,000m of altitude on a shady northeast slope, where the snow hardly transforms and settles during the short days of late fall. To make things worse, the report notes that wind had picked up that morning, creating a weak crust on top of loose, cold, fresh snow, prone to breaking.

According to recent reports, the avalanche site on the following day, with most of the terrain covered by freshly drifted snow. Photo: LWD Tirol.

According to recent reports, the second factor was exposure: the skier might have easily survived the fall if the terrain had been a clean snow slope, but he was on rocky terrain, where a simple fall can result in serious injuries. Most of all, the crevasse below created what the report described as a “terrain trap.”.

Fans of backcountry and ski touring are eager to hit the slopes with the first snowflakes, and the scarcely covered terrain may provide a false sense of safety from avalanches. But objective dangers go beyond the substantial powder avalanches and also include falls on icy slopes. In addition, the glaciers are dry after the summer, and the crevasses are wide open.

After a mild fall, snow is falling heavily in the Alps this week, significantly improving conditions for the region’s ski resorts. Most of them plan to open this weekend. The snow will also offer backcountry opportunities, but conditions will remain highly unstable.

Snowfall up to two meters is expected today in the Alps. Graphic by meteoexploration.com.

The avalanche report today by the Tiroler Avalanche Service (LWD Tirol) reveals low risk in the Austrian mountains, a remarkable risk (3 out of 5) in the Swiss Alps, and moderate risk (2 out of 5) in France.

According to recent reports, the avalanche forecast for today, November 19, in the Alps demonstrates remarkable (level 3-orange) risk, especially in Switzerland. Graphic: LWD Tirol.

3 Unprepared Hikers Rescued From Continental Divide After 11-Hour Search

📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 2 min read (453 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Thetrek

⏱️ ~2 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • An 11-hour overnight search and rescue operation in Colorado’s high country brought three stranded hikers safely off the Continental Divide early on the morning of November 15 after winter weather caught the group unprepared.
  • Recent findings suggest that grand County Search and Rescue (GCSAR) received the initial call at 5:01 p.m.
  • The group pitched camp at about 11,600 feet without adequate overnight winter gear or fire-starting supplies.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

An 11-hour overnight search and rescue operation in Colorado’s high country brought three stranded hikers safely off the Continental Divide early on the morning of November 15 after winter weather caught the group unprepared.

Recent findings suggest that grand County Search and Rescue (GCSAR) received the initial call at 5:01 p.m. on Saturday, November 14, according to a social media update. The hikers had lost their way amid heavy snow and treacherous trail conditions near the High Lonesome Trail, which sits near the Continental Divide Trail mile marker 1,340.

The group pitched camp at about 11,600 feet without adequate overnight winter gear or fire-starting supplies.

An initial response crew traveled up Rollins Pass Road on ATVs before continuing on foot deeper into the backcountry. Upon locating the trio, rescuers found them cold and exhausted and immediately provided warming gear, food, and support.

Rather than waiting until sunrise, field leaders determined that keeping the hikers exposed at 11,600 feet in worsening conditions posed too great a danger. A second team was deployed to help walk the group out in the dark.

Recent findings suggest that rescuers hike into the night. Photo via GCSAR.

Sources indicate that rescuers and hikers reached the ATVs by 3:10 a.m. on Sunday, and all personnel cleared the field by 4:18 a.m.

Backcountry Conditions and Safety Reminders.

In their report, GCSAR notes that full winter conditions have already arrived at upper elevations, bringing deep snow, high winds, freezing temperatures, and rapidly shifting weather that can easily obscure trails above treeline.

Officials advise anyone venturing into the mountains to pack proper winter layers and carry the ten essentials.

It has been revealed that GCSAR is staffed entirely by unpaid volunteers. The organization never bills rescue subjects and funds its gear, training, and rescue operations through public donations.

Featured image: Grand County Search and Rescue.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • It has been revealed that today, November 19, the Yamanashi Prefectural Police declared that they had ended the search for Chinese climber Chen Jie, 25, according to the Japanese national newspaper Mainichi Shimbun.
  • His two companions reportedly turned back because of deteriorating weather and inadequate equipment.
  • His father subsequently traveled to Japan and offered a reward of RMB500,000 ($75,000) for information leading to his recovery alive, or RMB100,000 ($15,000) for recovery of his body.

It has been revealed that today, November 19, the Yamanashi Prefectural Police declared that they had ended the search for Chinese climber Chen Jie, 25, according to the Japanese national newspaper Mainichi Shimbun. Chen disappeared November 8 on the main Yoshida Trail after continuing alone up 3,776m Mount Fuji during its closed season.

His two companions reportedly turned back because of deteriorating weather and inadequate equipment. Chen continued on his own without crampons or sufficient cold-weather clothing. His last video was sent that morning between 2,300 and 2,700m.

His father subsequently traveled to Japan and offered a reward of RMB500,000 ($75,000) for information leading to his recovery alive, or RMB100,000 ($15,000) for recovery of his body.

Sources indicate that ironically, Chen belonged to China’s Blue Sky Rescue Team, a volunteer search-and-rescue organization. His mother told local media that he had participated in rescues in China and had some mountaineering experience, including trekking and climbing in Nepal and Indonesia.

#68002. Tech Report: Fast Paced River Fords After Flooding on the Arizona Trail

📅 20 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 15m • 📚 Deep Dive (2915 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Thetrek ↗ Open Full Page

Tech Report: Fast Paced River Fords After Flooding on the Arizona Trail

📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 15 min read (2915 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Thetrek

⏱️ ~15 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • According to recent reports, this morning we got a nice early start at the room in Strawberry.
  • It was nice and cold out this morning, so the hot tub felt fantastic.
  • Sources indicate that right around 9AM we were all good to go, and Woods texted me to let us know that they had just pulled up.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, this morning we got a nice early start at the room in Strawberry. I wanted to get all packed up and then go in the hot tub first thing! That sounded like a wonderful way to start off the day. Last night I managed to coordinate a ride out of town with a few other hikers. The same kind man, Al, who we had breakfast with the other morning offered to drive a group back to the trailhead. About 5-6 hikers are getting back on trail at a road about 38 miles further south than where we’re getting back on trail. Al’s wife actually drove all of those hikers back to trail. Then Al was going to pick up Woods, Strix, and Leaf before coming to pick up Slide and myself around 9AM. That gave us plenty of time to go in the hot tub, shower, and have a little breakfast before hitting the trail.

It was nice and cold out this morning, so the hot tub felt fantastic. Slide and I soaked in there and then I took a final shower before we would be dirty hikers once more. The last couple of days off have been really nice. I needed the time to get some work done, and the trail needed some time to soak up all of the rain. I figure it we will still be dealing with the impacts of the storm for a little while, but hopefully it will be nothing in comparison to what it would have been like yesterday and the day before. After my shower I had a piece of pizza leftover from last night. Then I packed up the rest of my things and got ready to hit the road. We had talked about maybe walking down the road to the empanada place for breakfast. I absolutely love empanadas! But they didn’t open until 9AM and I didn’t want to make anyone wait for us, so we decided against it.

Sources indicate that right around 9AM we were all good to go, and Woods texted me to let us know that they had just pulled up. We loaded everything into Al’s truck and talked with everyone as we got ready to go. Strix has been dealing with some foot pain and is going to get dropped off right down the street to try and hitch into the larger town of Payson. Woods and Leaf are going to continue south on the trail just like us but will go into town sometime tomorrow from the highway crossing in 38 miles. That way they can hopefully link back up with Strix, and all continue on together from there. Slide and I are going to continue another 71 miles hopefully in the next 3 days and will head into the town of Payson in the evening. That will help to break up the next section of trail a little bit better so that we don’t have to carry as much food.

A bridge that the trail crossed over in the early evening.

The ride to the trailhead took about 30 minutes but we got there eventually. It was so incredibly nice of Al to offer us a ride. And he made sure that we all had his phone number in case anyone needed some help over the next couple of days. That was really sweet of him. Then we were back on trail once more! It feels really good to be back at it after another double zero to avoid bad weather here in Arizona. We have now taken 5 zero days in the 17 days that we have been hiking the trail, which sounds absolutely crazy. It is in stark contrast to the way that Slide and I both hiked last year on our CYTC hikes. But we have the time to do it and hiking in that weather would have been really miserable. If not seriously dangerous. There are a couple different river crossings that we will have to go through tomorrow and the next day which would have hazardous or even impassable during the heavy rain. I’m curious to see how deep they will be only a couple of days after the rain has passed.

Almost immediately when we began hiking south, we encountered patches of mud and areas where the trail was almost completely flooded. For the first couple of miles, we managed to navigate around the wetter sections while still keeping our feet dry. But that didn’t last long. Eventually there were areas where the trail was under about 4-5 inches of water consistently, and there was no good way around it. I was pretty happy though that the trail was wetter than it was muddy. Areas like this will often get a thick mud that sticks to your shoes and cakes on heavily. Walking in mud like that for miles can make your ankles and feet incredibly sore just from the weight of the mud alone. Slipping and sliding in mud can also make my hips and knees hurt, depending on how bad the mud is. At least the trail today was much more wet than it was muddy.

Recent findings suggest that A happy little mushroom just off the trail. All of the plants have been loving this rain.

When we were about 5 miles into the day the trail crossed over a dirt parking lot and trailhead. There were some large boulders surrounding the parking lot, so Slide and I decided to stop off there and enjoy a quick break. We’re only planning to hike around 20 miles today, so there is no need to rush. Woods and Leaf were somewhere behind us as well and it sounded nice to let everyone catch up. I was surprised how much mud and dirt was already coating my legs after only a handful of miles of hiking. The two of us hung out there for a while and then continued along. And right as we were leaving, I could see at least one of the girls approaching off in the distance. They weren’t far behind!

Caked in mud and dirt, only 5 miles after leaving town.

From there the trail continued through a forested area and we began to descend gradually. I could hear the loud roar of water off in the distance and began to wonder if we would be crossing the river that I could hear. Only a couple of miles after the trailhead where we had taken a break, we were now approaching a very large river. The trail did exactly what it always does when it requests you to cross a river. It descended all the way down until the trail disappeared and only the river laid before us. We had no choice but to cross it. The water looked deep and quite fast moving. I was not exactly eager to plunge into the freezing cold water. Slide on the other hand got right into the water and began to cross it. It’s always nice to gauge the water level on someone else before you also have to go through the water. We crossed right at the trail crossing and I could see the water rise to Slide’s upper thighs. He’s pretty tall so I knew that they water was going to be right up to the bottom of my shorts.

A river that we had to cross this morning.

In a recent development, I only had one trekking pole out which certainly wasn’t adequate for this crossing. The water was deep and very fast moving. With only one trekking pole I was not nearly stable enough. Plus, of course I was trying to record some videos of us crossing the water. I was glad that Slide was there on the other side. Otherwise, I would have probably had to pull my other trekking pole out to secure myself in that final stretch of the river crossing. But Slide just got back into the water and extended a hand to help me across that last little bit of river. Even though we had just stopped for a break less than an hour prior, we still decided to sit down there beside the river. I had a bunch of rocks in my shoes from crossing the river, and the girls likely weren’t far behind. They had each other so I wasn’t too worried about them. But they both are significantly shorter than Slide and me, so it seemed nice to wait around for them just in case.

Slide helping Leaf across the river.

Recent findings suggest that we sat there beside the river for a while, waiting to see if the girls arrived. And just as we were thinking about packing up and continuing along, I could see one of the girls crest over the hillside on the other side of the river. So, we decided to wait just a bit longer to let them get across. The first person to appear was Leaf, and we gave her some guidance for crossing the river. It was really deep though so Slide wound up just going over to her to help. He got into the river and met her about halfway through to help bring her to the other side. Then she joined us on the shore, and we sat and talked with her for a bit. In hindsight, I’m so glad that we waited for her. Because neither Slide nor I realized that the other hiker Wood’s had actually done a road walk earlier on in the day, which meant she was no longer heading in this direction. If we had continued on, then Leaf would have been stuck going through the fast-paced river alone. Knowing that no one else was anywhere close by behind her. I’m sure she would have been alright, but I was glad that we stuck around.

The sign by the trailhead when we finally got off the dirt road and reconnected to the AZT.

According to recent reports, before we headed out to continue along, we told Leaf that we were hoping to go around 20 miles. Hopefully she will go the same distance, and we can all camp together later this evening. She came out here to meet up with this group and hike with everyone, and now she’s basically alone. She’ll be able to link back up with everyone tomorrow, but it would be nice for her to not have to be alone on trail tonight. From there I wasn’t sure what to expect along the trail. That river crossing was a complete surprise to me, so who knows what is up ahead of us now. We wound up climbing for a while to get up and out of the area where we crossed the river. Once we got up top of the climb, the trail was completely dry and the trail turned in a double wide dirt road. Leaf had pointed out to us that the trail actually crossed over a road that we could continue along for a little while. It would wind up reconnecting with the AZT but might give a reprieve from any possible mud.

The section of trail that we were hiking through just before dark was really beautiful.

It has been revealed that after a mile or two we arrived at that dirt road crossing and decided to continue along the road as well. It sounded like a nice way to get a handful of miles in without too much struggle. The road was really nice and quite dry which was delightful. We walked through a bunch of different logging operations alongside the road. Trees were piled high in preparation of them being transported somewhere. We even walked by a logging camp with a bunch of recreational vehicles. I’ve heard about guys camping out and living at these types of logging operations. There were generators running and we saw a couple of guys and a dog running around. I wonder if they will have to hold off on logging for a while after all of the rain.

The sun beginning to set as we continued along the trail.

In a recent development, the road had a lot of long hills for us to climb and descend, but eventually we began going downhill continuously for a while as we got closer to the AZT. Then we passed by another trailhead parking area and turned right to get back on the trail. The trail began descending rapidly once we reconnected to it. And we went right past a junction for some kind of mine that you can walk to right off the trail. Some hikers left comments indicating that it was a great place to hide out in bad weather. But we decided not to explore the side trail down to it today. We’ll be hiking until after dark this evening most likely and didn’t need to get sidetracked. We did stop off for another break though to put some more layers on as it was getting later. And we hoped that if we sat for a break then Leaf might catch up to us as well. Both of us really wanted her to catch up so that she wouldn’t have to camp alone tonight.

Filtering water on the AZT with my platypus QuickDraw filter.

According to recent reports, the area that we were hiking through had numerous trailheads scattered throughout it, so we actually wound up seeing some day hikers not long after that. The trail also followed along a creek for a handful of miles toward the end of the day. It was great to have endless access to water if we needed it. We wound up stopping off and filling up on water sometime around 5PM, just so that we wouldn’t we wouldn’t have to worry about it for the rest of the night. And not long after that, the trail crossed over yet another trailhead. This one had a trail register as well, so I decided to leave a note for Leaf. I told her how much further we planned to go for the night in case she was close behind us and was hoping to camp together as well. Then we continued on with only a handful more miles to go for the day.

Standing up from a final break before we continued on into the dark.

Industry observers note that someone built this rock fort right next to the trail. I wonder how long it’s been there for.

The trail began to climb gradually after we left that trailhead. Which meant that we got wonderful views of the sunset as it began to light up the sky. It’s pretty typical for us to stop off and enjoy one final break before the sun goes down. Especially if we are hiking somewhere with great views of the sunset. This was too perfect to pass up. When we did get going again, we came across some cows that were hanging out right on the trail. I always feel bad for scaring the cows. We try to talk nicely to them when we go past, but most of the time you wind up scaring the cows either way.

The sunset this evening was incredible. It’s always my favorite time of the day!

Recent findings suggest that eventually the sun went down, and we continued on in the dark for a little while longer. The area that we were hiking through did not seem like it was going to accommodate our need for a camp spot. So, when we finally did turn a corner and see a fairly flat area we decided to take advantage of it. There were some cow pies on the ground, and it wasn’t the best spot I’d ever seen, but it would work for tonight. The two of us got our tents set up and were hopeful that any minute now we would see Leaf’s headlamp coming around the corner. But that actually never happened. She must have stopped off for the night before the sun went down. Once my tent was set up, I got comfortable and had a little bit of dinner. Then did my stretching and a little editing in my tent before calling it a night.

#68000. Climbers Forge New Route on Mount Shiva Despite Limited Acclimatization

📅 20 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 3m • 📚 Deep Dive (613 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Explorersweb ↗ Open Full Page

Climbers Forge New Route on Mount Shiva Despite Limited Acclimatization

📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (613 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Explorersweb

⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Benjamin Bosshard and Philippo Sala will never forget their first experience above 6,000m and the upcoming route they opened with Stefan Siegrist on India’s Bahai Jar, commonly known as Mount Shiva (6,142m).
  • Recent findings suggest that expeditions in the Indian Himalaya are usually quiet while they take place, because satellite phones and InReach devices are prohibited.
  • Sources indicate that siegrist had already visited the Chenab River Valley area in 2018 and climbed Shiva with Jonas Schild, but he still had designs on its unclimbed northwest ridge.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Benjamin Bosshard and Philippo Sala will never forget their first experience above 6,000m and the upcoming route they opened with Stefan Siegrist on India’s Bahai Jar, commonly known as Mount Shiva (6,142m).

Recent findings suggest that expeditions in the Indian Himalaya are usually quiet while they take place, because satellite phones and InReach devices are prohibited. After returning home, however, Stefan Siegrist reported the details, and the team’s cameraman, Christoph Detschmann, posted a video summary of the expedition:.

Sources indicate that siegrist had already visited the Chenab River Valley area in 2018 and climbed Shiva with Jonas Schild, but he still had designs on its unclimbed northwest ridge. At the end of September, he, Sala, and Bosshard reached base camp in the Kishtwar massif.

In a recent development, the three Swiss climbers were prepared to endure a long period of bad weather while acclimatizing. To their surprise, a good weather window opened right away. It was too good to let go, despite not being properly acclimatized and Sala and Bosshard’s lack of altitude experience. The window was expected to last just three days. After many “discussions and doubts,” they left base camp on October 3.

Industry observers note that sala had a headache during the first night, but the following morning, they were all totally focused on the climb, and the tension disappeared. “We assumed that we were unlikely to reach the summit on this attempt, and that we would therefore be wasting our only chance before a major storm [brought] the season to an end,” Siegrist explained. “So from then on, the idea was simply to climb higher and acclimatize, without any pressure.”.

A moment of the climb, filmed from a drone by Christoph Detschmann.

Along the way, they discovered they had left their stove at base camp. No problem in 2026: The expedition photographer used his drone to carry the stove up to them. The use of drones was a hot topic during the recent Piolets d’Or: To what extent are they compatible with alpine-style criteria? While most accepted that drones could scout routes or sections out of view of base camp, many considered using them to carry equipment up a face to be a red line.

On Shiva, Siegrist states the delivery of the missing stove “proved essential to the success of the climb.”.

The climbers spent their second night at 5,250m at the base of the northwest ridge. On the following morning, they had to decide whether to continue or retreat. They all felt well, but starting the highly technical ridge was a point of no return. At the same time, Siegrist recalls, they realized they really had a chance to summit. And so on they went.

It has been revealed that that night, they stopped at 5,700m in what Siegrist describes as a crucial moment. His partners had not been at that altitude before, and the latest forecast declared a storm the following day. They decided to wait and see what the morning looked like. No one slept at all that night.

The last meters before the summit. Drone image by Christoph Detschmann.

The sky was still clear when the team set off again at 4am, so they chose to keep going. “After a while, we finally reached the final slope, just 300m below the summit,” Siegrist wrote. By now, they knew they were going to make it. They reached the top at 7:44am, six days after arriving in Base Camp, and just in time to hurry down as the storm approached.

The climbers descended via the 1985 Japanese route (see topo below), and reached their base camp tents as it started to snow.

#67997. Two Inexperienced Teens Rescued After 20 Hours on Grossglockner

📅 20 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 2m • 📖 Standard (481 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Explorersweb ↗ Open Full Page

Two Inexperienced Teens Rescued After 20 Hours on Grossglockner

📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 2 min read (481 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Explorersweb

⏱️ ~2 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Two Germans, aged 15 and 18, spent almost 20 hours on Austria’s highest mountain before being evacuated by helicopter on November 15.
  • In a recent development, initially, police reported that the pair had reached the 3,798m summit and become lost while descending.
  • Recent findings suggest that their ordeal began around 11pm on Saturday, November 14.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Two Germans, aged 15 and 18, spent almost 20 hours on Austria’s highest mountain before being evacuated by helicopter on November 15.

In a recent development, initially, police reported that the pair had reached the 3,798m summit and become lost while descending. The younger climber disputes this, saying they turned back near an alpine hut at 3,454m because his companion felt ill.

Recent findings suggest that their ordeal began around 11pm on Saturday, November 14. The pair had no previous experience with such a serious mountain but had prepared by reading websites, watching videos, training physically, and asking others for tips. They did carry crampons, an ice axe, a helmet, a rope, a belay device, and extra clothing.

According to recent reports, it took them a long time before they decided to turn around. The descent went well at first, but one spot seemed too dangerous to them. To get around it, they followed someone else’s tracks in the snow, but these suddenly disappeared. While looking for a way, they got stuck in deep snow. The older boy called for help at around 6:30pm on November 15, according to Austria’s public broadcaster, ORF.at.

According to recent reports, at first, rescuers tried to guide the pair down by phone. More than two hours later, the boys were still stuck, so a helicopter was dispatched. The rescuers found the pair, exhausted, disoriented, and hypothermic, at around 2,800m.

In a recent development, A rescue helicopter brings the teens to safety. Photo: Mountain Rescue KALS.

Yesterday, rescue leader Peter Tembler criticized their lack of alpine experience and preparation. He told the German Press Agency that the pair lacked sufficient experience for the terrain and winter conditions. He also criticized their late-night departure.

According to recent reports, according to Tembler, a section that normally takes four to five hours took them almost 12. Other climbers reportedly advised them against continuing.

Tembler believes an increasing number of inexperienced people are attempting serious alpine routes, sometimes encouraged by social media accounts that downplay the difficulty. The disagreement has become a public debate about risk-taking, responsibility, and rescue operations.

Industry observers note that as Austria’s highest peak, Grossglockner is a magnet for climbers of all stripes and has more than its share of controversy. In January 2025, a man abandoned his less experienced girlfriend high on the mountain. She froze to death, and an Austrian court later convicted him of manslaughter for leaving her behind. This summer, an altercation occurred on Grossglockner in which a guide insulted a passing climber and nearly pushed him off a cliff. At the same time, veteran alpinists are still setting bold upcoming routes here.

According to recent reports, according to Der Standard, Grossglockner gets 8,000 to 9,000 ascents each year, with an average of two dozen rescues annually. Between 2005 and 2025, 29 climbers have died on the mountain.
