#67983. How Joe “Stringbean” McConaughy (Finally) Broke the John Muir Trail FKT

📅 02 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 11m • 📚 Deep Dive (2189 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Trailrunnermag ↗ Open Full Page

How Joe “Stringbean” McConaughy (Finally) Broke the John Muir Trail FKT

📅 02 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 11 min read (2189 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Trailrunnermag

⏱️ ~11 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • It has been revealed that joe McConaughy thought he would probably start a bit slower than François D’Haene when he went after the Frenchman’s record on the John Muir Trail (JMT) this September.
  • But when McConaughy got to Kearsarge Pass around mile 40, he was an hour off of D’Haene, who ran the Fastest Known Time (FKT) on the 223-mile trail through California’s Sierra Nevada in 2017, just months after winning UTMB for the third time.
  • In a recent development, “That was definitely a bit of a crack in the armor,” McConaughy told Trail Runner.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

(Photo: Andy Golich/Joe McConaughy).

It has been revealed that joe McConaughy thought he would probably start a bit slower than François D’Haene when he went after the Frenchman’s record on the John Muir Trail (JMT) this September. He guessed he’d be maybe 20 or 30 minutes behind in the early miles.

But when McConaughy got to Kearsarge Pass around mile 40, he was an hour off of D’Haene, who ran the Fastest Known Time (FKT) on the 223-mile trail through California’s Sierra Nevada in 2017, just months after winning UTMB for the third time.

In a recent development, “That was definitely a bit of a crack in the armor,” McConaughy told Trail Runner. “But I told myself that maybe he went out at more of a race effort, while my pace was better for a multi-day FKT.”.

McConaughy, known by his thru-hiking trail name, “Stringbean,” has more than a few multiday FKTs to his name. He’s set records on the Pacific Crest Trail, Appalachian Trail, Long Trail, and Arizona Trail. And he had two prior record attempts on the JMT, one of which earned him an unsupported FKT.

“I thought my experience could help me beat him,” McConaughy said.

Sources indicate that as he chased the ghost of the JMT’s past, McConaughy drew from his many multi-day FKTs and races. All of the miles and mistakes, successes and failures, and lessons and growth along the way helped him ultimately establish a fresh FKT of 2 days, 16 hours, and 15 seconds, taking nearly three and a half hours off a time that had stood for nearly a decade.

In rock climbing, climbers talk about “flashing” a route. It’s when they successfully climb the whole thing on their first attempt—without any practice or “beta” to help. McConaughy’s JMT effort was pretty much the opposite of flashing. The 35-year-old Seattle-based endurance coach was incredibly familiar with every mile of the JMT. Prior to his record setting attempt this fall, he’d covered the trail four times—the first in 2014—including the two prior FKT attempts. He’d also spent five summers guiding backpacking trips in the Sierra.

So when McConaughy ended up in a blizzard on Muir Pass with snowflakes landing in his eyeballs, it didn’t really stress him out or slow him down. If anything, it helped him move faster as he wanted to get up and over to warmer ground.

Sources indicate that “I’ve seen the worst that the Sierra can throw at you,” he noted, citing thunderstorms, blizzards, and rugged terrain. “I didn’t have to do a bunch of mental gymnastics, worrying about things I hadn’t experienced before. Instead, I could devote all of my energy to things that actually were issues.”.

Most of McConaughy’s complications during the record attempt were ones he expected to occur, was prepared for, and could handle. “The long climbs were long climbs and some of the descents take decades,” he remarked. But after numerous JMT attempts he knew “it could feel much harder.” A little over a day into his attempt he was two hours ahead of D’Haene’s splits.

The JMT is far from the only goal for which McConaughy’s persistence has paid off. He took seven swings at earning a Golden Ticket into the Western States 100 before clinching one at the Black Canyon 100K on his eighth try in 2025. He’s also raced the Cocodona 250 three times and has a trio of Barkley Marathons starts.

It has been revealed that “I like to think I’m more fun than a project-er, but when I look back, that’s pretty much my entire running career,” he stated. “I feel like it gives me purpose. I want to do routes that inspire me and motivate me and take what I’ve done wrong, or what I feel like I could improve on, and continue to experiment, tinker, and optimize.”.

He’s not as intense as a rock climber going after a seemingly impossible objective like the Dawn Wall, he swears. Rather, it’s about finding the sweet spot where he’s pushing himself to grow but having fun doing it. He’s not training to be the best at any given race or record attempt; he’s training to be the best version of himself for years to come.

“I get a lot of joy from sticking with the process, training with a smile, putting in the work to make a difference, and looking for opportunities to rise like a phoenix and perform the best that I can,”  McConaughy said.

Caroline Himbert, who is coached by McConaughy and set her own unsupported FKT on the JMT this July, helped pace McConaughy on the JMT this fall. “He goes back to things he’s failed at and tries to continuously learn and grow; he loves the science and spreadsheets and takes things seriously,” Himbert said. “But at the same time, he doesn’t take things too seriously and he keeps things fluid and fun.”.

In a recent development, as evidenced by the fact that it stood for nine years, the JMT record was stout. D’Haene is known for bringing a newfound level of professionalism to FKT attempts, with a full support staff, set of pacers, and film crew. But rather than seeing the competitive level of the record as a deterrent, McConaughy saw it as part of the draw.

“It’s the granddaddy of FKTs,” he remarked. “More people have attempted the JMT FKT than pretty much any other premier route that exists—and the fact that François [D’Haene] and Darcy [Piceu] were the [previous] record holders is an ode to the level of attention and competitiveness that it’s gotten.”.

Sources indicate that on his first attempt in 2022, McConaughy set an unsupported record of three days and one hour. But Jeff Garmire beat it by 13 minutes just 25 days later.

McConaughy knew he could do better, so he tried to reclaim the record in 2024. But he hallucinated in the final miles and wound up off-trail on a class-four scramble, much closer to life-and-limb-threatening risk than he’d anticipated. It was a wake-up call for McConaughy, who always considers what he’s asking of others when he chases a big goal. He’s now the father of a 6-month-old and knew he couldn’t end up in a similar situation—or worse—if he went back.

Sources indicate that “That experience made me really rethink what the record meant to me and ask myself if I wanted to do it again,” he mentioned, adding that it felt reckless to go for another unsupported record. But after much reflection, and many conversations with his wife Katie, he decided he had to go back.

“I knew I couldn’t exist as an athlete without trying to put my stamp on the JMT,” he noted. “This was my third time [attempting the FKT] on this trail and I wanted to give it my all, and use my best tips and tricks from every other effort to get the record.”.

According to recent reports, mcConaughy highlighted up with a 12-tab spreadsheet and 12 years of beta to guide his effort this fall. He thought some of the greatest opportunities for improvement lay in fueling, pacing, and recruiting an all-star crew to help him out. In his unsupported-style attempts, he’d had to carry all of his own food and gear with no supply restocks along the way.

Sources indicate that at Cocodona in 2025, McConaughy hit a wall that no amount of carbs could fix. He thought he knew how he needed to fuel to compete for the win. He’d done sweat testing and was experimenting with high-carb fueling. But he ended up with GI distress and struggled to breathe. He still finished in a respectable fourth place, but it was far from the finish he wanted.

Industry observers note that he started working with nutritionist Meredith Terranova, who suggested he was likely hypernatremic—too high of blood sodium concentration—during Cocodona. He wondered if trying to optimize his performance through a data-driven approach with high carb fueling and sweat tests meant he’d stopped listening to his body.

Sources indicate that so on the JMT he turned to real food like trail mix, purees, and waffles, especially on the significant climbs—of which there is no shortage with 38,000 feet of elevation gain to cover. He also used recovery drink mixes and fat- and protein-based fuels from his nutrition sponsor, Näak.

“I feel like sticking to more whole food was the biggest learning and the biggest difference maker in my performance,” he stated.

He also made up ground through a smarter sleep strategy. In his 2022 attempt, in which he finished six hours behind D’Haene’s record time, McConaughy slept for six hours. He knew there was an opportunity to trim down time spent resting while still sleeping enough to avoid dangerous hallucinations.

Industry observers note that he settled on taking a mere 40 minutes of sleep beneath a pine tree on Bear Ridge—around 28 hours in. He thought it might be prudent to get at least an hour but he decided to push it a little with 40 minutes, figuring he could always nap later if he needed it. When he got to his third night out on the trail he was still running strong, cracking jokes, and appreciating his surroundings, Himbert mentioned.

In a recent development, “You could tell he was having a good time and he was a ball of energy,” she stated. “I was with him more towards the end, and he was still moving so well. I think that’s the key with this trail; it’s so challenging but if you can still move well towards the end then you can crack these times. I think Joe really nailed it, and it went close to perfect.”.

McConaughy’s crew was one of his greatest assets. He learned some things about crewing the JMT after his crew missed him at Kearsarge Pass during his Pacific Crest Trail FKT in 2014. The PCT overlaps with the JMT for about 170 miles. He had to keep going on the PCT for two days with no sleeping bag, only a half-day’s worth of calories, and nothing warmer than a thin windbreaker. “We didn’t really know what we were doing,” he mentioned. Hence the 12-tab spreadsheet this go-around, which was largely for the benefit of his crew and the complicated logistics of supporting a record-attempt on the JMT.

According to recent reports, part of the beauty of the JMT is that it offers an uninterrupted tour of backcountry wilderness. The trail only crosses the road twice over the course of the entire 223 miles. That’s also what makes it a bear to support. Meeting McConaughy on the trail required hiking several miles and thousands of feet of climbing to deliver food and gear. Pacers ran monster sections—usually around 40 miles at a time. But his crew of pacers was up for the challenge, with a collective résumé that boasted JMT FKTs, podium finishes, and 200-mile runs.

Sources indicate that “Tara Dower talked about being a vessel on the Appalachian Trail, and I certainly had a similar experience on the JMT,” McConaughy stated. “I was able to appreciate the beauty of where I was and the excitement of doing this absurd endurance thing because my crew was always filling my cup instead of making me pour things out to keep going.”.

One thing that McConaughy has learned time and time again, is that he runs best when his cup is full.

“Gratitude and joy are the greatest performance-enhancing drugs,” he said.

While he was running, he thought about Katie, who was home solo-parenting so he could acclimatize to the altitude and run for 64 straight hours. He thought about his parents, who enabled him to get outside and run cross-country from a young age. He thought about the people who have supported his running career, and the friends who traveled to the Sierra to help him through the 223-mile journey. And he thought about the Sierra themselves, the mountains that have kept him coming back time and time again for the last 12 years.

It has been revealed that “I run my worst when I’m thinking about how far behind someone’s splits I am,” he stated. “When I caught myself doing that on the JMT, I thought, ‘This is doing more harm than good. You need to move forward at your own pace, and focus on the things that really matter.’”.

After shaving over three hours off such a long-standing record, McConaughy hopes that he’s reached an end with his JMT FKT attempts. With all of the time and effort he has dedicated to the JMT, it feels a bit like a fairytale ending: “The princess was saved,” he mentioned.

Now, he’s ready for a new goal, one he’s ready to chase to fuel his performance and fill his cup.

In a recent development, “It’s one of those moments where I realize I’m maybe more capable than I thought I was,” he stated. “And that makes it exciting to go back to Cocodona, or Western States, or another FKT, or any number of things to see what I can do.”.

Industry News: The World’s Most Cinematic Trail Running Is Hidden Above the Arctic Circle

💡 Key Takeaways

  • According to recent reports, trail Runner’s travel columnist Andy Cochrane has run all over the world, including five trips to the Lofoten Islands above the Arctic Circle in Norway.
  • As a travel writer, I fly an embarrassing amount.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that if you buy through our links, we may earn an affiliate commission. This supports our mission to get more people active and outside.Learn about Outside Online's affiliate link policy.

According to recent reports, trail Runner’s travel columnist Andy Cochrane has run all over the world, including five trips to the Lofoten Islands above the Arctic Circle in Norway. He shares his hard-earned recommendations on where to run, stay, and eat, what to pack for the unpredictable weather—and how to get there.

As a travel writer, I fly an embarrassing amount. Over three quarters of a million miles in the last decade, or roughly three laps around the Earth each year. That’s a lot of time in a pressurized tube sitting next to strangers, but perhaps a fair price to pay for the privilege of running trails all over the world, from Patagonia to Morocco to Greenland. Picking a favorite destination is difficult, but often actions speak louder than words. I’ve returned to one more than any other: the Lofoten Islands in Norway.

Hidden a hundred miles above the Arctic Circle, Lofoten is best known for its Viking heritage, red fishing  villages, and dramatic coastline—sandy beaches, turquoise waters, and walls of rock that rise 3,000 feet out of the Norwegian Sea. There are very few places in the world where mountains collide with the ocean in such a cinematic way, giving it the best of both worlds—and incredibly unpredictable weather.

Industry observers note that on my first trip to the Lofoten Islands in 2017, a snow storm shut down trails in the alpine, so I explored the lowlands, dabbled in fishing and kayaking, and enjoyed a nightly sauna. Since then I’ve returned four times to explore different corners of the islands and am planning to go back again next year, because there is still so much to explore, especially if you love empty trails and technical running. Here’s why I think Lofoten could be the next great trail destination and how you can visit before it gets too crowded.

It has been revealed that the Lofoten Islands are an archipelago in northern Norway that stretch from the mainland into the North Atlantic. At 68 degrees 54 minutes north latitude, they sit further north than most communities in Greenland and all but a dozen or so towns at the top of Alaska. The chain consists of five main islands and hundreds of smaller ones, connected by bridges and underwater tunnels. (Oh, the joys of Norwegian infrastructure!).

Sources indicate that combined, the islands cover a total of 474 square miles, roughly the size of the city of Los Angeles. However, they are home to just 25,000 full-time residents, most of whom live in Svolvær and Leknes. Suffice to say, the interior is remote and rugged; it’s common to find yourself on a trail without a single human in sight, despite the lack of trees and views in all directions.

According to recent reports, although there are offshore oil reserves nearby, drilling is prohibited in Lofoten (unlike much of Norway), which has allowed cod fishing and tourism to flourish. The landscape is a mix of granite spines and tussocked tundra, with a few birch and mountain ash stands sprinkled in. When storms roll in—which they do often—there is very little protection, which can be a humbling experience.

The trail network in Lofoten is a patchwork of everything from unmaintained user trails to heavily engineered routes like Reinebringen’s 1,978 stone steps. As a whole they skew towards the technical end of the spectrum; most are steep, rocky, and stout. It’s common to gain a thousand feet per mile or more.

Recent findings suggest that the vast majority of trails start near sea level and ascend through bogs and brush, climbing into the alpine via scree fields and off-camber granite slabs. Expect your shoes to get muddy and shirt to be saturated in sweat as you climb to the summit. Some marshes have wooden planks and some ridgelines have cairns, but they aren’t guaranteed. It’s best to always bring a good map and a better attitude.

According to recent reports, while there isn’t an official count of trails on the islands, a good estimate is around 150, including everything from short beach hikes to high ridge lines. For ambitious trail runners, the Lofoten Crossing is an unofficial 100-mile thru-route from Delp to Å, and uses a mix of local paths, beaches, and roads. It’s a great way to see the entire chain of islands, even if it skips some of the serene trails. A few of my other favorites are the steep climb up to Himmeltindan (2,700 feet in 2.1 miles), crossing the interior of Vestvågøya from Leknes to the eastern end, and almost any of the remote trails at the end of the archipelago near Å, many of which reside inside Lofotodeen National Park.

Industry observers note that lofoten sees over a million tourists each year, heavily focused on the summer months. The crowds get so bad in July and August that iconic trails like Ryten, Fløya, and Mannen are probably not worth visiting. In the spring and fall Lofoten becomes a lot more enjoyable, because it offers more solitude on the trails, open spots at restaurants, and generally friendlier locals. I have a slight preference for the fall, mostly because I reserve most of the spring for skiing, which also is pretty great in Lofoten.

It’s also worth considering the weather and daylight. For about a month from early December to early January, the sun doesn’t rise above the horizon. Days lengthen dramatically in the spring, from 6 hours in February to over 18 by the end of April. The Midnight sun rises in late May and sets in mid-July, offering 24 hours of daylight for a month and a half straight. Almost too much!

Weather is fickle all year but especially in the spring and fall, as temps float in the 40s and 50s Fahrenheit. Snow usually melts in May and the mountains undergo a rapid transition to green. In the fall the foliage turns to a golden and red mix, storms begin to batter the coast, and the Northern Lights illuminate the night sky as early as September. Thankfully saunas are common and help make cold weather running more enjoyable.

Getting to Lofoten takes more time than most destinations in Europe. The drive from Oslo is around 20 hours and the combination of train and ferry takes even longer. The fastest way to get to the islands is a flight to Bodø and then a puddle hop prop plane to Svolvær or Leknes. This saves time and helps avoid weather-dependent ferries, but is often more expensive.

I prefer to fly from Oslo to Narvik, which sits on the mainland adjacent to the islands, and rent a car. The drive takes between 2-4 hours, depending on where I’m staying, but is always worth it for the views. Plus, public transit is limited in Lofoten, so having a car allows me to get to quieter places. For example, the cinnamon rolls at Unstad are to die for—but the only way to get there is to drive (or go on a 80-mile round-trip bike ride).

Traditional fishing lodges, called rorbuer, are built on poles over the water. Many have been converted to cozy places to stay. My favorite is Hattvika Lodge in the town of Ballstad. The restaurant next door, Fangst, is one of the best in the area. For those wanting to stay further off the beaten path, Nusfjord would be a great option. For a wider selection of restaurants, consider a stay in Svolvær or Leknes. Regardless, it’s key to book early, because the best places fill up months in advance.

If someone told me the Offtrail Ultra was designed specifically for Lofoten, I wouldn’t blink an eye. The 5 mm lugs are perfect in mud and scree, the toe grip is great on granite slaps, the integrated gaiter keeps out debris, and the midsole is stable enough for the dynamic movements necessary in this terrain. Hard to imagine a better fit, honestly.

According to recent reports, designed for cold and wet weather, the Run Cold wool socks are designed with high-impact wear zones to help them last longer, but don’t feel overbuilt at all. Instead they are stretchy and comfortable, with a seamless toe to reduce chafing. They work well with tights and running pants, which I use in spring and fall running in cold climates like Lofoten.

Recent findings suggest that over the last few years I’ve trended towards running belts, but I make an exception for a place like Lofoten, where you want to bring a few extra things. The Triack has a snug fit with almost no bounce thanks to a bungee system that’s easy to adjust on the fly. Plus, with four easy-access pockets, I can carry spare layers, gloves, snacks, water, camera, and first aid easily.

The name is a bit of a misnomer, because it’s actually made of merino wool. The wool helps regulate temperature better than other materials, keeping you warmer at the start and cooler when you heat up, not to mention not smelling after days of use. I love the hood and neck gaiter for colder days, and how the hoodie works great under a raincoat, too.

Latest Update: The Best Trail Running Shoes for Fall 2026

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that the best trail running shoes boost our confidence on singletrack to scree fields, sand to slick rock. They’re comfortable and nimble and help us run fast or forever, depending on the adventure. As the days grow shorter and colder we’re also looking for shoes that excel under a wide variety of circumstances, like wet leaves, rime ice, and snow. And as the weather deteriorates, we’re also leaning more on road-to-trail models for the days when the roads and paths are calling our names.

In a recent development, over two to four months of testing on varied terrain across Santa Barbara to Boulder and Nebraska to Fresh Hampshire, our testers Lisa Jhung, Cory Smith, Johnathan Beverly, and Abby Levene provided detailed feedback on fit, comfort, speed, traction, cushioning, and their joy of running. The result is Trail Runner Magazine’s best trail shoes for fall 2026. Considering that the “best” shoe can run differently on someone else’s feet, our review is specially curated with a shoe claiming the title of each chosen category it achieves best. For even more models, check out Outside’s guide to best trail running shoes for fall.

Weight: 7.5 ounces (men’s 8.5), 6.2 ounces (women’s 8) Stack Height: 28.5–21.5 mm Drop: 7 mm Sizing: 7-12.5, 13, 14, 15 (men’s), 6-11 (women’s).

Pros and Cons + Responsive and springy + Weightless feeling underfoot + Good ground feel + Excellent traction – Runs small (go half a size up) –Expensive.

Sources indicate that if the Norda 005 was a car, it would be the Mercedes AMG E63S Wagon. That is to say: it’s quiet performance luxury. IYKYK, as the kids say. Coming in at just 214 grams (7.5 ounces) for a men’s U.S. 8.5, it’s one of the lightest trail running shoes on the market. It’s also made from the highest quality materials: A Biodyneema upper makes it both durable and highly breathable. A slick of Vibram “Megagrip Elite” rubber renders the outsole ultra tacky on the trails while rolling over the roads. And, perhaps most importantly, the midsole is made completely from a proprietary Mouse Arnitel TPEE—a supercritical foam generally only used in small amounts because of the cost—making the shoe featherlight, energetic, and highly durable.

In a recent development, and the simplicity of the design lets the quality shine. As such, it’s a light, fast trail running shoe that can do it all. We’d turn to this shoe for anything from easy days on mixed surfaces, to “fast” trail 100-milers like Western States or Ultra-Trail du Mont-Blanc. Trail Runner managing editor Abby Levene wore one pair of the Norda 005 for the Tour du Mont Blanc, a five-day, 110-mile adventure through the Alps, and she didn’t think about her feet once. There is no higher praise.

In a recent development, the midsole is tuned to be slightly firmer than the superfoam in road racers and thus provides an energetic, bouncy ride that doesn’t trampoline you in wild directions off the trail. While the lack of a plate may disqualify the Norda 005 from being a true trail “super shoe,” don’t mistake semantics for inferiority. We didn’t miss a carbon plate here, and its absence allows for enhanced ground feel and adaptability to varied terrain. The foam and rocker deliver a smooth roll and plenty of precision.

Sources indicate that the only real downside to this shoe is the price tag. But sometimes, you get what you pay for. Read our full review of the Norda 005.

Weight: 9.5 oz (men’s), 8.4 oz (women’s) Stack Height: 32–28 mm Drop: 4 mm Sizing: 7-13, 14, 15 (men’s), 5-12 (women’s).

Pros and Cons + Excellent traction + Lightweight and nimble – Slippery laces require double-knotting.

According to recent reports, we’ve tested every version of the Saucony Peregrine since the model’s debut in 2011, and this sixteenth iteration just might be our all-time favorite. The shoe has long been capable of making us feel nimble on rugged terrain, with its great balance of ground feel and cushioning, plus traction on all kinds of trail, wrapped up in a lightweight package. But version 16 takes the Peregrine’s trail capabilities to new levels, and at $150, it’s an easy pick for Best Value.

In a recent development, the upgraded Vibram Megagrip outsole grips rock slabs with aplomb, while the four-millimeter lugs dig into loose dirt and soft ground (though some sandy-trail testers craved even deeper, toothier lugs). The balanced midsole—not too springy, not too mushy, not too thick—delivers a strong connection to the trail while still feeling responsive and shock absorbing, even during wild descents. The flexible, breathable mesh upper with added toe protection kept out trail debris and warded off snags from roots and branches.

The fit of this trail running shoe somehow made a variety of testers feel like it was custom-made for them. It locks down the heel, and the just-roomy-enough toebox allowed toe space to breathe while maintaining control. “The fit is just perfect,” said a tester. “I feel secure and supported from heel to toe, and side to side.”.

Weight: 10 oz (men’s), 9 oz (women’s) Stack Height: 33.5 mm–25.5 mm Drop: 8mm Sizing: 7-13, 14 (men’s), 5-11 (women’s).

Pros and Cons + Great traction + Outstanding foothold – Cushioning may feel too firm for some.

It has been revealed that the Salomon Genesis 2 earned mountain-goat status among our crew, providing outstanding traction over loose dirt and rock. Its supportive Matryx upper—constructed with thin, high-tenacity yarns and durable Kevlar—secures narrow and wide feet alike via Salomon’s quick-pull lacing system. The forefoot offers slightly more room than version 1, enhancing overall comfort without sacrificing agility.

The outsole, made of Salomon’s Contagrip rubber with toothy, 4 mm lugs, provided excellent traction on all surfaces, giving us confidence, even on scrambles over large rocky slabs and slippery descents.

While the EVA-blend midsole runs firm, it offers direct trail feedback. “This shoe makes it fun to pick a line and charge,” noted one tester. “I felt completely present instead of mindlessly rolling over obstacles.”.

According to recent reports, for technical runners who prefer softer cushioning, we also recommend the La Sportiva Prodigio Pro. (Read our full review of the La Sportiva Prodigio Pro here.).

Weight: 11.7 oz (men’s), 9.5 oz (women’s) Stack Height: 39–31 mm Drop: 8 mm Sizing: 6-15 (men’s), 5-12 (women’s).

Pros and Cons + Extremely versatile + Comfortable for all-day wear – Traction could be better.

The Nike Trail Pegasus 5 has been our top choice for road-to-trail runs for several seasons, so we were concerned that its newly branded replacement, the Nike ACG Pegasus Trail, would mess with its winning formula. But as soon as we stepped into the upcoming model, we breathed a sigh of relief. The shoe is just as comfortable as its predecessor and, after testing, has proven to be just as capable on and off roads and over gravel, continuing its reign as the most versatile shoe in this roundup.

Industry observers note that the midsole foam—Nike’s injection-molded ReactX—feels responsive and cushions comfortably on concrete, pavement, and hard-packed dirt. The outsole traction, from 3.5 mm lugs made of the brand’s proprietary “All Terrain Compound 2.0,” is tackier on wet terrain than the previous version, but still pales in comparison to Vibram MegaGrip.

What makes this shoe work from roads to singletrack trails is the fit and foothold. Even our most narrow-footed testers felt a secure hold without any pressure points, which allows precise footing on trails, no matter how steep or rocky. This shoe’s versatility makes it a great pick as a one-trick pony for the casual runner who doesn’t need a lighter, faster race shoe, and a solid choice for travel.

Weight: 9.5 oz (unisex) Stack Height: 40–34 mm Drop: 6 mm Sizing: 5-12,13 (men’s), 6.5-13.5, 14.5 (women’s).

Pros and Cons + Extremely lightweight for a 40 mm stack + Great stability – Premium pricetag.

Industry observers note that brooks has a reputation for building a great shoe and sticking to that formula, giving loyal fans a consistent ride, model after model. The tradeoff? It can make the brand seem boring. The all-new Brooks Cascadia Elite shatters that mold. It’s one of the most exciting shoes Brooks has introduced in years, and arguably one of the most exciting trail releases of the year.

Despite sharing a name, the Cascadia Elite is nothing like the everyday, cushioned Cascadia trail runner: It’s a trail racing super shoe that is lighter, faster, and more nimble. The standout feature is the 100% PEBA midsole paired with a carbon-infused PEBAX plate that strikes a perfect balance between a springy and stable ride. On smooth, flowy single track in Santa Barbara, CA, running in the Cascadia Elite felt almost effortless, and a ton of fun.

Recent findings suggest that 40 millimeters under the heel is a lot of foam to deal with, but the ride never felt squishy or overly bouncy in off-camber footing. A wide platform, paired with a flexible, embedded horseshoe-shaped plate, keeps the Cascadia Elite from being tippy. That width does come at a cost, though; picking tight lines through technical terrain requires precise footing to keep from getting wedged between rocks.

It has been revealed that if you’re in the market for a trail running shoe, first consider the type of trails you run on regularly: do you tackle rugged, mountainous terrain, or stick to mellow dirt paths? Some trail shoes can handle both adequately, while others are specialized and excel in one or the other. Shoes with smaller lugs are generally better on smoother, firmer terrain, whereas shoes with deeper, more aggressive outsoles are optimized for steep, muddy, or rocky trails. If you like to feel the trail and dance around rocks and roots, you’ll likely prefer a light, more minimal shoe, but if you’d rather let the shoe roll over trail variations, cushioning and protecting while you zone out, you should look for a shoe with a thicker midsole.

Once you’ve narrowed the search to a certain type of trail shoe, you need to find a pair that complements your unique body and stride. Every runner’s body, gait, speed, experience, and ride preferences are different, so every runner will interact differently with each trail shoe. The shoe that your best friend or your sister-in-law loves may be uncomfortable for you and make running feel slow, sluggish, or even painful. Finding the perfect pair of trail running shoes is a seriously personal affair.

In a recent development, the process for choosing the best running shoes is a matter of finding the models that both fit your foot and also feel best when you’re running. To determine fit and feel, there’s no substitute for trying the shoes on and running in them.

When assessing fit, first pay attention to length. You need room at the end of your toes as your feet lengthen during their dynamic movements on the run. A rule of thumb is to allow a thumb’s width between your longest toe and the end of the shoe. Runners often wear a running shoe a half or full size bigger than their street shoes.

According to recent reports, ensure that the shape of the sole and the upper matches your foot shape. The sole should be as wide or wider than your foot for the whole length, and match the curve of your arch comfortably. The shoe should hold your foot securely over the instep, while allowing the ball of the foot and the toes to splay and flex when you roll forward onto them. Your heel shouldn’t slip when you lift it, and the arch should be able to dome and lengthen naturally. Nothing should bind or rub as you roll through the stride.

If the shoe fits, it’s time to take them on a short run on a treadmill, around the store, or, ideally, down the block and back. Every trail running shoe has a unique ride created by the type and density of foam in the midsole and the geometry of that foam: its thickness, width, heel-to-toe drop, molded sidewalls or flares, and forefoot flexibility or rocker shape (plus, in an increasing number of models, the presence of and type of embedded plate). Each of these elements interact with each other and your stride to determine how the shoe reacts on landing, how much it cushions, how stably it supports, how smoothly it transitions from landing to toe off, and how swiftly and powerfully it rebounds.

In a recent development, the best way to choose trail running shoes that complement your body and stride is to find the ones that feel right on the run. Benno Nigg, the world-leading biomechanics professor who proposed this method of shoe selection, calls it the “comfort filter,” but makes clear it is far more than how plush the shoe feels when you step into it. What you want to assess is whether the shoe allows and supports the way your feet want to move, what Nigg calls your “preferred movement path.” In the right shoe, while running at your normal pace, you will touch down where you expect to land, roll smoothly and stably through the stride without noticing the shoe, feel both cushioned from and connected to the ground, and push off naturally, rapidly, and powerfully. When this comes together you’ll know that you’ve found your pair.

It’s likely that several shoes will feel good on your feet. To find the most comfortable, it helps to compare them back to back, like an eye doctor will do with corrective lenses: flipping between “A” or “B,” “1” or “2.” You may also find that different shoes feel better at different paces or level of fatigue, and you may want more than one pair. In fact, research reveals that wearing a variety of different shoes is one of the few proven ways to reduce injury risk as it appears to vary the stresses on your feet and joints.

Industry observers note that running shoes have long been marketed and sold as prescriptive devices to help runners stay healthy, but there is little scientific evidence correlating shoes, or any specific shoe properties—like cushioning or pronation control—with running injuries. Medical professionals say that it is highly difficult to determine whether a runner needs a certain type of shoe, and studies have shown that prescribing shoes using traditional methods like treadmill gait analyses or wet-foot arch height tests don’t consistently reduce injuries.

Don’t assume that you need more cushioning or more stability if you have sore joints, or if you’re a heavier runner, or if you’re a beginner—evidence doesn’t support many common beliefs. The best way prevent injury is find two or three different pairs that feel right on the run, ease into using them, and vary your shoes, your running surface and your pace regularly (plus avoid rapid increases in your training load and work on improving your mechanics).

Each season, we evaluate new releases from top outdoor brands, distributing samples to testers based on foot shape and local trail conditions and preferences. For this fall revision, we evaluated 5 new models alongside 91 previously tested shoes to select the best trail running shoes on the market.

It has been revealed that over two to four months of testing on varied terrain across the country (from Santa Barbara to Boulder, Nebraska to New Hampshire), our team provided detailed feedback on fit, comfort, traction, cushioning, and responsiveness. We combined these reports with our own trail testing to select category winners and top recommendations for every type of runner.

Recent findings suggest that freelance journalist, editor, and author Lisa Jhung has researched, tested, and written about running shoes for the past decade and a half, much of that time for Outside. She coordinates a fleet of female shoe testers out of Boulder, Colorado, and claims her home office is a perpetual obstacle course of cardboard boxes and piles of running shoes. Lisa’s written about gear of all kinds for numerous national magazines as both an editor and freelancer, including a stint as the shoes and gear blogger and trail running microsite editor for Runner’s World.

Recent findings suggest that A high school jumper and occasional sprinter/hurdler, she started running—really running—after walking off the collegiate volleyball team, and moved on to road and trail races of any distance, triathlons, adventure races, and mountain running. She’s happiest testing rugged trail shoes on gnarly terrain, and also loves a good neighborhood jaunt…but is almost always looking for ribbons of dirt. Lisa is the author of Running That Doesn’t Suck: How to Love Running (Even if You Think You Hate It) and Trailhead: The Dirt on All Things Trail Running.

Recent findings suggest that cory’s passion for running started over 30 years ago in high school when he became the number six ranked runner in the nation at 3000 meters his senior year. After high school, he competed at Villanova University, earning two NCAA Division I Championship showings. Today, he’s determined not to let age slow him down and competes on the national master’s circuit, running a 4:12 (4:30 mile pace) 1500 meters and 9:04 (4:52 mile pace) 3000 meters in 2021 at age 43. He prefers a hard track workout or tempo run over an easy long run any day but also appreciates a challenging trail or mountain run.

Industry observers note that his obsession with running shoes started in 2014 when he wrote his first shoe review for Gear Institute. Since then, he’s tested and reviewed hundreds of running shoes, clothing, and gear for Outside, Runner’s World, Footwear News, and other outlets. He has a soft spot for speedy shoes over heavy trainers but loves dissecting all shoes equally and thinking like a product engineer to explain the why behind every design detail. Cory is the Founder of Run Your Personal Best, an online running coaching business, and since its inception in 2014, has coached runners to over 100 Boston Marathon Qualifying times.

One of Cory Smith’s go-to routes for testing trail running shoes:.

Jonathan fell in love with running his freshman year of high school and swiftly became fascinated with finding the perfect pair of running shoes. That quest got a boost when he became editor of Running Times in 2000 and started receiving every upcoming model as they were released. The parade of shoes continued while he served as shoe editor for Runner’s World, then editor of PodiumRunner, and currently fitness gear editor at Outside. Having now worn nearly every running shoe created in this century—and a fair amount of those dating back to the early models of the ’70s—he’s given up on finding the one best and now relishes the wide variety of excellent options.

Sources indicate that once a 2:46 marathoner regularly doing 50+ mile weeks, recent injuries and his age have reduced his volume and slowed his pace—but he still enjoys an uptempo workout or two each week. Beverly is the author of the book Your Best Stride which explores how each individual’s gait—and thus shoe preference—is unique. He enjoys getting scientists’ take on latest shoe trends and trying to describe the nuances of each shoe’s ride.

The Rules of Trail Running Etiquette, from the ATRA President

📅 06 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (1013 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Trailrunnermag

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish

💡 Key Takeaways
  • It has been revealed that as the president of the American Trail Running Association (ATRA)—a title that sounds more impressive than it is—and co-author of The Ultimate Guide to Trail Running,” which is now in its third edition, I know a little about the proper behavior of trail runners.
  • To me, the “rules” of trail running are quite simple and boil down to two principles: respect nature, and respect other owners.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that as the president of the American Trail Running Association (ATRA)—a title that sounds more impressive than it is—and co-author of The Ultimate Guide to Trail Running,” which is now in its third edition, I know a little about the proper behavior of trail runners. And as a six-decade trail veteran myself, I also know a little about the improper behavior of trail runners.

To me, the “rules” of trail running are quite simple and boil down to two principles: respect nature, and respect other owners.

According to recent reports, those two tenets blossom into about 10 “strong suggestions” for sustainable, copasetic trail experiences, but, like with the Golden Rule, it all comes down to showing respect. Here are the basics of what you should know when you hit the trails:.

Close any gates you open, don’t disturb the wildlife or livestock, and respect private land and get permission to enter.

Take only photos and pack out at least as much as you brought in, including gel wrappers. If needed, wear shorts, a jacket, or hydration pack with zip pockets to stow rubbish found on the trail.

In a recent development, don’t disturb wildlife as frightened animals may be dangerous. Steer clear of trails that disturb sensitive habitats during nesting or mating seasons. When passing horses, use special care and follow directions from the horseback riders. Consider turning around and going another direction when faced with large herds of animals.

In a recent development, don’t play your music loudly, engage in boisterous conversations with your fellow runners (or through speakerphone), or listen to headphones so loudly that you are unaware of your surroundings. Along the same lines, do your social media influencing elsewhere. Nature is not your recording studio. We don’t want to hear you, and you ought to be able to hear others.

Recent findings suggest that we expect the same of cyclists. This should be obvious but, then again, all of this should be.

In a recent development, as trail runners, we move relatively quickly, especially when we seemingly emerge from nowhere on unsuspecting trail consumers. This may be alarming, so anticipate and give a courteous and audible announcement of your presence and intention to pass hikers on the trail by stating something along the lines of, “On your left,” or “Trail,” as you approach. Keep an eye out for those wearing headphones, as they won’t hear your warning. Be courteous when passing, slowing down or stopping if necessary to prevent accidental contact. Be ready to yield to all other trail users (cyclists, hikers, horses) even if you have the posted right of way.

This is likely to be controversial, but consider not bringing your dog on group runs and, when you do run with your dogs, be sure to leash them and keep them under your control when necessary to prevent any wildlife disturbances. Be sure to pack out their (and your) waste.

Be cognizant that off-leash dogs often chase wildlife and degrade the outdoor experience of other trail consumers.

Greet and say “Excuse me” to those you see and pass on the trail. This should be a common practice if for no other reason than to alert others to your presence and not frighten anyone. Similarly, be sure to stay in control of your speed, especially when you could cause rocks or other trail features to fall.

If you startle someone, apologize, and thank them if they’ve stepped aside. A little kindness goes a long way on the trail.

Don’t cut the switchbacks or widen trails by running around puddles,downed trees, or when it is too muddy.

Sources indicate that don’t create your own trails by running off preexisting, well-marked trails. When multiple trails exist, run on the most worn. Stay off closed trails and obey all postings.

Industry observers note that run single file in the middle of a trail, even if it’s laden with a fresh blanket of snow or thick mud. Go over, not around, obstacles like puddles,rocks, or downed tree limbs, as that widens trails, damages vegetation, and causes unnecessary erosion.

In other words, participate in trail maintenance and give back to the trail community.

In a now-infamous Outside opinion piece of seven years ago that went viral, Marc Peruzzi claimed that trail runners are lazy parasites. Ultrarunner and lawyer Stephanie Case wrote a response piece, saying more could be done, agreeing with my stance that “we are guilty as charged … we need [to do] more. A lot more.” Case continued, “Indeed, as trail running continues to increase in popularity, it will become even more crucial that we expand our volunteer and conservation efforts.”.

Industry observers note that so, carry your weight and do trail work. Volunteer. Go plogging on your local trails.

It has been revealed that technically, those ascending are supposed to have the right of way but, in practice, people often yield to descenders, likely due to speed and momentum. Be polite, maintain control, and be prepared to yield to other users, including horseback riders.

Split larger groups into smaller groups as bigger numbers can intimidate other people and have a greater environmental impact on trails.

If you come across someone in distress, stop and check whether they need help.

According to recent reports, don’t become a liability by taking risks, getting lost, or ignoring trail closures that require dangerous rescues. Carry proper clothing, nutrition, and hydration so as not to put yourself at risk of exposure. Safety first is always a good rule.

If running alone, familiarize yourself with the area where you proposal to run and let at least one other person know your intended route. Be prepared for the weather and conditions when you start your run and plan for the worst, given the likely duration of your run. Know and respect your limits and report unsafe conditions and activities to the proper authorities.

Trail running is beautifully simple. So is being a courteous trail runner. Follow these tips for proper etiquette and keep the trails safe, welcoming, and wild!

Abodde Ski Essentials Waffle Pouch.

Vuarnet Legend 02 Original Sunglasses.

Are you overwhelmed by the sheer number of items in stores that simply slap the words “ski” or “après” on them in the hopes that the word alone makes it a good gift for skiers?

We hear you. Gifting items that skiers will actually love and use can be intimidating. Especially when it comes to a holiday gift where seemingly everything from cocktail napkins to candles is ski-themed (and no shade to either; we do love a perfectly scented pine candle).

It has been revealed that whether you’re shopping for the skiers on your list or just browsing for yourself, scroll away; our editors have chosen every item on this list wisely, and we have some pretty good taste. If you’re looking for gifts for hardcore skiers check out our recommended gifts for those who eat, breathe, and talk skiing.

Quickly gaining on pickleball as the newest pastime obsession, mahjong is all the rage right now. If you happen to have a mahjong-loving skier on your holiday gift list, you’re in luck. This alpine-themed “Let It Snow” tile set from Mahj & Co is absolutely adorable. It comes with 160 tiles adorned with different wintry scenes, including evergreen trees, a crackling fire, a snow groomer, snowflakes, and, of course, skis and skiers, with a canvas storage bag included for easy cleanup and stowing away. Surely your favorite maj-er needs a set for the ski condo this winter. —Samantha Berman, SKI Executive Editor.

For anyone who spends winter chasing snow, Gray Malin’s newest photography collection, SNOW, is a stunning reminder of what makes skiing special. Known for his aerial photography, Malin shoots mountains, ski resorts and snowy landscapes from a perspective few of us ever see. The images range from the anticipation of a storm day to a mountain town blanketed in fresh snow—perfect for the artsy skier who loves to linger over a good book. —SB.

A great ski sweater should do more than look good by the fire. Made from 100 percent Responsible Wool Standard–certified merino, the Rockcraft Wool Crew is warm yet breathable, moisture-wicking and odor-resistant on long days on the slopes. Its chunky five-gauge Shaker knit traps heat without sacrificing comfort, and raglan sleeves allow easy movement. With timeless style and the durability to be handed down for generations, it’s the perfect sentimental gift for your favorite skier. Also comes in men’s. —SB.

We love UGGs, just not for clomping around a snowy ski town after dark. Until now. The new men’s Classic Mini Outpost is a sturdier, more weatherproof option for hitting the bars or grabbing dinner after a day on the mountain. Waterproof suede and seam-sealed construction keep feet dry, a plush lining made with upcycled wool adds warmth, and a White Spider rubber outsole grips slick sidewalks. It’s a practical, stylish pick for post-ski hours. —SB.

Sources indicate that few things say effortless alpine style quite like a great pair of Vuarnets. The French eyewear brand has been part of ski culture for decades, and the Legend 02 sunglasses have the history to prove it. Jean Vuarnet wore the original frames when he won Olympic downhill gold in 1960, and more than 65 years later, they’re still in vogue. Made in France, these classic frames feature Vuarnet’s signature mineral-glass lenses, known for their optical clarity and contrast. Choose the Skilynx lens for a version designed specifically for mountain environments. They’re equally at home on a sunny ski-resort patio, wandering through a European mountain village, or skinning up for a few spring turns. For the skier who appreciates good design as much as good snow, these are a timeless gift. —Sierra Shafer, Editorial Director, Lifestyle.

According to recent reports, A cold beer after skiing is one of life’s simple pleasures. Cold fingers holding that beer? Less so. KAVU’s delightfully superfluous solution is a fleece mitten with a built-in pocket for your drink. Yes, it’s essentially a koozie for your hand and your beverage, and frankly, I wish I’d thought of it first. Is it necessary? Absolutely not, which is why it makes a great gift for your favorite parking-lot après regular. —SS.

Sources indicate that celebrating a ski day by dipping bread into melted cheese is an elite, unbeatable experience, but you don’t have to travel to the Alps to indulge. Le Creuset’s Alpine Signature Fondue Set brings the ritual right to your kitchen table. The enameled cast-iron pot retains heat beautifully, while six color-coded forks help everyone keep track of their bread. It’s a splurge, but it’s also the kind of gift that will become a tradition for years to come. As for the best recipe? My friend JF, an expert skier and even more accomplished fondue enthusiast, has entire books on the subject. His advice, which I’ll pass along as my holiday gift to you: Rub the inside of the pot with a cut garlic clove before adding the ingredients, use a combination of Gruyère and Emmentaler, and finish with a pinch of nutmeg. Whatever the recipe, double it. —SS.

In a recent development, I own several Rumpl blankets and use them year-round. Think of them as your favorite insulated jacket, only massive enough to share. At parking-lot après, nothing beats throwing one over your lap in a camp chair. They’re just as useful wrapped around your shoulders while you cheer on your U12 racer bashing through slalom gates in subzero temps. A built-in clip keeps the blanket in place, leaving your hands free for whatever libations or cowbells the occasion calls for. I keep one in my car all winter, partly for emergencies but mostly because there’s always a reason to pull it out. With recycled synthetic insulation and a water-resistant shell, it’s warm, packable and endlessly useful. And yes, I’m suggesting you gift yourself one. Ho, ho, ho. —SS.

Hygge meets performance in this cozy fleece that doubles as an ultra-plush midlayer. We love the longer, relaxed cut that covers your backside, and the high, fuzzy collar is pure comfort when the snow starts swirling. The recycled pebbled pile is warm, quick-drying and moisture-wicking under a shell, though it’s so plush it’s almost overkill for skiing. Where it really shines is après and around town, thanks to fun prints in three colorways and men’s and women’s cuts. —Jenny Wiegand, Associate Gear Director.

Long winter nights call for warm pajamas. Hanna Andersson’s flannel PJ pants are so cozy you’ll want to wear them under your snow pants. They come in several ski-chic patterns that look good on the whole family, and they’re perfect for skiers who want something soft to climb into before dreaming of powder all night. —Giorgia Menetre, Senior Social Media Strategist.

Recent findings suggest that nothing beats taking off your ski boots and slipping into cozy slippers. If you’re like me, you want a pair that lasts, has a solid sole and isn’t the same old tan suede. L.L.Bean’s Daybreak slippers check every box. The wool clog-style upper keeps toes warm, the slip-on design makes them easy to pull on and off, and the durable rubber sole offers just enough traction. They’re perfect for the skier who wants to be cozy and stylish after a day on the slopes. —GM.

Review: Oboz Katabatic Storm GTX Winter Hiking Boots

📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (820 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Sectionhiker

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish

💡 Key Takeaways
  • It has been revealed that the Oboz Katabatic Storm GTX is a fresh waterproof and insulated hiking boot from Oboz, known for its popular 400g Bridger 10″ and 200g Bridger 8″ insulated mid winter hiking boots.
  • According to recent reports, if you’re a hiker, but you don’t hike in winter, you’re missing out on a lot of fun.
  • Several companies, including La Sportiva, Hoka, and Salomon, have attempted to introduce lightweight mids and trail runners for winter use with mixed success, because there are so many different types of winter hiking outings, from trail running and snowshoeing to light mountaineering, all targeting different user types, temperature ranges, complementary gear types, and trail conditions.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that the Oboz Katabatic Storm GTX is a fresh waterproof and insulated hiking boot from Oboz, known for its popular 400g Bridger 10″ and 200g Bridger 8″ insulated mid winter hiking boots. Modeled after cross-country ski boots, the Katabatic Storm GTX is a lightly insulated mid-height boot insulated with aerogel-based Solarcore bonded to a Gore-Tex liner, providing waterproofing and warmth without added bulk. The result is an active winter boot with about 80% of the warmth of Oboz 200g insulated Bridger boots, that’s robust enough for use with lite traction aids like Kahtoola Microspikes or Hillsound Trail Crampons.

According to recent reports, if you’re a hiker, but you don’t hike in winter, you’re missing out on a lot of fun. Gone are the bugs, roots, and rocks that can make three-season hiking unpleasant. The trails are less crowded, and there are lots of new skills to learn and gear to play with. In the past 15 years, winter footwear has gotten lighter and lighter due to advances in insulation technology, material science, and manufacturing practices. The introduction of lightweight traction aids, like microspikes, was a real inflection point because they could be used with footwear that has lightweight, flexible soles, requiring no special training like rigid mountaineering boots and crampons.

Several companies, including La Sportiva, Hoka, and Salomon, have attempted to introduce lightweight mids and trail runners for winter use with mixed success, because there are so many different types of winter hiking outings, from trail running and snowshoeing to light mountaineering, all targeting different user types, temperature ranges, complementary gear types, and trail conditions.

With that in mind, the Oboz Katabatic Storm GTX is a winter hiking boot, not a trail-running shoe, because its sole is too rigid. It is lightly insulated, with about 80% of the insulation of a 200g Thinsulate boot, and is good for temperatures down to about 15 degrees as long as you are moving and not standing still. It has enough front toe-kick rigidity to work with traction aids like Kahtoola Microspikes or Hillsound Trail Crampons without causing friction on top of the toes, which can lead to blisters or cold toes because of reduced circulation. The boots have a gaiter hook, making the boots compatible with gaiters. The outsole has lugs that provide good traction on snow and frozen slush when you’re not wearing a traction aid.

Fitwise, the Katabatic Storm is true to size. That stated, they’re patterned on cross-country ski boots, with a quick-lace system and a zippered top cover, which makes them a little time-consuming to put on and hard to adjust if you use an articulated lacing technique that requires different pressure at different points along the lacing track. I’m not a huge fan of either, but they fit me well enough, hold my foot securely, and don’t cause any hot spots inside.

In a recent development, I was a little leery of the Katabatic Storm GTX when I learned they only have a warmth value of about 80% of a 200g insulated winter hiking boot. The insulation they do have is only located in targeted areas such as underfoot, over the toe, and through the tongue, but not along the sides and around the heel. The shoe is designed for movement and managing the heat it generates, but not for standing around.

Why would that be an matter? As a winter hiker, I generally recommend buying insulated boots that will keep your feet warm when you’re not moving and are standing still. This is especially true if you hike in the backcountry where you may have to wait a long time, say 8 hours or more, for search and rescue to come and help your injured hiking partner while you wait with them, or if you have to slowly walk an injured hiker out into the wee hours of the morning. That’s not the time to wear a lightly insulated boot designed only for movement. That might sound overly conservative, but I have participated in backcountry winter rescues that ran into the early hours of the following day, and we were all very glad we were wearing heavily insulated boots.

According to recent reports, the insulated Oboz Katabatic Storm GTX boot is lightweight and comfortable, even on challenging hikes that require traction. I just wish they were available with more insulation that’s equivalent to the 400g Oboz 10″ Bridger insulated winter hiking boots I wear today. If they were, I’d wear them on every winter hike. As such, they’re ideal for shoulder season weather and spring conditions where there’s ice and slush on trails, but temperatures are warmer during the day. Because they are only lightly insulated, I reserve them for winter hikes on warmer days and close to accessible trailheads where local SAR crews can muster and arrive relatively quickly in an emergency.

Disclaimer: Oboz donated boots for review.

#67930. How to Shoot a Shotgun (and Hit Every Bird) Like Your Granddaddy Did

How to Shoot a Shotgun (and Hit Every Bird) Like Your Granddaddy Did

📅 14 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 11 min read (2171 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Outdoorlife

⏱️ ~11 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • We may earn revenue from the products available on this page and participate in affiliate programs.
  • In a recent development, don Zutz, 43, has hunted and fished all his life and has won or scored high in many skeet and trap tournaments.
  • He was a lifelong duck hunter and had never had any trouble hitting his share of waterfowl.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

We may earn revenue from the products available on this page and participate in affiliate programs. Learn More ›.

In a recent development, don Zutz, 43, has hunted and fished all his life and has won or scored high in many skeet and trap tournaments. He was the 1964 Wisconsin skeet co-champion in 12 gauge with 100 straight and shot 150 straight in the shootoff. This story was originally published in the November 1976 glitch of Outdoor Life.

Harry couldn’t understand it. He was a lifelong duck hunter and had never had any trouble hitting his share of waterfowl. His season birds-to-shells-fired average was quite impressive. That very morning, in fact, I had watched him drop a lone honker and a pair of passing mallards with only four shots. And on previous occasions when he forsook his beloved blinds for pheasant hunting, he had more than held his own.

But Harry’s bubble burst when I suggested that we switch to open-bored guns and visit a few grouse covers after our early-morning duck hunt. It was a new world for him. Three roaring flushes from grouse netted him only half a dozen empty shells to reload. Then he missed a spiraling woodcock. Harry was beside himself with frustration and embarrassment.

“How can I be deadly at dawn and then turn into a flub by midday?” he growled.

Recent findings suggest that at first I didn’t pay attention. Anyone can have a bad day on grouse. When he continued to growl about his troubles over a hot cup of coffee, however, the reason for his bad showing became obvious.

According to recent reports, “I guess those fantails are just too fast and tricky for me,” he mused. “When ducks and geese come over, I’ve got plenty of time to measure off my lead, but I simply can’t get ahead of these crazy grouse and swing with them—especially when they’re twisting through the brush!”.

In a recent development, anyone who is conversant with the various wing-gunning methods immediately realizes that Harry had been using the wrong technique in the thickets. Instead of building his lead with a fast swing, he had used the deliberate, precise method of leading that he had perfected during all those years of dedicated duck hunting. And because it had also worked well on pheasants in the open, Harry had never questioned his method. For him, a carefully held sustained lead was the way to go. It was his one and only wingshooting technique.

Sources indicate that but deliberate shotgun pointing doesn’t work on fast-breaking game in thick cover. The hunter simply cannot measure off a precise lead and maintain it on a grouse that is threading its way through branches. Harry found out that a versatile wingshot selectively employs different methods of leading flying targets, depending on what he is shooting.

There are four basic techniques for slapping a lead on speeding birds, clay or feathered: 1) the sustained lead, otherwise known as the maintained lead; 2) the swing-through method, alias the fast swing; 3) the pull-ahead system; and 4) the snap shot (see sketches).

Sources indicate that the one Harry had been perfecting in duck blinds, lo those many seasons, was the sustained lead. This is the method called “maintained lead” by the late, great D. Lee Braun, an outstanding Remington skeet and trap pro, in his popular book “Skeet Shooting with D. Lee Braun.”.

The shooter visualizes the amount of lead he will need for a given target flying at a given speed and then brings his gun up ahead of the target by that approximate distance. Swinging at about the target’s speed, he then adjusts for the exact lead and continues swinging on the bird’s apparent line of flight until he is satisfied that the alignment and forward allowance are perfectly correct. The trigger is pulled while the gun maintains the established lead and swing speed. If the shooter judges his lead correctly, and if he maintains his lead and swing speed by following through properly, he should center his birds.

Recent findings suggest that the sustained lead, like all the others, is subject to human error. The shooter who gets lazy during his swing will slow down unwittingly and shoot behind. Ditto for the gunner who tries being too precise, because any tendency to aim a scattergun like a rifle results in tightening up, which also slows the swing. The most common failing, however, is stopping the swing at trigger time, thus cancelling out the forward allowance.

Many hunters miss with the sustained-lead method because they don’t measure off enough lead. In other words, they overestimate shot-string speed. Even at skeet’s meager 20-yard range, the low-house target at Station 3 and the high-house clay at Station 5 (right-angle-birds) require a full four-foot lead if you use this method. Passing ducks doing 70 feet per second at 40 yards require an 8½-foot lead, even with a high-velocity load of 4’s doing 1,330 feet per second at the muzzle. Stretch that range to 60 yards, and the lead increases to 14 feet! In other words, you might visualize a rowboat between the duck and your shotgun’s muzzle while also keeping the swing crisp and smooth at the duck’s speed!

A sustained lead is best employed in the open on targets flying a steady course. It is natural when hunting doves, ducks, and geese, firing at crossing skeet clays, and for certain pheasant-hunting situations.

According to recent reports, but the sustained lead can’t be used effectively in the brush on fast-flushing birds. There isn’t enough time, and the game seldom flies a steady course. I pointed this out to Harry.

“Guess I’ll have to start snap shooting, if I want some grouse,” he said.

I didn’t like that idea either, and tried to dissuade him. Snap shooting is the least-scientific and least-consistent shotgun technique. It consists of nothing more than picking a spot ahead of the moving target, pointing the muzzle at that spot, and firing. There is no swing; there is no attempt to coordinate with the target’s speed; there is no follow-through. The gun is merely snapped, or poked, and it is virtually stationary, when the shot charge is triggered. If the shooter “guesstimates” right, he scores. Otherwise it’s a miss. And misses always outnumber the hits.

Sources indicate that this is not to say that snap shooting doesn’t play a role in modern wingshooting. When a hunter is caught completely off guard and can’t recover in time to make a coordinated swing, his only chance lies in a snap shot.

Recent findings suggest that in my opinion, about the only time snap shooting is really best is when you are trying for cottontails in the brambles. Those bounding, zigzagging, change-of-pace artists seldom allow you to take a smooth swing, and a hunter must resort to the “poke-and-hope” method. (For very different opinions on snap shooting, see Robert W. Woodruff on quail in “Five Topflight Gunners Tell How” in the October 1976 matter of this magazine, and Peter Miller on woodcock on page 72 of this issue.).

Industry observers note that many skeet and trap shooters use a variation of snap shooting that they call spot shooting. This specialized technique has arisen because most clay-target shooters already have their guns mounted and pointed at a specific spot when the claybird appears. They do not have to bring their guns to their shoulders from a low, field-carry position. In trap, the first bird of doubles is often spot shot, because the shooters know exactly where it will be. Many skeetmen “spot” the high-house bird at Station 1 and the low-house disc at Station 7. But since a hunter doesn’t walk around with a mounted gun, and since he doesn’t know when or where the birds will appear or how they will fly, spot shooting has little application afield.

Industry observers note that “I’d sooner see you try the swing-through method,” I told Harry. “It’s more dependable and consistent, and once you get the timing right, it can be lightning quick. In fact, some people call it the fast swing instead of the swing-through.”.

“Well, right now I’ll try anything,” Harry muttered, spinning the cap back onto his thermos.

Recent findings suggest that I explained that the shooter starts his gun behind the target. He then swings aggressively, catches up with the bird, and strokes right through it with a muzzle speed faster than the target’s flight. The mental command to fire is given just as the muzzle passes the moving mark, and the gun continues its accelerating swing along the target’s line of flight.

Theoretically, the correct lead is built up by the rapidly swinging gun while the shooter’s muscles respond to the mental command to fire and while the trigger yields, the firing pin falls, the primer ignites, the powder burns, and the shot charge clears the barrel. The faster the swing, the longer the lead will be. The muzzle moves ahead of the target during the shooter’s physical responses and the gun’s lock and combustion time.

Industry observers note that the swing-through system can be applied to more different hunting, skeet, and trap situations than any other method. I’ve even come to favor it over sustained lead for distant birds, because the accelerating, “heave-ho” swing needed to generate leads of eight to 15 feet after coming from behind develops a gun momentum which, in turn, insures a good, positive follow-through.

It has been revealed that unfortunately, however, some people can’t handle the true swing-through method. They don’t feel comfortable starting behind the bird. They are doubtful about swinging with gusto, and lack the timing needed to coordinate trigger pull with swinging muzzle.

It has been revealed that harry was one of them. After years of starting his gun ahead of ducks and geese and taking a deliberate, measured lead, he didn’t like swinging from behind and firing with no visually apparent lead.

But there was still hope. The following weekend I had him try a variation called the pull-ahead method. With this technique the hunter starts by bringing his gun up right on the bird. Then he builds up gun momentum by pulling ahead for a very short distance. Once he has gun alignment and momentum, the shooter moves the muzzle ahead of the bird. When the right amount of daylight appears between muzzle and bird, the trigger is pulled while the swing continues to accelerate. The amount of visual lead is supplemented by the time that elapses during the shooter’s body responses, the function of the gun, and the shot bore travel.

Recent findings suggest that the pull-ahead method does require good timing. There is only one point during the accelerating swing when the muzzle is in correct juxtaposition to the target. In general, though, the average person masters the pull-ahead faster than he does the swifter movement required by the true swing-through.

Sources indicate that although the pull-ahead method hasn’t received much publicity, I’m certain many shotgunners use it unwittingly while thinking that they are employing the true swing-through. Thousands of skeet and trap shooters align directly on their clays first and then generate leads merely by swinging crisply ahead. The business portion of their swings never starts behind the targets, and yet many of them think they are swinging through. There’s nothing wrong with that, of course, but I believe a shooter should try to understand exactly what he is doing, not what he thinks he’s doing!

Industry observers note that in the field, pull-ahead shooting works nicely with incoming birds and close-range shots at upland birds. It also works well with rabbits when the cover is fairly open. This method is faster than sustained lead, less complex than the swing-through, and more dependable than snap shooting.

Read Next: How to Miss Fewer Birds.

According to recent reports, harry picked it up easily. He felt comfortable coming up with the muzzle on the bird rather than behind it, and he liked seeing daylight between barrel and bird. But he knew better than to look for a precise, measured lead. He still uses the sustained lead for ducks because there is more time and open sky. In the brush, he found, it is simply a matter of getting on target, swinging ahead briskly, and letting go with a positive follow-through.

This doesn’t mean pulling ahead can be used for all kinds of shooting. I seriously doubt that its abbreviated swing, starting on the bird, can develop enough gun momentum to generate the really long leads needed for distant crossing shots at waterfowl.

To be a versatile wingshot, the scattergunner must have more than a single swing/lead system in his repertoire. He should learn the strengths and weaknesses of all four basic techniques, practice them with claybirds until the movements are automatic, and then apply the appropriate method as field conditions and individual shots dictate. There is no other way to become a successful all-around performer with the bird gun.

#67929. Latest Update: The 10 Best Walleye Fishing Tips for Early Ice

📅 14 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 7m • 📚 Deep Dive (1369 w)
