Public-Land Sales, Energy Dominance, and Data Centers: What Interior’s Master Proposal Really Means for Outdoorsmen

📅 18 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1434 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Outdoorlife

⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Less than two months after a dinner at the White House with leaders of hunting and angling groups in which President Trump and Secretary of the Interior Doug Burgum confirmed support for conservation priorities, Burgum has formalized the Trump administration’s plans to shrink the federal estate and to site industrial data centers and energy infrastructure on America’s public lands.
  • As we reported last week, the intentions are outlined in the Department of the Interior’s five-year strategic initiative that extends through 2030.
  • The 28-page plan is short on details but long on statements about the department’s role in domestic energy “dominance,” “unleashing the potential” of America’s public lands, and pursuit of “public-private partnerships.” In addition to his role at the helm of the Department of Interior, Burgum also chairs the White House National Energy Dominance Council.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Less than two months after a dinner at the White House with leaders of hunting and angling groups in which President Trump and Secretary of the Interior Doug Burgum confirmed support for conservation priorities, Burgum has formalized the Trump administration’s plans to shrink the federal estate and to site industrial data centers and energy infrastructure on America’s public lands.

As we reported last week, the intentions are outlined in the Department of the Interior’s five-year strategic initiative that extends through 2030. The document serves as a blueprint for implementing the priorities of the Bureau of Land Management, U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service, Bureau of Reclamation, National Park Service, and Bureau of Indian Affairs, among other Interior agencies.

The 28-page plan is short on details but long on statements about the department’s role in domestic energy “dominance,” “unleashing the potential” of America’s public lands, and pursuit of “public-private partnerships.” In addition to his role at the helm of the Department of Interior, Burgum also chairs the White House National Energy Dominance Council.

The few detailed directives contained in the five-year proposal note Interior’s intention to “decrease the size of the federal estate by offering to states, localities, and Tribes the opportunity to purchase federal lands” in order to better focus the department’s resources on “nationally significant federal lands.” The strategic plan further emphasizes Interior’s pursuit of “strategic rights-of-way agreements, land exchanges, and direct transfer of lands in support of reliable energy production and transport.”.

And the strategy specifically calls for redirecting revenue from the Land and Water Conservation Fund, which is funded by offshore oil and gas leasing revenue, to private-land easements rather than outright purchase of land by the government for recreation and resource purposes. The fund provides about $900 million annually to acquire land, improve existing properties, and invest in communities’ cultural and outdoor recreation assets.

Sources indicate that the Department of Interior’s strategy’s mention of possible land sales provoked quick push-back from lawmakers from both parties who recall the tsunami of opposition to inclusion of federal land sales as part of the 2025 Significant Beautiful Bill. Language that would have funded tax breaks by selling large parcels of public land was eventually withdrawn from that bill, which was later signed into law by Trump.

According to recent reports, both of Montana’s Republican senators, including retiring Sen. Steve Daines, who sits on the powerful Senate Energy and Natural Resources Committee, told the news agency Politico that they were not consulted on Interior’s strategic plan and would oppose the idea of land sales. Yesterday, Burgum, responding to growing criticism of the land-sale language, told Fox News that national parks would not be sold. He called public-land supporters’ reaction to the strategic plan “manufactured hysteria.”.

But the renewed conversation around the topic, along with the proposal’s focus on energy development and investment in “Super Intelligence” infrastructure, raises the question: How seriously should America’s hunters, anglers, and outdoor enthusiasts take Interior’s blueprint, or is the strategic plan simply glossy “shelfware” that will be ignored as a new Congress convenes in January and other priorities shove it to the background?

“The thing about these intends is that they don’t really hold a lot of authority,” says a government affairs executive who didn’t have permission to speak on the record. “The agencies have to put them out periodically, but this is not a chapter-and-verse regulatory document or a change in the statute. Instead, you can read it as a sort of statement of purpose.”.

According to recent reports, in order to execute sales or transfers of federal land, they note, the Interior would have to undertake a formal land-use planning process with opportunities for public comment. That’s a core provision of the Federal Land Policy and Management Act. But some conservation groups are signaling that a newly introduced bill working its way through the lame-duck Congress this week, the Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act would undermine many of those land-disposal requirements. And the administration’s undercutting of the BLM’s Resource Management Prepares further weakens norms that have kept land transfers a rare exception.

Related: Senate Poised to Vote on Affordability Bill that Hunters, Anglers Worry Is a Trojan Horse for Public-Land Rollbacks.

A more present worry isn’t outright land sales, which are overwhelmingly opposed by America’s hunters and anglers. It’s the long-term lease of federal lands for hyper-scale data centers and energy facilities, says Randy Newberg, a longtime public-land advocate and podcaster.

In a recent development, “Within this vision plan is an awful lot of what I’d call greasing the skids for private development of public land, which in all aspects is quasi-ownership of public land,” says Newberg. “Given the transactional nature of this administration, I worry about sweetheart deals that help your buddy who is friends with the president or cabinet secretary to develop data centers or oil and gas facilities, you name it.”.

Newberg claims the outcome is the opposite of conservation.

“Under that vision document, you can just about bet that our public lands will become far more industrialized than any of us probably ever expected.”.

Recent findings suggest that no one should be especially surprised to see land transfer discussed at this vision-document level. After all, it’s a plank in Republican Party platforms in several states, including Montana, where party leaders last summer amended the position confirming their support for public-land transfer but also encouraging public access.

Montana’s GOP ratified the updated platform in June to read “Support transferring federally managed lands to the state with a transition initiative and continued public access.” The previous version had simply encouraged transfer of federal lands to the states “in order to secure statehood equality and provide for better management of public lands.”.

Interestingly, even the polarizing Project 2025 document, organized by the Heritage Foundation to prioritize policies of the incoming second Trump administration, doesn’t explicitly advocate transferring federal land. On the other hand, the document’s section outlining Department of the Interior priorities — maximizing energy production on federal lands, rolling back protections for national monuments, and weakening environmental reviews — are all reprised in Burgum’s five-year proposal.

Industry observers note that one of the few times the current Congress pushed back on administrative priorities in the second Trump term was to remove the land-transfer provisions of the Big Beautiful Bill. That opposition was led by Montana Rep. Ryan Zinke (R), the former Secretary of Interior in Trump’s first term, who later founded the Public Lands Caucus in Congress. But the next Congress, with majority Democrats energized by successes in this month’s mid-term election, is likely to demand oversight and review of federal agencies, including Interior.

One of the incoming freshmen, Democrat Sam Forstag, took Zinke’s western Montana seat by about 9 points. It’s the first time in 30 years that Montanans elected a Democrat to represent them in the U.S. House of Representatives. Forstag is a U.S. Forest Service smokejumper and union leader who ran on issues of affordability and against politics that “puts working people last.”.

Speaking from Washington, D.C., yesterday as he rushed between meetings and caucused with fellow freshmen, Forstag claims that public-land management has the potential to be a rare bipartisan issue.

“The notion of shrinking the federal estate and selling off our public lands sounds damned concerning to me,” Forstag said. “I think particularly as we’re seeing a change of leadership in Congress, this is the matter I see as having the most potential for not just bringing the [Democrat] caucus together but building bipartisan support. Republicans who may not have stood up publicly when we needed them the last couple of years are coming around that when it comes to actual people, public lands are not a partisan issue. They’re one of the last places where you don’t have to be rich to get access to it. [Public lands] are a reason Montana is a place worth living while costs skyrocket.”.

Forstag, who hopes to land an assignment on the House Committee on Natural Resources, states he considers talk about selling or leasing federal lands for data centers or energy infrastructure to be a “distraction.”.

Read Next: The Rush to Build Data Centers on Public Lands Is Worse Than You Thought.

Recent findings suggest that “The way you fix affordability isn’t selling off what little bit working people still have,” he states. “The way you fix affordability is not building a data center in the wilderness. It’s getting private equity the hell out of housing, and reinvesting in things like Community Development Block Grants, which have been systematically underfunded for decades while billionaires got tax cuts.”.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Southeastern Ohio is known for its heavily wooded rolling hills and the big bucks that live there. Margaret Fuller of Newly introduced Plymouth has hunted a small piece of private land there for years, and it’s where she was hunting this past weekend. In particular, she was looking for a giant 200-class buck she’d come to think of as “the Monarch.”.

The major deer started showing up on trail camera about a month ago, although only at night. He was hitting scrapes near one of Fuller’s favorite ladder stands, and that’s where she hunted on Friday.

Sources indicate that “It was bitter cold that day, but I hunted from the morning until noon,” Fuller tells Outdoor Life. “I went inside to get warm for a while, then went back out that afternoon and hunted until dark.”.

That day she spotted a smaller buck about 50 yards from her stand. The deer was working along a trail toward her, but seemed to sense something was wrong and slipped away.

In a recent development, fuller returned to that same stand the next day — her birthday — anyway. It’s the same spot she killed a 178-inch buck in 2022 during the firearms season.

“I didn’t get on stand until about noon,” says Fuller, a financial program manager for the Ohio Department of Natural Resources, “because I was so cold from the previous day’s hunt.”.

About 3 p.m. she heard an ATV roaring on the neighbor’s property and she thought her hunt that afternoon was over.

According to recent reports, “But a few minutes later I heard something in the woods, and then I caught a little movement,” states Fuller. “I stood up, grabbed my crossbow, and saw it was Monarch.”.

He was at 50 yards and coming to a scrape along the same trail the little buck had walked the day before.

Sources indicate that “I was worried the Monarch would spook, too, like the smaller buck did. I knew I had to shoot soon before he caught my wind.”.

The buck began stopped to rub his rack on a tree, then started walking closer to Fuller.

According to recent reports, “I knew I had to stop him before he got to the place where he could smell me, so I grunted,” says Fuller. “He stopped when I grunted, and I shot him at 30 yards.”.

Instead of running, the buck dropped right there. Her shot had struck the spine, and the deer didn’t get up.

Fuller called her sons and husband, then climbed down from her ladder stand.

In a recent development, “I was on cloud nine,” she claims. “I’ve been hunting deer since I was 14 with my dad, and I’d have given anything for him to have been with me and see this buck … And it was on my birthday, too!”.

In a recent development, the family helped Fuller snap photos and field-dress the massive nontypical, which had 20 points. Then they butchered the deer at home.

The whitetail, which Fuller estimates is 5½ years old, was scored at 213 inches by Buckmasters measurer Toby Hughes.

“I’m over the moon,” notes Fuller, who credits her success, in part, to “sticking with hunting even in the coldest weather.”.

Read Next: Old-School Whitetail Wisdom for Deer Hunting When the Weather Finally Turns Cold.

She also adds that practicing meticulous scent control with her clothing and using a cover scent probably didn’t hurt, either.

Recent findings suggest that “But the best thing is the joy of having my sons and husband involved in hunting. Everyone helped me and that family camaraderie is really special.”.

Escape Winter With These 6 Underrated Desert Trail Runs

📅 13 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 8 min read (1595 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Trailrunnermag

In his research for his upcoming book, “The 50 Classic Trail Runs of America” Andy Cochrane ran hundreds of trails across the U.S. These are his six favorites across the Southwest that come into season when most of the country is hibernating.

With all due respect to Presidential Traverse, Teton Crest, and Wonderland, the most sought-after one-day trail running route in the U.S. is the Grand Canyon Rim-to-Rim-to-Rim. Every spring and fall runners flock to Arizona to test their luck on this double lap of the big ditch, despite the National Park Service strongly advising against it. (Signs around the Grand Canyon warn of heat illness, elevation, and difficult evacs.).

Some have called R2R2R an obsession—while I’m not sure I would personally go that far, I do see the argument. I’ve run the route three times and each trip I find myself more enamored than the last. On my last visit in 2023, a peak autumn weekend with nearly perfect temps and all the water facets still running (the NPS shuts some of them down seasonally), I saw hundreds of runners attempting R2R2R. That’s a tiny fraction of the four and a half million people who visit the park each year, but very busy for a trail run.

According to recent reports, however, that was before the closures. The North Rim of the Grand Canyon was shuttered for most of the 2025 season due to the Dragon Bravo Fire, which burned 149,000 acres and 118 buildings. Then, on August 29th, 2026, a flash flood struck Phantom Ranch at the bottom of the Grand Canyon, killing three and forcing 82 others to be evacuated by helicopter. Trail damage was widespread, taking out footbridges and much of the park’s water line. The North Kaibab Trail, parts of the Bright Angel and South Kaibab trails, and sections of the River Trail remain closed with no set date for reopening.

It’s getting colder and darker across most of the country. That means one thing: It’s desert season. In lieu of a double dip into the Grand Canyon—and to open your mind to the endless possibilities elsewhere—I’ve compiled a list of my six favorite trails across the American Southwest. All of them are in my upcoming book, “The 50 Classic Trail Runs of America” (which you can pre-order now!). They cover six different states and four unique desert ecosystems, so there is plenty of variety to choose from.

Unlike the rocky singletrack of the Northeast, the forested trails of the upper Midwest, or the alpine ridges of the West, running across the Southwest desert is a singular experience. Limited shade, even less water, and direct solar radiation create obvious hydration challenges. The temperature swings dramatically from near freezing overnight to scorching heat midday. The trails themselves are a mix of surfaces, from soft sand to loose scree to firm slickrock, with many—including the ones listed below—being very remote.

Beyond the physical experience, running in arid environments carries a different emotion, too. I often find myself in a quiet and contemplative mental space, passing by ancient saguaros, joshua trees, and prickly pears while trying to stay alert for subtle movements of rattlesnakes, lizards, and coyotes. Running in the desert is, simultaneously, the antidote to life’s complexity and a plague of endless possibility.

Industry observers note that there are four distinct desert ecosystems in the U.S. The northernmost is the Great Basin, which covers most of Nevada and parts of neighboring states, making it the largest desert in the country. With frigid winters, it’s filled with sagebrush instead of cacti. Just south is the Mojave, the smallest of the four, which is home to Death Valley and Joshua Tree. Further south is the Sonoran, the “green desert,” with large saguaros and rainfall in both summer and winter. Last, the Chihuahuan, covers West Texas and southern New Mexico, and is known for succulents like Agave, Yucca, and Creosote.

Hidden in one of North America’s most remote national parks, Big Bend, the Outer Mountain Loop is a 32-mile circuit featuring a stark ecological contrast between the Chihuahuan Desert and the high-alpine Chisos Mountains. Beginning and ending in the Chisos Basin, a sky-island that’s home to rare species like the Colima Warbler, the trail plunges down stone steps and rolls across the sun-scorched flats of the Dodson Trail before making a grueling 3,000-foot final ascent up Blue Creek Canyon. Early Spanish explorers called this isolated region El Despoblado.

Why I love it: Getting to experience both sky islands and the solitude of the Chihuahuan desert.

Recent findings suggest that spanning 39 miles from the edge of the Navajo Nation to the Grand Canyon’s South Rim, the Little to Substantial Colorado route is the less conventional way to explore one of the country’s most popular national parks. Tracing the historic Hopi salt journeys, the route plunges down Bekihatso Wash, follows the Little Colorado to its confluence with the Colorado River, passes sacred sites, scrambles obstacles like the Papago Wall, and passes by billion-year-old rock. With a 4,700-foot grind up the New Hance Trail at the end, it’s just as challenging and rewarding as rim-to-rim-to-rim.

Why I love it: It’s so close to the most famous one day trail route in the country, but still unheard of.

According to recent reports, crossing the national park from east to west, this 37-mile rolling route passes two distinct deserts—the higher Mojave and the lower Sonora—as you wander by long shadows of Yucca brevifolia (Joshua trees) and massive, weathered granite batholiths. Championed by the activist Minerva Hamilton Hoyt after decades of cattle grazing and mining exploitation, this sandy sanctuary strips away the crowds, offering sheer solitude as runners cross ancient mountain passes, gaze down at the dark expanse of the Salton Sea, and experience a desert communion.

According to recent reports, why I love it: it’s the one place in America that feels straight out of a Dr. Seuss book.

It has been revealed that one of the most remote routes we considered for the book, this 64-mile trek traces the ridgeline of the Toiyabe Range. Like Outer Mountain, this area is a sky island, a rare ecosystem in which the valley below is a scorching hot desert, but the trail itself is a lush forest of aspen and bristlecone pines, some 3,000 years old. Despite being Nevada’s longest named trail, Toiyabe is off-trail in nature, with significant routefinding and some sections of unrunnable terrain.

Why I love it: Remote and rugged, it’s a good test of navigation and alpine movement of all sorts.

Recent findings suggest that perched above Albuquerque, this 26-mile trail follows a limestone ridge along the backbone of the Sandia Mountains, with 360-degree views of the Rio Grande Valley below. Sandia is Spanish for watermelon, named after the ridge’s unique sunset alpenglow that turns the cliffs deep pink, with green conifers on top representing the rind. The trail features wildflowers, ponderosas, spruce, and white fir, and can be accessed via an aerial tramway, providing easy access without sacrificing its rugged, aesthetic appeal.

Why I love it: Quick and easy access paired with absolutely beautiful sunsets.

It has been revealed that winding through one of Southern Utah’s most distinctive landscapes, the 30-mile Bryce Canyon Traverse links the heavily trafficked northern amphitheater where thousands of hoodoos, rock fins, and natural arches create a natural maze with the primitive Under the Rim Trail to the south. Crossing a geological marvel shaped by erosion and freeze-thaw cycles over millions of years, the traverse is the best way to see it all. Heading southbound allows runners to catch sunrise over the spires before descending into remote backcountry, which is the direction we recommend.

Why I love it: There’s no place in the world with the same density or volume of hoodoos.

It has been revealed that desert running presents many challenges that the Mafate X can handle. Deserts are often oven-hot, so having a woven, high-airflow upper is ideal. They are rocky and filled with pokey things, so having a taller stack with soft PEBA foam is a bonus. They are loose, so having Vibram lugs adds a level of stability and confidence. And, with uneven ground, a wide base makes your feet feel much more planted, too.

On long, sweaty days, sunscreen only goes so far. I take extra precaution and wear a Tahoe sun hoody, which delivers UPF 50+ protection against harsh UV rays, paired with a light polyester-spandex knit that wicks sweat off my skin and dries promptly. And, integrated thumbholes and a fitted hood keep my hands and neck completely covered without restricting movement.

For most desert runs I recommend stashing water the day before, but if you aren’t able to, having an extra large running pack is key. Kiprun’s 10L has room for a bladder in the back and two flasks up front, which is ideal for long desert stretches. The harness keeps the pack secure and large front pockets make it easy to access your phone, electrolytes, snacks, or sunscreen on the go.

My favorite drink mix, Fuel combines essential electrolytes like sodium, potassium, and magnesium to replace minerals lost in heavy sweat. It tastes good, prevents cramps, and the added zinc supports fluid retention in hot conditions. Using a low-GI carb from beet sugar, it also provides steady energy without blood sugar spikes or crashes, which is great for longer days.

10 of the Hottest Hunting Suppressors on the Market in 2026

📅 18 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 11 min read (2188 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Outdoorlife

⏱️ ~11 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • In a recent development, we may earn revenue from the products available on this page and participate in affiliate programs.
  • According to recent reports, it’s never been easier to get a suppressor for your hunting rifle.
  • I’ve been shooting every new suppressor I can get my hands on for years, and these are the best ones that I have used.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, we may earn revenue from the products available on this page and participate in affiliate programs. Learn More ›.

According to recent reports, it’s never been easier to get a suppressor for your hunting rifle. But choosing one, for a first-time buyer, can be intimidating. There are thousands of options on the market and narrowing it down to the best can for your hunting rifle isn’t easy if you don’t know what to look for. So many latest suppressors are hitting the market that what was a top-of-the-line can a couple years ago is just average today.

I’ve been shooting every new suppressor I can get my hands on for years, and these are the best ones that I have used.

This is one of the best hunting rifle suppressors I have ever used. Like many others that are leading the pack, it’s 3D printed from titanium, making it both strong and economical. It measures 5 inches long and weighs just 5.75 ounces. Despite its lightweight profile, it’s very quiet. In fact, it’s substantially quieter than several other popular suppressors — something I noted on a recent antelope hunt.

Industry observers note that this is one of my top picks because it’s simple, rugged, quiet, and you’ll hardly notice it on your muzzle. It is direct thread only and, because threads are cut into the suppressor itself, they cannot be changed like a HUB-compatible suppressor. For a hunting suppressor, that’s a feature, not a bug. At $900, this is a really good value. Many top-level hunting suppressors will cost you $1,000 or more.

In the year since its introduction, Airlock has released 30-cal and 7mm versions of the Zero Gravity, as well as a 3.7-ounce Zero Gravity Nano, which is designed for bolt-action centerfire .22 cals like the 22 ARC, 22 Creed, and .22-250 Rem. It’s slightly larger than a rimfire suppressor, but satisfyingly quiet.

Sources indicate that the Nomad Ti XC is another excellent option for a hunting suppressor. Its 3D printed design allows for modern baffles and reduces weak spots. The front and rear of the can are threaded and it is compatible with HUB rear mounts. I prefer using a Silencerco Ti direct thread adapter on the rear, and the standard .308 front cap. Other companies like Salmon River Solutions are making accessories like a directional brake that threads into the front cap to further reduce recoil and tame down cartridges like the .300 PRC. As pictured, the suppressor weighs less than 10 ounces and works wonderfully for anything 30-caliber and under. A nice feature is the inclusion of deep tool notches which makes removing the HUB mounts easy without worry of damaging the suppressor.

Another great option, if you want a shorter overall length for your rifle, is the Nomad TiOTB, which has a chamber that extends back over the barrel. This suppressor has the same interchangeable endcaps, but works exclusively with a thread-over-brake mount.

I’ve been shooting the TiTrex 300 Ti for several months now, and this is one of the best options for a general-purpose hunting suppressor out there. After all that shooting, it still only weighs 9.5 ounces, and it offers great mounting and front-cap modularity.

In a recent development, A couple years ago, the Silencerco Scythe Ti was one of few .30-cal silencers that light, but it’s been plagued by weld failure issues. The TiTrex 300 Ti is also made of titanium, is slightly lighter, and uses HUB mounts at the rear and an open-source front cap that works with the Silencerco Bravo front mounts. You can use a normal endcap or the short endcap brake, which helps reduce recoil, and both have great spanner wrench notches. It’s also compatible with some aftermarket Endcap brakes like the Salmon River Solutions Grim, which can help cut recoil even more.

The TiTrex has a 3D-printed body and baffle system that is rugged, durable, and even full-auto rated. This is a great option to use with a front brake as a competition can, but that can also work well on your hunting rifle. It would also be a solid choice as your first suppressor. A unique feature is that the serialized portion of the suppressor is a stainless-steel band at the rear of the can, that can be moved to a different core if you manage to wear the original out or damage it somehow.

There are three big trends in hunting suppressors in 2026, and the Buckskin 30 from Tenet tackles all of them. First, it’s 3D printed. Additive manufacturing has allowed companies to rapidly develop and prototype suppressor models while reducing weak points like welds on thin titanium.

According to recent reports, second, it incorporates a front brake. Suppressors reduce recoil by slowing gases as they exit the muzzle, and incorporating a brake on the front tames them even further. The Buckskin features a built-in brake that is non-adjustable and won’t come loose.

Third, it’s light. It’s printed with titanium and mine weighs 8.5 ounces — making it the lightest .30-cal suppressor I own. I’ve used this suppressor on my 20-inch 300 PRC, several 6.5 Creedmoors, and have been putting a lot of rounds through it on a 16-inch 7mm Backcountry. It does a great job at reducing recoil while adding minimal extra weight.

Recent findings suggest that if you want more adjustability and increased recoil reduction, the Tenet Limited 30 is another suppressor to look at. These are more expensive, but feature a removable front brake that cuts your rifle movement dramatically. Mine has a two-port brake and, while the first generation of brakes tended to blast your face with gas, the recently-released gen 2 brake has small steps in the curved brake to disrupt that gas impulse. It’s much more pleasant. If spotting your impacts with larger cartridges is important to you, a can like this fits the bill.

In the days of year-long waiting periods, modularity was king for hunting suppressors. While modular cans have their place, a simple dedicated hunting silencer is hard to beat. This fully 3D-printed titanium can from Unknown Munitions weighs about 11 ounces and features a reflex design, meaning the rear portion of the suppressor goes back over the barrel. That reflex expansion chamber allows a shorter portion — about four inches — to stick out in front of your muzzle. This improves balance and gives you a more compact package than the average 8-inch suppressor. The reflex design also creates a noticeably duller sound signature, whereas some produce a very sharp, snappy sound.

According to recent reports, these are available in .30 caliber as well as 6.5mm and 6mm options, and models and fit over 0.75-inch diameter steel barrels and the OGL model fits larger carbon-fiber barrels. This suppressor isn’t modular, so you need to ensure compatibility before you order. Also check out their Reaper suppressor, which I haven’t had the chance to use, but should be another top contender.

Sources indicate that I’ve used several of B&T’s Print-X series of titanium 3D-printed suppressors and have been impressed by all of them. Their modular VERS36 Ti model, however, deserves special recognition. To my knowledge, this is the lightest modular 36-caliber suppressor on the market, and it’s way cheaper than similar, more primitive cans were several years ago. If you’re wanting to get a suppressor to start out with, or to use on multiple hunting rifles, this is your jam.

It has been revealed that it’s got 36-caliber baffles and comes with a .360 front cap. The rear is HUB-compatible and B&T makes nice titanium direct-thread adapters. You can get smaller front caps as well. If using on smaller cartridges or you just need a shorter overall package, the front section is removable. This is a flow-through design with spiral baffles that works well on bolt actions and gas-guns alike. It’s ideal for cartridges like the .350 Legend, but will work on anything with a .360-diameter bullet or smaller. I received mine through Silencer Central and it can be delivered to your door.

It has been revealed that the StingerWorx Evo Hunter is a lightweight suppressor that’s more affordable than the 3D printed titanium cans, and it’s also much more serviceable. A downside of most printed suppressors is that there isn’t a great way to remove large amounts of carbon buildup from the baffles. Soaking and ultrasonic cleaners help, but a lot of shooters want a suppressor that can be disassembled and manually cleaned.

The Evo Hunter is just over 10 ounces, and it gets there by using multiple materials. It has a titanium blast baffle and chamber to provide a long service life, but uses an aluminum baffle stack downstream of that — where heat and abrasion isn’t as intense. If damaged, that front baffle stack is replaceable. Additionally, the Evo Hunter is compatible with StingerWorx’s front brake if you’re looking for additional recoil reduction. It’s got HUB threads at the rear and the blast chamber is deep enough to work with a variety of over-brake HUB mounts that you might already have. For the light weight, versatility, and serviceability, this can is a great value.

There are lots of suppressors out there and, because many of them are so similar, lots of good ones can get lost in the mix. Because we cover a lot of leading-edge ultralight cans, don’t think that we don’t pay attention to budget options, too. There are bottom-tier suppressors that are very cheap — often made of mostly aluminum — that will work, but can also leave buyers dissatisfied. When it comes to bang for your buck, stainless steel is still one of the best materials for a more affordable can. The first suppressor I ever bought was a large .30-cal stainless can. It was durable and affordable and its weight was the only downside.

According to recent reports, the Banish HNT 30 SS is a great example of a modern great value. It’s compact and, at 13.8 ounces, not excessively heavy. It’s suitable for virtually any hunting rifle .30-caliber and smaller, and similar in size and form to the lightweight Banish Backcountry titanium can. It’s got hub threads at the rear and comes with a direct-thread adapter. If you’re looking to try a suppressor for hunting and want a good-quality can, this is a great place to start.

In a recent development, if you’re looking for maximum suppression of your significant-bore cartridges, the Goliath Gen 2 from Liberty Suppressors is an excellent option. This beast of a silencer is 10.25 inches long by 2 inches in diameter and designed specifically for cartridges like the .458 Socom, .450 Bushmaster, and .45/70 Gov’t. While big, this can is relatively light. It’s got twice the volume of suppressors like the Silencerco Hybrid 46, but weighs only about 4 ounces more (22 ounces total). This is a perfect fit for anyone hunting with a short-barreled .458 or .450 Bushmaster, or a trapper-style .45/70.

The suppressor has a titanium sleeve and titanium baffle stack that’s removable and serviceable so you can shoot cast lead bullets and clean out lead fouling — unlike sealed suppressors. I’ve had a Liberty .22 rimfire can for many years, and this is essentially a much larger version of that. I’ve been shooting it on my .45/70 and it’s working wonderfully on my .338 ARC SBR with subsonic ammo.

One of the best values in lightweight modular suppressors is the BDE from Primary Weapons Systems. I’ve been shooting the 5.56 model for the last several months, and it combines smart manufacturing with durability, value, and the kind of modularity a lot of hunters want. The BDE has hub threads at the rear, a blast chamber segment, and a 3D-printed main baffle segment. Forward of that, it has removable individual threaded baffle segments topped with an end cap.

According to recent reports, this is a sealed suppressor, but baffles are designed to allow gasses to flow better and reduce backpressure, making a great option for both a bolt gun and AR-style semi-auto. Each segment of the can has wrench notches making disassembly easy, and you can customize to the platform you’ll be shooting. This has been living on my .223 practice bolt-action and the irregular surface contours do seem to help break up mirage. The BDE is also available in .30- and .36- caliber models, all with customizable baffle configurations.

Picking through the many different suppressor options can be daunting, and most good suppressors perform similarly. To find one that you’ll be happy with, consider details like construction and weight, but also the level of modularity you desire, or whether you’re just looking for a good value. If one of these isn’t quite what you’re looking for, I hope that seeing these options and features will help you home in on the model that you will be most satisfied with. The suppressor market is constantly evolving, and we will continue to use and test suppressors with the goal of helping you make the most informed decisions possible.

#67889. Old-School Whitetail Wisdom for Stalking Cornfields During Deer Season

📅 18 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 19m • 📚 Deep Dive (3897 w)

Old-School Whitetail Wisdom for Stalking Cornfields During Deer Season

📅 18 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 19 min read (3897 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Outdoorlife

⏱️ ~19 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • There are two things that my friend Harvey Wilcourt loves more than anything else.
  • Harve and I had scheduled a day of winter fishing for walleyes, and the initiative was to meet at a well-known parking area near the lake and then decide upon a particular frozen-over bay that might offer the best results.
  • At first, I shrugged my shoulders, not knowing in which direction he might have headed.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

There are two things that my friend Harvey Wilcourt loves more than anything else. One is ice-fishing, and the other is eating peanuts. It might not sound as though that bears any relation to whitetail deer hunting, but one time it actually helped me to collect a very significant buck.

Harve and I had scheduled a day of winter fishing for walleyes, and the initiative was to meet at a well-known parking area near the lake and then decide upon a particular frozen-over bay that might offer the best results. As it happened, however, car trouble delayed my arrival by more than an hour, so naturally, when I finally reached our meeting place, Harve had already headed out onto the ice-shrouded lake.

At first, I shrugged my shoulders, not knowing in which direction he might have headed. Then, I happened to look down at the ground near his parked vehicle, and guess what I spotted? Right, peanut shells! Right then, a wide smile came across my face because I instantly knew that tracking Harve would be easy.

Industry observers note that in most places, the trail was relatively thin, but occasionally I’d come to an abandoned hole in the ice where shells littered the entire area. Then, the trail would lead off into the distance to another hole, and then still another. Eventually, I spied my partner in a distant channel, and we spent the remainder of the day fishing together. Without the discarded peanut shells showing the way, I might have never located Harve and might have ended up fishing solo that day.

The irony is that several years later, I duplicated the same type of feat, but this time the trail eventually led me to an eight-point buck. To the best of my knowledge, whitetails don’t maintain any particular fetish for peanuts, but they do love corn. And after filling their paunches in a cornfield, it’s quite common for them to carry off a cob in their mouths and continue eating from it as they travel to a nearby bedding site. Sometimes, they’ll finish with the cob along the way and let it fall to the ground right there. Other times, they’ll carry the cob all the way back to the actual bedding location, perhaps to snack upon later.

In any event, I had been hiking along the edge of a large cornfield near my home in southern Ohio, and in coming upon a threadbare trail exiting from the corn, I had found a partially eaten cob. Recalling my amusing experience with Harvey, I decided to follow the trail, and just inside the leading edge of a nearby beech forest I discovered another cob on the ground, and then still another. All of the cobs were in various stages of deterioration, so I knew that they had been dropped at different times over a period of weeks. Large, fresh deer tracks of uniform size and large droppings provided additional clues, and eventually, more than 300 yards into the timber, I came upon a lone bed. That confirmed I was in a buck’s bailiwick, because had there been tracks of varied sizes and several beds, I could have inferred that the deer were only does.

In a recent development, after resting the area for two days, I snuck back into the spot and quietly fabricated a makeshift blind behind a convenient blowdown overlooking the trail. Later, when there was just enough light to make a shot, a gray shadow materialized in the distance, traveling right along the trail. My arrow caught the eight-pointer at the base of the neck, and after sprinting 50 yards, the buck collapsed in a heap.

Recent findings suggest that it’s no secret that bucks and corn go together like bacon and eggs, and we have plenty of all of those commodities, especially throughout the Midwestern agricultural belt. In fact, after talking recently with my local extension agent, I learned that in 1986, in the nine major farming states stretching from Ohio to Minnesota, more than 46 million acres of land were planted to corn.

Moreover, acquiring hunting permission in agricultural regions is invariably easier than it is on other privately owned lands because of the extensive damage often inflicted by wild animals. In Wisconsin alone, it was estimated that during 1986, deer destroyed more than $22 million worth of corn, and this cost each farmer an average of $490. Add to this the combined losses of alfalfa, soybeans, truck garden crops and other foods that whitetails regularly dine upon, and it should come as no surprise that though a majority of farmers certainly enjoy seeing deer on their land, they don’t take kindly to whitetail populations reaching such levels that they severely cut into the farmers’ annual incomes.

The exasperating problem that most hunters face is how to effectively hunt those often mammoth and intimidating cornfields.

The first task is to confirm that deer are indeed using the corn, and this is easily ascertained by merely hiking the perimeter of the field and looking for tracks entering and leaving the food plot. Obviously, the best time to do this is either after a rainy period, when the ground is soft, or after several days of light snowfall.

If the region has been experiencing several weeks of dry weather, however, and the terrain is like hardpan, tracks are not easily detected. It is in this case that other types of insight must be applied to the hunting situation. For example, one time I discovered a cornfield where many stalks had been knocked down and countless partially eaten ears were on the ground. Initially, I thought that I had found a mother lode of deer activity, but I was dead wrong.

In a recent development, as I learned later, several raccoons had been at work. The telltale giveaway — pointed out to me by a friend who is a serious naturalist — should have been the fact that the ears were only partially eaten. Raccoons rarely eat an entire ear of corn; instead, they knock down a cornstalk and bite off just the tender tip of the ear, then move on to the next stalk.

If the cornfield borders a climax forest, corn-hungry squirrels may also give the false impression that deer have been at work. But in this situation, the animals climb the stalks, nibble away at the ears, stuff their cheeks and then retreat to their dens, where the scavenged kernels are placed in storage. This leaves the ears still attached to the stalks but gives them a ragtag, moth-eaten appearance.

Recent findings suggest that if deer are working the corn, however, the clues to look for in the absence of tracks are scattered cobs on the ground that have been cleaned of almost every kernel of corn. Also keep on the lookout for droppings.

Once it has been determined that deer are hitting a particular cornfield on a regular basis, the best mode of hunting must be decided upon. And contrary to what you might expect, the best method of hunting is not necessarily the tactic you might like to use most, but rather the one that most appropriately falls in line with the agricultural cropping practices in your region.

Recent findings suggest that in many areas, conventional harvesting methods are engaged in sometime during October or November, when the corn is brown and cured. The picking operation leaves the cornfield in a stubble-like condition, yet there remains on the ground plenty of spillage residue to attract the interest of local deer. Under these conditions, with the previously standing cornstalks no longer present and the concealing cover therefore eliminated, midday hunting is virtually out of the question. The animals will predictably visit the corn only in the early morning hours or at dusk. If hunting pressure is intense in the region, the deer may even be strictly nocturnal in their feeding.

Industry observers note that conversely, in many other regions, it is becoming an increasingly popular agricultural practice to leave corn standing in the field for as long as possible. With grain-elevator storage costs escalating like never before, and future market prices always uncertain, many farmers nowadays are simply delaying their harvesting either until such time as they have a specific need for the corn for stock feed or until the price increases, which it often does in February or March. Consequently, the hunter now finds that he can effectively hunt the cornfields not only early and late in the day, but also during the midday hours.

Regardless of whether a solo hunter elects to use bowhunting equipment, a rifle, a slug-loaded shotgun, a muzzleloader or a handgun, there are four options to choose from when hunting standing corn: sneak-hunting in and around the corn; sneak-hunting in and around nearby heavy-cover regions; taking a stand designed to intercept the animals coming to the corn; or taking a stand designed to intercept the animals as they leave the corn.

Still again, the right method to use may not necessarily be the hunter’s favorite way to hunt, but it must be geared to existing conditions. The foremost determinant that I rely upon to make my decision is the presence or absence of wind — assuming there is standing corn, of course.

Recent findings suggest that on a windy day, I do not want to be in a tree stand. Wind is the result of downdrafts of cold air meeting warm air. Therefore, no matter which direction the wind is coming from, it will have a tendency to force scents down toward the ground, and this will readily give away a hunter’s location. Compounding the problem is the fact that deer do not like to move on windy days because the wind disallows the effective use of their sense of hearing. Calm days, on the other hand, or those during which the wind is only slightly and gently blowing from one specific direction are ideal for quietly waiting on stand for the deer to walk by.

Just the opposite is the case when hunting in and around the cornfield itself. Now is when a hunter wants the windiest conditions possible. This is because when whitetails bed during the midday hours, they feel most secure and safe by retreating into the heaviest, thickest cover they can find. In many agricultural regions, the terrain surrounding cornfields, such as gullies and forest lands, simply does not offer hiding cover that is as thick as that in the cornfields themselves. Consequently, the whitetails will commonly bed right in the cornfields in these areas.

Now it becomes obvious why the very time to hunt these cornfields is during periods of high winds. It is because under blowing conditions, a cornfield is a very noisy place. The leaves are dry and brittle later in the season, and the loud rustling and crackling noises that they make in the wind cover up so much human error in prowling around that a hunter can quite easily walk right up on deer without them suspecting his presence.

According to recent reports, moreover, a hunter doesn’t have to worry about his scent when hunting in a cornfield. Wind in a cornfield is a tricky thing. It hits the stalks and broad leaves and bounces every which way. As a result, deer in a cornfield may catch a hunter’s scent, but in most cases they will not be able to determine the direction from which it’s coming. As a result, they lock up, or freeze, in position because they know that if they attempt to run, they may blunder right into trouble. And if the hunter then happens to step into the right row of corn, he may have an easy shot at a stationary buck.

In going back to calm days, during which patiently waiting in a tree stand or ground blind is the preferred method of hunting either standing corn or stubble fields, there are two tricks that I use to properly locate my stand. First, it’s necessary to engage in enough scouting to know in advance where trails are located. It must be remembered, however, that it’s quite common for deer to leave a cornfield via a different trail than the one they used to enter the field, assuming, of course, that the deer are bedding somewhere other than in the corn itself. Therefore, a morning stand to intercept the deer leaving the corn will undoubtedly be in a different place than an evening stand that has been set up to ambush deer coming from their bedding areas to the corn.

In a recent development, thus, what a hunter initially wants to do after locating trails is to ascertain what time of day they’re being used. The direction in which tracks are pointing is a sure clue — if the tracks are pointing toward the corn, they were probably made in the evening; if they are directed away from the corn, they probably indicate an exit trail that the animals use in the morning. Also, the hunter should be on the lookout for corncobs. Because deer obviously do not carry cobs from their bedding region back to the cornfield, but do carry cobs from the field to their bedding sites, the presence of intermittent cobs along the trail indicates in no uncertain terms that the travel route is a morning trail.

As a general rule, I do not like for either a morning stand or an evening stand to be too close to a cornfield where deer are feeding. If possible, depending upon his evaluation of the terrain, a hunter should try to situate his stands or blinds 100 to 200 yards from the cornfield so that he can overlook the exit and entrance trails that the deer are using to enter or leave the food plot.

Recent findings suggest that there are several good reasons for this strategy. To begin with, the largest bucks in any given region do not like to expose themselves unnecessarily in broad daylight, especially in regions where hunting pressure is intense. They can pretty much be counted upon to leave the cornfield at the very hint of early morning’s first light. Because it may still be too dark to shoot accurately, the hunter wants to be farther back down the trail that the deer are using so that by the time they reach the stand location, it will be fully light enough to see.

Industry observers note that conversely, in the evening hours, the very largest bucks seldom enter a cornfield when the sky is still brightly illuminated. They like to linger back in the shaded, heavy cover of their bedding areas, sometimes not actually entering the cornfield until after full dark. Naturally, therefore, if a stand or blind is positioned close to the cornfield, by the time the deer reach the location, it will be too dark to see.

Sources indicate that in all of this, it should be kept in mind that though the hunter doesn’t want to position his stand too close to the cornfield for either a morning or an evening watch, neither does he want his stand too close to the bedding area that the animals are using. This is simply too risky because the animals are very likely to detect the hunter as he tries to approach his stand site; and if they are spooked from the very region that they previously considered the safest place to be, they may not return for many days.

Industry observers note that in fact, it’s worth mentioning that during the course of scouting, I always move slowly but make plenty of noise. Sometimes, I even whistle to myself as though I’m engaged in some type of routine outdoor work such as that of a surveyor or forester. Whitetails are accustomed to this type of minor disturbance, and they will simply circle around the intruder. And because the deer have the opportunity to hide or sneak away undetected, they’ll still have full confidence in the security of their chosen area, prompting them to return shortly after I’ve left.

Recent findings suggest that later, when I return to begin my hunting vigil, I stalk my stand. I actually sneak up on it just as though I were stillhunting through the woods. By doing this, the chances of any nearby deer recognizing my presence are much lower.

Pursuing whitetails when they’re actually in the corn is one of deer hunting’s most challenging and exciting endeavors. But the hunter should remember two things: If the terrain surrounding the cornfield is devoid of thick security cover, meaning that the corn itself is the very best place to hide and bed, the deer will probably cling to the corn all day and every day. This is especially the case if water is readily available in rain-filled puddles or tractor ruts. The second thing to remember — again — is that the windiest days are the best days to hunt.

It has been revealed that simply sneak-hunting around the perimeter of the cornfield can put venison on the meat pole, particularly during the early and late hours of the day, when the deer are feeding and have a tendency to work along “edges.” I’ve most often found this to be the case when the cornfield is bordered on one or more sides by lush hay meadows planted to some legume such as alfalfa, red or white clover or lespedeza. This is because it’s rather uncustomary for whitetails to gorge themselves on a single food type, as they are opportunists in their feeding habits and like variety in their diets. Therefore, if you know of a cornfield bordered by some other equally preferred food, you’ve hit paydirt!

Recent findings suggest that in sneak-hunting around the perimeter of a cornfield, a hunter shouldn’t expose himself in the open by remaining along the outside edge. Instead, he should stay one or two rows inside the edge of the cornfield — just far enough in so that he’s concealed yet can still see along the outside edge and into the adjacent, secondary food plot. The only exception to this rule is when the cornfield butts up directly against a brushy thicket or other bordering cover. In this case, the hunter can remain along the outermost edge of the corn and move slowly along with minimal chance of detection.

If the entire outside perimeter of the cornfield has been worked and no deer have been seen, it’s now time to assume that the whitetails are deeper within the confines of the corn, where they are most probably either feeding or bedding.

If the hunter is familiar with the terrain from previous scouting missions — before the corn was planted — he should try to recall the locations in the field where there were rock piles, soupy swales, sand pockets and the like. These exist in many fields, and farmers simply plow and plant around them. Once the surrounding corn has grown high, however, such places are hidden from view, and they are the very types of locations where deer commonly like to bed. The hunter should sneak up on these places during windy conditions, and he might very well shoot an unsuspecting deer right in its bed.

If firearms are being used and several hunting partners are working together, staging drives is an excellent way to push deer through the corn to the opposite end of the field, where standers are likely to have shots. But there are a few vital points to bear in mind when using this method. If the cornfield is large, it is imperative that a large number of drivers — spaced no more than eight to 10 rows apart — be employed, because otherwise the deer, reluctant to leave the security of the cover, will tirelessly circle and sneak back between the drivers. Consequently, if there are only a few hunters participating in the drive, only smaller cornfields where the animals can be moved effectively in a predetermined direction should be hunted.

Also, in the interest of safety, drives in cornfields should ideally include stand hunters placed in tree stands, or at least on some other elevated vantage points such as hillsides or knolls. This way, they will be able to look down and through the rows of corn to see both the escaping deer and their approaching partners. Likewise, when they shoot from such higher locations, the angles of their shots will be acutely downward, rather than horizontal.

Bowhunters can also enact drives in cornfields, but instead of hunting parallel with the rows in an attempt to push deer to standers in the distance, they should hunt perpendicular to the rows. In this type of situation, no hunters need be placed on stand.

Along the edge of the cornfield, the bowhunters should be spaced about 100 yards apart. The team leader at one end of this drive line should then use his arm to signal the first hunter on the far end to enter the field. As this hunter enters the first row, he should look right and left, then move on to the second row, and so on. After about 30 seconds, the drive master should then motion the next hunter to enter the cornfield in the same manner. What results is that instead of a straight and even drive line moving through the field, there is a diagonal shift across the field. Therefore, if a hunter enters a row and sees a deer he wants to shoot at, he can do so to either his right or left with complete confidence in safety, knowing that his partners to either side are far ahead of or behind him. If he does not wish to shoot, the deer will usually run parallel to the rows and eventually offer a shot to one of the next hunters in the line.

Industry observers note that finally, one of the shrewdest ways I know to evaluate potential cornfield hunting situations, especially in unfamiliar regions, is to go to a local airport and hire a small plane to fly over the terrain. Most pilots charge an average of $30 per hour, and if two hunters split the expense, the cost per person is not prohibitive. But most vital, in one hour of flying about 500 feet above the ground, a hunter can learn more about an area than he can in two weeks of driving back roads and scouting on foot. A topographic map should be brought along, and the location and configuration of every cornfield in the region should be marked. Adjacent terrain and cover should be carefully examined, and it then should be easy to determine with a high level of accuracy how deer are living, moving and feeding in each specific region.

Read Next: Old-School Whitetail Wisdom for Deer Hunting When the Weather Finally Turns Cold.

According to recent reports, believe me, if there are cornfields in the region you strategy to hunt, you can be sure that bucks are in the corn — if not continuously, then at least intermittently. In either case, you should make the effort to be on hand, too, and when you leave, the chances are excellent that you’ll be dragging your deer behind you.

This story, “Deer By The Ear,” appeared in the November 1988 glitch of Outdoor Life.

A Routine Invasive-Species Survey in Lake Ontario Turned Up Something Much Stranger

📅 18 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 2 min read (443 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Outdoorlife

⏱️ ~2 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Routine research in the Great Lakes system morphed into an unusual catch this fall.
  • Fish and Wildlife Service survey crew caught a rare yellow burbot in October, according to a statement last week.
  • “The finding is notable because burbot populations in the lake are extremely low,” the agency wrote on Nov.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Routine research in the Great Lakes system morphed into an unusual catch this fall.

Industry observers note that A U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service survey crew caught a rare yellow burbot in October, according to a statement last week. The fish came from Oswego Harbor, Fresh York, which is on the southeastern side of Lake Ontario. It’s a significant find for more than just its color variation.

“The finding is notable because burbot populations in the lake are extremely low,” the agency wrote on Nov. 10. “The species typically inhabit deeper, cooler waters than those found within the harbor.”.

Industry observers note that running the full length of an arm, the off-colored native burbot had xanthochromism, a genetic mutation that causes an animal’s pigment to be excessively yellow or orange. In fish, it displays on their scales and fins, but it can also show up on furred animals. It’s less common than albinism in the wild, but it’s also not unheard of.

A 6.6-foot orange-Creamsicle nurse shark turned up with the same condition, plus albinism, in 2024 in Costa Rica, and the first case of xanthochromism in a sunset-colored snook in the Gulf was documented in 2024.

According to recent reports, the variation might be appealing to fishermen, but it’s less fun for the fish themselves. Their bold coloring reduces their ability to hide within their habitat, which means they’re easy prey and often have shorter lifespans.

The deadly-bright hues look similar to banana trout, but that’s a different scenario.

It has been revealed that palomino trout, or bananas, are popular stockers for pond practice. They’re also covered in shades ranging from yellow to orange, but they’re bred that way on purpose. Hatcheries breed them from a mutant rainbow trout strain that lacks the dot pattern but keeps the bow’s notorious red lateral stripe. Despite the golden color, they aren’t related to California golden trout. The strain traces to a single yellow-mottled rainbow fingerling found at a West Virginia hatchery in 1955 and was introduced to anglers in 1963.

Read Next: These Are the Biggest North American Catfish of All Time.

According to recent reports, as for the yellow burbot in Oswego, it wasn’t released. Its body condition was in decline, so the fish was sent to Cornell University College of Veterinary Medicine to be studied. It’s one of many fish analyzed during the region’s Aquatic Invasive Species Survey. The goal of the survey is early detection of a problem throughout the many bodies of water in the Great Lakes system, including harbors and rivers. Researchers use electrofishing, fyke nets, and gill nets to collect specimens for the survey.

#67884. The Most Unexpected Ski Adventure in North America Might Be in Michigan

📅 20 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 5m • 📚 Deep Dive (936 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Skimag ↗ Open Full Page

The Most Unexpected Ski Adventure in North America Might Be in Michigan

📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (936 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Skimag

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • It’s breakfast in the main yurt, so the girl from the kitchen is again standing on a chair and rubbing the dome of a snow globe.
  • Sources indicate that “Grant us snow, almighty spirits of winter,” she begins, raising the globe above her head.
  • The Midwest is a peculiar place for a ski pilgrimage.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Marcus Caston, Mt. Bohemia, Mich. (Photo: Keri Bascetta).

It’s breakfast in the main yurt, so the girl from the kitchen is again standing on a chair and rubbing the dome of a snow globe. Eyes shut tight, she shouts over the gathered skiers.

Sources indicate that “Grant us snow, almighty spirits of winter,” she begins, raising the globe above her head. “By your power, give us powder. Amen.” She is our shaman.

“Amen,” we all murmur along and mean it.

The Midwest is a peculiar place for a ski pilgrimage. But on Michigan’s isolated Keweenaw Peninsula, known as “the fin,” Mount Bohemia has no shortage of true believers. And they’re not coming for the corduroy. This expert-only backcountry resort is ungroomed, technical, and seriously steep. Signs across the mountain are clear: NO BEGINNERS ALLOWED.

While skiers scour the globe for powder, Michigan has been sitting on one of the country’s most unlikely stashes. Bohemia sees almost 300 inches annually, with no snowmaking. Here, bad weather is usually good news. Arctic air sweeping over Lake Superior’s warmer water produces storms that bury the Keweenaw. This lake-effect snow is remarkably light and dry—the kind you’d travel to Utah or Japan to find.

On paper, Bohemia’s numbers seem modest: 900 vertical feet, 585 acres, and just two lifts. Yet over 90 percent of its runs are black diamond or better, including the region’s only triple-blacks. Boho has the untamed feel of backcountry skiing, minus the skinning. Its dozen or so named territories—mostly sprawling glade districts—each have distinct temperaments.

“It can take two or three visits before guests get a feel for the mountain,” says Vern Barber, Bohemia’s general manager.

It has been revealed that I spend one morning adrift in one of the territories, Extreme Backcountry, a half-mile-wide expanse of Bohemia’s toughest terrain. Its high-angle tree runs, cliff drops, and narrow chutes kept funneling me onto unexpected lines. Supposedly, somewhere out there is a frozen waterfall drop I never managed to find. I wasn’t going to hit it. I just wanted to look.

Now I’m farther out in Middle Earth, another territory, surfing Boho’s longest runs through twisting hardwoods. Less steep, but somehow more exhausting. This is where skiers come to explore, hunting for pockets of untouched powder.

I stop at a trail marked “Helm’s Deep.” It took several attempts to find this place. Even then, it felt like an accident. The entrance is just a gap interrupting the tangle of trees—my only way down. Two clicks of my poles, and I drop in.

Dry powder explodes on my first turn. Branches rake both sleeves as I weave between trunks. Each bank hides what lies ahead. I barrel over a blind rise straight toward a stand of maples. I slash hard right and spray snow against the bark. Off balance, I slip through a drift and down a steep-sided gully.

Recent findings suggest that “You’re rowdy,” I grunt as the trees finally open. With room to breathe, I find my rhythm. Ahead lie 30 yards of untracked pillows. I point my tips and charge.

By the time I pop out at the bottom, a throng of skiers is already waiting. Not for a chairlift, but for a bus. Bohemia’s farthest backcountry runs spill onto Lac La Belle Road, where a fleet of buses collects those who make it out of the woods. Over four days, I’ve shuffled through far more bus lines than lift lines. With luck, the next shuttle will be the elusive ABBA bus, plastered with Swedish memorabilia and bumping “Dancing Queen.” Today, I’m not so lucky. I climb into a regular bus for the day’s last ride, legs shot.

As we pull into base, the parking lot is just getting started. Around a fire barrel, a haggard congregation passes bottles and joints. Skiers still in bibs boil noodles on camp stoves between RVs and Sprinter vans. This crowd feels familiar—as if every little ski hill I grew up on in Michigan sent its most adventurous regulars.

Recent findings suggest that the village itself is a jumble of yurts, stitched together by gangways. It houses bars, a hostel, and a surprisingly elaborate Nordic spa. Its 30-person hot tub was dubbed “dude stew.” But Vern claims they don’t call it that anymore.

Recent findings suggest that for a place that wears you out by noon, Boho has a strange amount of energy after dark. Inside the North Pole Bar, skiers running on beer and pasties belt out “Country Roads” with the band. The party stumbles outside to packed pools and saunas. Much later, some hooligans will hike halfway up the frontside and sled down on stolen cafeteria trays. I am one of them.

On my last morning at Mount Bohemia, a particularly nasty blizzard has blown in off Lake Superior. Word is spreading through the yurts: high winds and whiteout have shut down the lifts. The buses aren’t running.

Recent findings suggest that skiers gather at the back of the village, their helmets and jackets already covered in powder. Out of the blowing snow, a single snowcat materializes. Vern himself is behind the wheel. The wind forces him to park at an angle to wrestle the door open. Skiers cram aboard, a handful at a time, bound for the summit.

It has been revealed that I join the others in line. We laugh and curse as the snowcat is swallowed again by the whiteout. Powder is piling up around our shins. Above us, the glades are already buried. I can’t feel my toes. It’s a perfect day.

Not a bad place for a pilgrimage.

Industry News: The Burris Buck: How I Tagged the Biggest Mule Deer of All Time

💡 Key Takeaways
