  • This scene unfolded in southern Idaho on Nov.
  • Recent findings suggest that “1,200 miles from home hunting a latest bird,” wrote Kyle Stokke in an Instagram post on Nov.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Two unbelievable sights in one spot: a dog trapped in a deep fissure in the ground, and a crew lowering a man into that fissure to save her.

This scene unfolded in southern Idaho on Nov. 8. After a traveling bird hunter’s pointer fell some 60-feet into a basalt crack while hunting wild birds, he had to call in a professional rescue team for help.

Recent findings suggest that “1,200 miles from home hunting a latest bird,” wrote Kyle Stokke in an Instagram post on Nov. 12. “[I] was naively unaware of the unique dangers in these new environments.”.

A post shared by Kyle Stokke (@kyle.stokke).

Stokke posted a four-minute rescue video last week. Earlier posts show him hunting upland birds with two dogs: a German shorthaired pointer and a Labrador retriever. The trio camped while traveling 1,200 miles cross-country from the Midwest to Idaho. Trouble started when the GSP, Esther, fell into a deep fissure.

It has been revealed that “Good gracious!” an unseen rescuer says in the video. “She is down there a freaking long ways.”.

According to recent reports, esther fell at least 60 feet. The fissure went deeper than that, but she landed on a ledge above the true bottom. In the video, you can hear her whines echo up the crack as Stokke, filming from above, reassures her.

In a recent development, “It’s okay Esther,” he says. “You’re a good girl.”.

In a recent development, magic Valley Paramedics has a dedicated unit called the Special Operations Rescue Team. SORT is a highly trained, 20-person volunteer crew specializing in low- and high-angle rope rescues.

“The biggest challenge was finding exactly where she was,” Chad Smith, SORT team leader, tells Outdoor Life. “Sound travels differently in the canyon. You could hear her so she seemed close, but she wasn’t. How sound travels in there is really deceiving. It threw us off a little bit.”.

In a recent development, SORT averages 20 rescues a year in Twin Falls and Jerome counties. In Smith’s 15 years with SORT, the team has rescued four dogs from fissures, including another bird dog stuck in a similar crack during a previous hunting season. Esther’s rescue happened to fall on the first day of SORT’s semiannual, three-day training exercises.

“The rescue truck is pulled out and everyone is practicing anchors when the supervisor asks if we want to rescue a dog,” reads a post by the organization. “Who can say no to a dog? Training shifts gears real quick.”.

The video shows the team straddling a 2-foot-wide black void hidden in flat sagebrush country.

In a recent development, “Wow! I can see her,” says someone offscreen as one rescuer, Trevor Churchman, is slowly lowered into the tight divide on a harness, ropes, and straps rigged to a large tripod set over the opening.

“Tell Kyle she’s doing good,” says Churchman. “She’s walking around and she’s wagging her tail.”.

A few minutes later, both man and dog are hoisted out of the crack, and Esther, apparently unharmed, is handed to Stokke. He’s visibly shaking in the video and sounds emotional, but manages a “thank you” for the crew and a “whoa” to keep Esther steady, since everyone is standing near the edge.

In a recent development, “Okay guys, remember there’s an edge there,” a rescuer says. “We don’t have a lot of you guys on ropes.”.

The two-hour rescue took place in terrain shaped by prehistoric volcanic activity. Tunnels, lava tubes, cliffs, caves, and crevices run through much of the area’s undeveloped public land. (If that’s hard to picture, think of the better-known volcanic landscape at Craters of the Moon National Monument and Preserve, 90 miles north of Twin Falls.).

Water filters through the porous basalt rock formations, creating seeps, springs, and waterfalls that feed the Snake River, which has carved a deep canyon that’s home to the dramatic spray of Shoshone Falls.

Recent findings suggest that “When hiking around the canyon, cracks in the rock can be quite deep,” the rescue team warns. “This one was deeper than 45 feet. We could not see the bottom, and they can fill with tumbleweeds making them look like level ground. So watch your step.”.

It’s rough, remote country that attracts extreme adventurers like BASE jumpers. And it can surprise even experienced bird hunters, such as Stokke, who assume they’re hunting in relatively flat country.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that we may earn revenue from the products available on this page and participate in affiliate programs. Learn More ›.

In a recent development, simms has long been an industry staple for fishing apparel, most notably waders and outerwear. I’ve tested and reviewed many Simms products, including its Challenger lineup of rain gear. While that gear has always performed well, its target market is clear: dedicated recreational anglers. I’ve never bothered to test how Simms outerwear handles the trials and tribulations of everyday use by commercial deckhands or saltwater captains because, frankly, why would I? That’s not the audience it’s intended for, and I wouldn’t expect rain gear designed for landlocked fly anglers to hold up for someone used to hauling crab traps in salt spray and freezing rain all day.

Enter Simms’ new Rip Line Pro series of rain gear, the manufacturer’s first attempt at a truly hardcore jacket and bibs designed specifically for watermen. The Rip Line Pro series forgoes much of the aesthetic and, shall we say, fanciness of Simms’ standard recreation-oriented rain gear in favor of pure, rugged functionality. From the moment you see the Rip Line Pro jacket and bibs, it’s clear they aren’t meant for a hike down to your favorite blue-ribbon trout stream. Pick them up and feel them in hand, and that point is driven home. This is not casual rain gear, and it doesn’t sacrifice performance for looks. It’s designed for abuse of the highest order, the kind dished out by Mother Nature on the open sea.

So, how does it handle that? The look and feel right out of the box make a promise, but does the Rip Line Pro series deliver? To find out, I spent a few weeks putting this gear through the wringer in one of the best testing grounds I could think of: the Chesapeake Bay in late fall and early winter. Read on to see how the Rip Line Pro performed.

When it comes to testing gear, sometimes the timing doesn’t line up. Given the monthslong drought in the Mid-Atlantic leading up to my test, I was worried that might be the case here. As it turned out, that worry was misplaced. Exactly one day after the Rip Line Pro gear arrived, the forecast called for an epic deluge paired with extreme wind and storms. It was the perfect blend of miserable fishing conditions for testing rain gear. Lucky me.

Recent findings suggest that the forecast proved accurate, and the weather was extreme, almost to a fault. I spent the first few hours of the morning sheltering from lightning under a dockhouse on the water. The Rip Line Pro gear will protect you from a lot, but I don’t think “lightning strike” is on the list. Thankfully, the electrical portion of the storm passed, and I had the rest of the day to fish in a constant downpour and gusting wind.

Industry observers note that after a few hours of fishing from a kayak in the rain and getting sprayed with salt water, the first thing I checked was the areas where most rain gear performs worst: the wrists, neck, and ankles. These are typically the hardest spots to protect because they offer a direct path for water to get beneath the rain gear, and they still need to allow some comfort and range of motion. The Rip Line Pro did an outstanding job of keeping moisture out of all three. The wrists and forearms were the most impressive. They feature an extended 1-millimeter neoprene cuff beneath the outer layer that lets this jacket perform almost like a full dry top. Not only does it keep rain out, but the neoprene cuff creates a seal that kept water from flowing down the sleeve even when my arm was fully submerged. I was equally impressed by the neck. While it doesn’t have the full neoprene seal of the sleeves, the hood design and zipper-and-Velcro combination created an impressively form-fitting seal that kept water from dripping down my back or chest. Finally, the ankle cuffs on the bibs did an excellent job of keeping spray and rainwater away from my feet. I was wearing ankle-height deck boots, and the leg cuffs paired perfectly with them to create an angled seal where no water could enter.

According to recent reports, next, I inspected the storage, namely the various dry pockets on both the jacket and bibs. Each has a well-designed, easily accessible exterior pocket sealed by a watertight zipper and tucked beneath a Velcro storm flap for extra protection. Exterior pockets on rain gear are always a gamble, but accessible waterproof storage is crucial. The pockets on the Rip Line Pro jacket and bibs performed exceptionally well, even after I opened and closed them many times throughout the day to reach various items. Nothing seeped through the pockets to the interior of the suit, and the pockets kept everything inside them dry and functional.

In a recent development, dry storage and adjustable cuffs matter, but ultimately the most important job of rain gear is keeping you dry all day long. While I was impressed with how well the Rip Line Pro kept water out of various areas throughout the day, the real test would be how wet and cold I got after fishing in rain and wind for upward of 12 hours.

The answer? Not very. For me, the most impressive part of this gear is the overall protection it offered from the elements. After we returned to the boat ramp and loaded our gear, it was time to strip off the rain suit and inspect the damage. No matter how dry you think you are, a bit of unforeseen moisture usually gets through any rain gear after a long day. Apart from a few wet spots where my shirt had been exposed during the day, I was basically bone-dry. The jacket and bibs also did a great job of blocking wind chill. I had underestimated how well that was working during the day, but looking back, I realized how much the gear kept the wind from affecting my comfort. Not that I needed confirmation, but watching my fishing partners shiver miserably and wring out sopping undershirts provided a sense of warm relief, both physically and emotionally.

Protection from the elements, plain and simple. I’ve worn many bibs and rain jackets over the years, some designed for comfort and others for function. The Rip Line Pro does the best job I’ve found of marrying the two, though function is still clearly the priority.

Once you’re fully suited up, this rain gear makes you feel practically invincible, protected by an impenetrable shell of armor. I’m not saying it’s bulletproof, but I could feel an unrealistic sense of confidence building while I wore it. The materials not only kept me bone-dry through a full day of torrential rain but also provided exceptional wind protection during gusts upward of 30 knots. When it comes to protection from extreme water and wind, the Rip Line Pro series is as good as it gets.

According to recent reports, with extreme weather protection as the focus, it’s easy to understand why some other features take a back seat. That noted, there are still a few areas I’d like to see Simms improve.

The most noticeable is the lack of mobility. The four-layer construction and fully waterproof material make this gear weatherproof, but they also make it rather cumbersome. Simms added articulation points and adjustable areas where possible, but there’s still room for improvement. At times, I felt a bit like a piece of vacuum-sealed meat, or a video game character bolted into a mech suit. Yes, I felt invincible, but I also had a harder time than I care to admit squatting to grab a sandwich from the cooler.

Insulation is another area that could be better. The Rip Line Pro gear does an incredible job of protecting you from water and wind, but it doesn’t have much interior insulation for true winter use. That’s easy to offset by layering proper cold-weather clothing underneath, but I could see a built-in cold-weather liner helping. Perhaps Simms will release a “winter” edition of the Rip Line Pro in the future with a wool liner or something similar.

The Rip Line Pro series of rain gear is not for everyone. In fact, I would say the target market for this gear is fairly narrow. Most casual anglers and outdoor enthusiasts can get by with less extreme, less expensive rain gear and never have an concern. While this gear is fantastic at keeping you dry, I could see it being overkill for an after-work outing during a light summer shower.

However, what the Rip Line Pro series is designed to do, it does extremely well, and the people who need this type of gear will appreciate it. The Rip Line Pro series is built for serious anglers and people who spend as much time on the water as on dry land. As with any gear in the fishing space, the more purpose-built something becomes, the less universal appeal it tends to have. That said, if you fish as much as I do, serious rain gear becomes less a matter of convenience and more a matter of necessity. The Rip Line Pro jacket and bibs offer the type of performance and functionality I value, and I’m sure many other anglers, deckhands, and charter captains who try them will agree.

#67855. Historic Drought Looms Over Arkansas Duck Opener. What Few Ducks Show Up Face Heavy Pressure

Historic Drought Looms Over Arkansas Duck Opener. What Few Ducks Show Up Face Heavy Pressure

📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1340 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Outdoorlife

⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Sources indicate that if you asked any serious waterfowl hunter to name their dream duck-hunting destinations, Arkansas would be at the top of nearly every list.
  • Recent findings suggest that yet in 2026, Arkansas’ waterfowl season is suddenly looking bleak.
  • For 14 months Arkansas has been without any serious rainfall, leaving rich croplands and, more importantly for ducks, wetlands, drier than they’ve been in decades.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that if you asked any serious waterfowl hunter to name their dream duck-hunting destinations, Arkansas would be at the top of nearly every list. Its classic flooded hardwoods and bayous along with the state’s rich rice and grain fields, lure massive flights of puddle ducks and geese to its hallowed waters every year. This has made Arkansas stand out above other southern states as the beating heart of the Mississippi Flyway.

Recent findings suggest that yet in 2026, Arkansas’ waterfowl season is suddenly looking bleak. A historic drought has many duck hunters worried ahead of the Nov. 21 opener, as the serious lack of water could bring duck hunting to a standstill. Duck hunters on both public and private land may have some serious decisions to make to safeguard ducks and future duck seasons.

For 14 months Arkansas has been without any serious rainfall, leaving rich croplands and, more importantly for ducks, wetlands, drier than they’ve been in decades. Every corner of the state is under a severe drought status, with some areas being more than 20 inches behind in cumulative rainfall totals.

To put the drought in perspective, this is slated to be the state’s third-driest October through January since record keeping began in 1895.

This leaves the Arkansas Game and Fish Commission with very little water to spare, to the point where the agency expects it will only be able to flood around 40 of its more than 70 moist-soil public-land hunting units.

Industry observers note that “In my 50 years of duck hunting in Arkansas, I don’t remember it ever being as dry as this,” notes Brent Birch, founder of Arkansas’ Greenhead magazine. “It’s been this way all summer and well into the fall. And even with the prospects of a Super El Niño, we have nothing the forecast that says it’s going to resolve anytime soon.”.

Without an incredible amount of rainfall in a short amount of time, Birch and other waterfowlers around the state are worried not only about not having places to hunt, but that the ducks may not even show up.

“So far, we are seeing a few groups of gadwalls, pintails, and other early migrating ducks but not in anything close to their usual numbers,” Birch says. “And when it comes to incoming mallards, you can pretty much forget it. It’s just too dry for them. The fact is the closer it gets to 2027 under these conditions, the worse the entire duck season is going to be. And if we don’t start getting some wet weather soon to push ducks down here, we’re looking at a poor outlook for the entire season.”.

It has been revealed that the reason that Arkansas waterfowl hunting is so good is that it lies at the north end of the historic feeding grounds for ducks and geese in the Mississippi Flyway. Once the cold sets in around their spring and summer breeding grounds in Canada, the birds come south to binge on Arkansas’ rich wetlands throughout the winter. However, with the current drought, the fear is that the incoming ducks will be forced to fly elsewhere.

“Ducks coming south to Arkansas aren’t like ducks in northern states,” says Ducks Unlimited Arkansas regional biologist Jake Spears, who lives in Jonesboro. “Northern birds are more apt to feed in dry fields so long as they have a body of water to roost on nearby. However, in the Southern U.S., they stop feeding in fields and primarily feed in water. They look for things like water plants and waste grains in flooded fields, which Arkansas currently just doesn’t have.”.

Spears worries that many ducks are going to fly to Arkansas and then be forced to turn northward again or keep driving south.

“The ducks need food so they may go to Louisiana, or Kansas, or Missouri — wherever they can find that food source,” says Spears. “Which is going to leave both public-land duck hunters and even most hunting clubs just completely out of luck.”.

Sources indicate that private-land duck-hunting clubs are a popular option for many Arkansas hunters and visiting nonresidents, as even during droughts, most clubs can pump water to create duck habitat and attract birds. The 2026 drought has been so bad, however, that many clubs won’t even have the water to pump.

Sources indicate that this is especially troubling to some public-land waterfowl hunters, who worry that the private hunting clubs that can still pump water may end up attracting what few ducks do make it to Arkansas. This could result in a season that benefits the haves over the have-nots.

It has been revealed that “I think hunting clubs are the only thing that’s going to make Arkansas appealing for ducks right now,” Spears says. “Most of the smaller rivers, sloughs, and backwaters we have on public land can be walked across in flip-flops right now. So the clubs that have the option to flood fields and create habitat are where the birds are going to be. But with the water table so low, clubs with the ability to pump will be few and far between, so any ducks that do show up during the season are going to have to be babied quite a bit.”.

Sources indicate that the fact is that if the drought continues in Arkansas, duck hunters on both public and private land alike are going to have to weigh their priorities. Drought conditions are going to be tough on ducks that migrate through Arkansas, and hunting pressure will make surviving the migration harder even for birds that aren’t killed.

This leaves duck hunters with a choice to make.

It has been revealed that “It’s going to come down to responsible management on all sides because if we want to maintain the ducks we have, we have to be careful with them,” Birch says. “There are several components to management. It’s not just hunting and the noise of guns, we must be careful disturbing the ducks in any capacity. Your vehicle is an matter because you’re going to bump ducks going in and out of your hunting area, and you’re going to have to be real careful with how many days you hunt and how many hours you hunt in a day, because you’re going to have to let the birds rest.”.

With Arkansas’ duck season lasting a total of 51 days with two relatively short splits, hunters looking to limit out consistently are going to be putting serious pressure on what will already be a limited resource.

So instead of hunting hard, both Birch and Spears recommend self-imposed bag limits and time on the water so that the resource can continue to both be conserved and shared.

Industry observers note that “My suggestion to any duck hunter in Arkansas is that if you have ducks on your property, take care of them,” notes Spears. “With the limited resources, they aren’t going to be able to handle a lot of pressure. You’re going to have to limit how much you hunt and how many birds you shoot, and not be afraid to cut your hunt short. Get a few birds and then leave so the ducks can get back to the water to feed.”.

Read Next: Has Hot Cropping Ruined Duck Hunting? Here’s What the Data and Biologists Say About How Flooded Corn Affects Waterfowl Migration.

While there is hope that conditions will change, the fact is that the whole of Arkansas’ 2026 duck season may be a nonstarter for many hunters. That short-term pain, however, could help future duck seasons look a little brighter. Spears and Birch are hopeful for a future where water and the waterfowl will eventually return, filling the skies and waterways like flowing veins and once again making Arkansas the beating heart of the Mississippi Flyway itself.

“We need to be good stewards of the resource,” urges Spears. “Hunters should do everything they can to keep [ducks] around and not shoot them off what water we do have.”.

As a hunter and outdoorswoman, I have been wearing heated socks for years. Just like my trusty heated vest, they have kept me in the field for longer, enjoying the activities I love, whether that’s tracking a whitetail or hiking with my kids. Socks are often an afterthought in the world of outdoor gear. However, they’re actually one of the most important pieces. After all, our feet play an essential role in body temperature regulation. Warm feet allow proper blood flow, moving heat to other parts of your body. When you get cold, it can make for a miserable outdoor experience—which is where heated socks come into play.

While there are plenty of warm socks out there, heated socks take cozy to the next level, with rechargeable batteries powering them up. To find the warmest pairs, we tested the best heated socks for both men and women through hours of hunting, camping, and just spending time outside.

In a recent development, these Gerbing heated socks are unlike others in that they warm up both the bottom and top of your feet via a heated microwire. My husband recently wore them on a Missouri hunt and said the only thing that kept him out there were these heated socks. With a generous battery life of up to seven hours, we never had to worry about them losing charge out in the woods and they provided more than enough warmth. Designed for comfort and performance with a moisture-wicking wool blend, these socks are ready for the elements.

The sizing for these socks is unisex. We reviewed the L/XL, which fit true to size for a men’s size 10.5 wide. The heat panel runs the entire length of the bottom of the foot, providing warmth across your whole foot. If you have worn heated socks before, you know the wire can be annoying and uncomfortable. Fortunately, Gerbing used a microwire in its design for maximum comfort—no wire digging into your skin.

These are the most expensive heated socks we reviewed; however, the quality and performance are well worth the price. Plus, the heating elements are backed by Gerbing’s lifetime warranty, so you have peace of mind.

Savior Heat heated socks use powerful 7.4V 2200mah rechargeable batteries to maximize warmth for hours on end. With three available heat settings, they can reach temperatures of up to 140 degrees. We like that they have a high over-the-calf design with a no-slip elastic band that keeps them securely in place. The socks are made with breathable CoolMax technology that prevents your feet from getting sweaty once they’re warm. Available in four color options, the socks come in unisex sizes to fit a range of foot shapes and sizes.

Recent findings suggest that the large batteries are one of the biggest highlights of these socks. They provide a lot of power and up to seven hours of high heat on one charge. You can charge them simultaneously, and in just a few hours, they’re fully loaded and ready to go. However, they can also be a negative. Because of their size, they sometimes struggle to stay in place and can bunch up in the socks. Savior is also a good choice for the budget-conscious shopper—you can get a pair for under $80. Plus, Savior offers a 30-day money back guarantee or a free replacement should you be unhappy with your socks.

If you’re looking for the best heated socks for hunting, look no further than this pair from Snow Deer. The socks—which are available in a range of sizes and colors—come with a 7.4V battery that offers three heat settings that you can customize for as much or as little warmth as you’d like. They’re crafted from a CoolMax fabric blend that’s cozy without being stifling. Your feet will actually be able to breathe in these babies, which is vital when you’re wearing your hunting boots for hours and hours.

The innovative heating system eliminates the feeling of wires, ensuring a seamless design and making these Snow Deer heated socks more comfortable than other options out there. They’re user-friendly, with easy temperature adjustments and charging. While they primarily heat around the toes, the socks work well in tandem with a good pair of insulated hunting boots for cold weather to help you stay outside for longer.

According to recent reports, actionHeat is well-known for making outstanding heated gear, and these rechargeable heated socks are no exception. Powered by an ActionHeat 3.74V battery along with FAR infrared heating and heat-reflective technology, they provide warmth for more than seven hours of use on a single charge. The breathability factor makes these socks ideal for outdoor activities like hiking or winter sports like skiing or snowshoeing.

Recent findings suggest that the heating element is located at the bottom part of the foot, providing 70 percent more coverage than Ororo’s previous model. FieldSheer heated socks come in both men’s and women’s sizes and designs. They have a compression-like feel with ample arch support to prevent foot pain. In terms of comfort, I also really liked the contoured battery, which allowed the battery to fit snugly against my calf.

In a recent development, these Fieldsheer socks are controlled via a mobile app. There, I was able to adjust the heat setting and monitor the battery life. What’s really nice is that you can control each sock separately. Plus, you can even connect other heated gear—like heated vests or heated gloves—to the same profile. I personally really appreciated the battery life percentage monitoring capability. Even though the battery is the smallest out of all the ones we reviewed, it still lasts up to 10 hours on the lowest heat setting.

It has been revealed that with the high percentage of merino wool, these socks have a solid heat retention rating. However, they offer less coverage than others on our list—the heated area only covers from the upper part of your sole up to your toes.

Recent findings suggest that through years of wearing heated socks, I have narrowed down exactly what makes a quality pair. The style and comfort may fluctuate depending on the brand, but the factors below should apply to all. Of course, you’ll also want to take into consideration your own needs to make sure they’re met.

After handpicking which heated socks to include in our review process, here’s how I evaluated each pair during testing and research:.

According to recent reports, when dealing with anything that depends on battery power, the type of battery is important. You don’t want to invest in a pricey heated sock just for the battery to die. Rechargeable batteries are cost-effective and convenient. They are also more environmentally friendly, reducing the excess of disposable batteries in landfills.

However, rechargeable batteries have limited charging cycles and will require replacement. Batteries such as lithium-ion may provide more stable and reliable performance and minimize charging times.

In a recent development, socks normally come in grouped sizing; they are “one size fits most.” Since most heated socks for men and women come up over the calf, factor your calf size into your size choice. Most of these socks are unisex, so if you have a need women’s size or a wide option, take that into consideration as you weigh your pros and cons. Always refer to the socks’ size chart to determine the best fit for your feet.

In a recent development, durability is always high on my consideration list. When making a gear investment, you want something that is going to last but also that won’t break the bank. Consider the materials used. Wool, for instance, has a high heat retention rating and will last through seasons of use.

In a recent development, also think about frequency of wear. What is your intended use? An avid outdoor enthusiast who plans to wear their heated socks almost daily will require a more durable option than someone who will just wear them a handful of times for weekend adventures.

Sources indicate that yes, heated socks are a great investment. I’ve worn them for years and they’re a game-changer. Of course, it also depends on your specific needs and intended use.

Recent findings suggest that the lifespan of your heated socks will vary depending on use and base materials. Follow the manufacturer’s instructions for washing and drying and avoid using harsh detergents to help them last longer. As for battery life, rechargeable batteries will slow down over time and start losing their charging power. Fortunately, if the sock itself is still holding up well, you can just purchase a new replacement battery to remedy that matter.

Industry observers note that yes, each pair of electrical socks comes with a mesh laundry bag. Remove the batteries, cover the plug (if applicable), and clip to secure the pocket. Wash on delicate and hang to dry. That mentioned, be sure to check the care instructions for your specific socks before washing.

In a recent development, heated socks are a prime example of how advanced technology for outdoor gear has become. When choosing the best heated socks for you, weigh the performance of the batteries and the durability of the material with how comfortable the socks are. You want to get the most out of your footwear, so we recommend investing in a pair that will keep you doing the outdoor activities you love for longer, like the Gerbing Ultimate or the Snow Deer heated socks. Your feet will be happy, and so will you.

Stephanie Case Just Ran 100 Miles in Antarctica. She Doesn’t Even Like the Cold.

⏱️ ~8 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • In 2025, a photo of Stephanie Case breastfeeding her infant daughter, Pepper, at an aid station during a 100K ultra in Northern Wales went viral, and the human rights lawyer and ultrarunner became the face of postpartum badassery.
  • Now, she’s officially the first woman to run 100 miles in Antarctica.
  • According to recent reports, “The whole idea for this race came after I had my daughter and people were asking me if I was going to start to settle down,” Case, 44, shared with Trail Runner from her home in Chamonix, France.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In 2025, a photo of Stephanie Case breastfeeding her infant daughter, Pepper, at an aid station during a 100K ultra in Northern Wales went viral, and the human rights lawyer and ultrarunner became the face of postpartum badassery.

Now, she’s officially the first woman to run 100 miles in Antarctica. Case took on the November 8 challenge in part to prove that the things she did before becoming a mom weren’t behind her. If anything, she could come back and do them even better.

According to recent reports, “The whole idea for this race came after I had my daughter and people were asking me if I was going to start to settle down,” Case, 44, shared with Trail Runner from her home in Chamonix, France. “They were criticizing me after I came back for my first race postpartum, telling me that I was selfish to be taking that time to train. So I wanted to go out and really prove to myself and remind myself that I could keep doing big things.”.

Recent findings suggest that actually, major is an understatement. Of the eight runners who started the Antarctic Ice Ultra 100 miler on Union Glacier, Case was one of four finishers, and second overall. Her finishing time of 17 hours, 31 minutes and 39 seconds, a clip of 10:31 per mile, smashed the former overall course record by five hours. Only Yusheng Ni, a top ultrarunner from China with experience racing in Antarctica, ran faster in a new best-ever mark of 17:02:24.

Here’s the kicker: Case doesn’t even like running in the cold.

In a recent development, there’s cold, and then there’s Antarctica cold. The race started at 1 a.m. under a 24-hour sun, with temperatures as low as minus 35 degrees Fahrenheit—roughly 35 degrees colder than a typical kitchen freezer. And with fierce polar winds, no exposed skin is safe.

Industry observers note that “I’m someone who doesn’t like when the house goes below room temperature. My partner and I are constantly having a fight about where we set the thermostat,” Case shared. “So this was going to be a substantial challenge for me. I knew that I wasn’t going to love it. But I’m Canadian. There’s no bad weather, there’s just bad clothing, they say.”.

In a recent development, finding the right gear was one of the biggest priorities in Case’s preparation. She reached out to other runners who had completed the Antarctic 100-miler in previous years to glean their insight. One offered an unexpected tip: Apply sunscreen inside of her nostrils, since the sun reflecting off the snow can burn there, too.

She also worked with The North Face, one of her sponsors, to design a custom shoe specifically for the conditions. Breathability was key: She didn’t want moisture trapped inside the shoe, and the sole needed to remain flexible in extreme temperatures. There was also the matter of laces. Frozen laces—or having to tie them with mittens on—were not an option. The solution was a BOA closure system, which let her tighten the shoes by turning a dial. The design also included an integrated, insulated but breathable gaiter and removable spikes she could screw into the soles if conditions got icy.

It has been revealed that the setup worked better than she could have hoped. Case wore two pairs of socks—a thin liner underneath a wool pair—and didn’t change them once during the entire race.

“I just set it and left it,” she noted. “And it was one of the things I was most stressed about, because with hands, you can put on more gloves. You can have hand warmers. But toe warmers don’t work when you’re running. They can’t fit in the shoe. And I knew if my toes were cold, I was just going to be screwed. And they were toasty the whole time.”.

As for the rest of her clothing, Case had to consider another challenge: her sweat rate.

“I’m a heavy sweater. Even in just mild cold temperatures, I sweat a liter an hour, and in warm temperatures up to two liters,” she said. “So I knew that I would be at a pretty significant disadvantage, because when you sweat, your gear gets wet and then you’re screwed.”.

Her strategy was to dress as lightly as possible through her core while keeping her hands, feet and face warm and protected. In the coldest stretches, she wore winter tights under wind pants, along with a thin base layer, a midlayer, and a shell on top. At some points, she stripped down to a thin base layer and shell.

“As long as I kept moving, I was fine,” she remarked. “But I wouldn’t be able to kind of stop and walk if something went wrong.”.

Sources indicate that she never quite felt warm, and some exposed skin on her face did get frostbitten. But she managed to find moments of equilibrium.

“I felt comfortable at times. And then other times I feel like I was just constantly on the edge,” she noted. “I wasn’t freezing, but I was cold. But as long as my feet were OK and my hands were OK, then I was fine to keep moving.”.

The temperature wasn’t the only feature of Antarctica that concerned Case. She describes herself as a “mountain goat.” Living in Chamonix, she’s accustomed to steep trails and vert—not the flat, repetitive terrain of Antarctica’s 38-loop course.

Sources indicate that working with her coach, Meghan Roche, she shifted her training toward flatter ground and faster running. The change paid off: during her workouts, Case set personal records at several distances, from the 10K through the marathon.

In a recent development, “I had a love-hate relationship with it,” she said of the training. “But the funny thing was that every time I had a training session, I was getting PRs, because I just don’t run on flat ground.”.

She also tested her gear in a cryotherapy chamber during a trip to Geneva, Switzerland, spending 20 minutes in temperatures that gradually warmed from minus 148°F to minus 22°F. The goal wasn’t so much to acclimate as to understand what the cold would feel like and test her logistics. The session made her rethink her fueling plan: Pulling off gloves, unzipping a shell, and drinking from a flask in those conditions would be too cumbersome.

Instead, her camera operator doubled as her crew, handing her a SIS gel and flask every loop. While most competitors visited the aid tent every lap or two, Case aimed to go ten loops—roughly a marathon—between stops. She had to cut the first stretch short when her balaclava froze into a solid block of ice, but after that she managed three 10-loop stints.

The aid station offered some reprieve, with ramen noodles, mashed potatoes, shots of maple syrup, and Rice Krispies treats, but even small tasks there got complicated. Taking her gloves off for just 30 seconds to go to the bathroom could mean waiting 20 minutes for her hands to warm up again.

“There was not a single minute during this race when I kind of just relaxed and allowed myself to switch off,” she states. “In any other 100, I can usually just kind of push past [discomfort], but there, one tiny mistake could end the race for me.”.

Industry observers note that as Case recovers at home with collagen mask treatments to heal her frostbitten cheeks and nose, her next challenge is already on the calendar: becoming the first woman to complete the Montane Arctic Spine, a 500-kilometer race in February. This time, she’ll be on Nordic skis, pulling a sled and traveling solo, with checkpoints as far as 50 miles apart. She’ll need to melt her own snow, pitch her own tent, and carry out the journey without a crew.

She hopes Antarctica has prepared her for an even harder task.

“Sometimes the way to get through a really scary thing is to line up an even scarier thing afterwards,” she remarked.

It has been revealed that beyond that, Case is developing a project called “94 Degrees,” a film that will show her running the gamut of conditions from minus 40 degrees Celsius in the Arctic to 54 degrees Celsius at Badwater in California’s Death Valley, a 94-degree Celsius spread. (She’s qualified for Badwater but still needs to apply for an invitation, so that part isn’t yet confirmed.).

Industry observers note that and in the meantime, she’ll continue her work for the U.N. while serving as the President of Free to Run, a non-profit organization that uses sport to empower women and girls in conflict-affected areas. And she’ll soak up all the cuddles she can with Pepper, now 2, while sharing stories of that one time she ran 100 miles in Antarctica. It’s a story that almost sounds like a fairy tale.

“I actually brought one of her toys, a penguin rubber ducky, with me on the trip, just as a reminder of her,” Case stated. “And then this penguin came out on the course and actually ran alongside me for part of it. I’ve been showing her photos and videos … but still … it’s all kind of unbelievable.”.

#67852. Old-School Whitetail Wisdom for Filling Your Tag After Opening Day

Old-School Whitetail Wisdom for Filling Your Tag After Opening Day

📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 16 min read (3245 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Outdoorlife

⏱️ ~16 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • These days, a buck can’t grow to trophy proportions on hard-hunted public lands by folding up under the pressure exerted by the opening-day crush of hunters.
  • Industry observers note that some substantial bucks live in locations that allow them to avoid the opening weekend crowd by slipping into the sanctuary offered by state parks, game refuges or private posted land.
  • But the whitetail is a homebody at heart, and he is most comfortable on his loosely defined home turf.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

These days, a buck can’t grow to trophy proportions on hard-hunted public lands by folding up under the pressure exerted by the opening-day crush of hunters. A whitetail lives the 3½ years necessary to grow a bragging set of antlers by learning to cope with the annual influx of hunters during the season’s first days. Every opening day that the buck survives increases his chance of surviving the ensuing openers, as well.

Industry observers note that some substantial bucks live in locations that allow them to avoid the opening weekend crowd by slipping into the sanctuary offered by state parks, game refuges or private posted land. Others crawl into the most inaccessible and gosh-awful cover their “territory” has to offer — the kind of place hunters walk around, rather than through — and stay there until the crowds leave. And on more than one occasion, I have found a bruiser buck in a tiny, secluded patch of isolated cover — the kind of place most hunters never think to look in.

But the whitetail is a homebody at heart, and he is most comfortable on his loosely defined home turf. You can bet that once the steady crack of opening day rifles slackens to only an occasional pop, those big bucks will be right back to business as usual. And that is the precise reason why your best chance for bagging a wall-hanger occurs after the opening day madness has subsided.

Where you begin your search for that after-the-opener buck hinges upon one factor: the rut. Many states plan their firearms seasons to coincide with the rut, offering their hunters every opportunity to harvest the surplus bucks. Other states, bound in tradition, open the season after the main rut has ended. If you are planning to travel out of your home state to hunt whitetails, it makes sense to hunt a state where the season coincides with the rut, all other criteria being equal.

A mature whitetail buck is a different character during the rut than he is after it. A buck’s sole purpose at that time is to procreate, and this he does with obvious enthusiasm and the stamina of a teenager. There are stories abounding in every deer camp in the country of the crazy antics performed by bucks under the spell of the “rutting moon,” such as lovesick bucks strolling across open fields in broad daylight. Others tell tales of bucks putting their noses to does’ tracks and following those tracks, even after being shot at and missed several times. Rut-crazed bucks, while under the influence of a powerful rush of hormones, have even been known to either pick fights with or attempt to mate with assorted farm livestock.

Industry observers note that so rampant are the stories that I’m afraid there exists a whole contingent of deer hunters laboring under the false assumption that all a hunter needs do to down one of these crazy buggers is to walk into the woods, lean up against a stump and wait for one of the poor, sex-addled dummies to saunter on by. Although such tactics work just often enough to keep the myth perpetuated, plenty of hunters have been sitting against stumps for more unsuccessful years than they will probably admit, and they’re still waiting for a buck to wander by.

According to recent reports, hunting whitetails during the rut and after the opening weekend of the season isn’t easy. You must employ all of the skill and woods savvy you have. Any breaks you receive because of a buck’s overactive glands should be considered a bonus.

It has been revealed that after the opener, I refine my hunting strategy for big bucks by determining what stage the rut is in. This is key because the stage of the rut will determine where I concentrate most of my midweek hunting efforts.

Sources indicate that the whitetail buck is ready to breed long before the first doe enters estrus. During this period, the buck runs off excess energy by beating up saplings, sparring with bushes and, on occasion, duking it out with other bucks. In the process of making rubs on bushes and trees, the buck deposits scents that tell the rest of the whitetail community who was there.

In a recent development, scrapes begin to show up in increasing numbers as the level of testosterone builds in the buck’s system. The buck paws out scrapes and leaves his scent both in the bare earth of the scrapes and on overhanging branches above the scrapes. Again, this is a means of communicating with other whitetails. The message to does is that the buck is now standing at stud, and it tells other bucks that they had best move along if they know what’s good for them.

In a recent development, A buck will paw out most of his scrapes in areas where they are most likely to be seen or smelled by does. Openings in woods, old logging roads and the edges of woodlots are common places to encounter scrapes. A buck may make a dozen or more scrapes, and he’ll check some of them daily, making sure they are free of debris and liberally doused with musk/urine. These are the scrapes to hunt over.

However, once the does begin cycling into heat, the dominant bucks that handle the bulk of the breeding chores are often so busy accompanying, tracking and servicing does that they neither have the time nor the need to freshen their scrapes. But if you find a string of scrapes that have not been freshened for several days, it doesn’t necessarily mean that the rut is over or that the buck that made the scrapes is hanging from someone else’s game pole. It may mean that the buck is out doing his job.

It has been revealed that the best way to determine what stage the rut is in is to spend a day or two in the woods prior to the hunt. If fresh scrapes abound, you will be hunting the pre-coital period, and a stand near a scrape line is going to be hard to beat. If, on the other hand, you find that more than half of the scrapes are old and abandoned, it’s a good bet that the big bucks are out taking care of the does, while the lesser bucks are still hanging around their scrapes, waiting.

In a recent development, if you just don’t have time to get into the woods prior to the season, you can get a good idea about the stage of the rut by speaking with area game managers, milk haulers, rural school bus drivers, postal carriers, loggers, trappers, farmers, grouse hunters, bowhunters or others who spend most of their time in deer country. If the bucks are chasing the does, chances are these people will have observed some of the activity.

Why all of the fuss over determining what stage the rut is in? Because it makes a massive difference when you have to decide how you want to hunt after the opening weekend of the season.

When the season begins, if the actual breeding season has not yet begun but bucks are busy pawing out new scrapes and freshening old ones, chances are the bucks will curtail this activity during the high-pressure days at the beginning of the season, resuming their rounds once the hunters thin out. I like to have at least a half-dozen scrape lines pinpointed prior to the opener, and I check them after the opening weekend for any sign of activity. I then concentrate my hunting efforts near the “hottest” scrapes.

If your pre-season scouting and snooping indicates that the actual breeding season is in progress, then hunting over scrapes may not be your best option for tagging a really good buck. Remember, it is often the significant, dominant bucks in the area that handle the bulk of the breeding chores. Even in an area with an excellent buck-to-doe ratio, a breeding buck can be kept so busy that he has little time or need to tend his scrapes. Often, a buck will spend 24 hours with the same doe, breeding her several times before her cycle ends. At this time, it is the doe, not the buck, that determines where the pair will travel. Though I would not totally rule out hunting in the vicinity of inactive scrapes at this stage of the rut, there are other options that I’ve found give me a better chance at tagging a big buck.

Recent findings suggest that one of my favorite methods during this period is to concentrate my hunting efforts in areas where I have encountered good numbers of does in the past. Does and fawns tend to hang around together, and they routinely congregate in specific areas, often bedding as a loosely knit group in a favorite swale or sunny hillside. I can’t direct you to these “ladies-only bedrooms,” but I’ll bet there is such a place in the chunk of woods you hunt.

You can locate these places that hold special favor with the does by simply noting those areas where you encounter the most doe activity. After a few years of hunting the same ground, a familiar pattern becomes apparent.

On several occasions, I have located a hotbed of doe activity by simply listening to other hunters. When you hear a hunter complain that he sat on his stand and saw 15 does but not a single buck, find out where he was sitting. You can bet that when the time is right, there will be a buck or two sniffing around the vicinity.

Sources indicate that A dominant buck ranges well out of his home area during the actual breeding season. I don’t think he goes out of his way looking for does so much as he is drawn out of the territory when following the tracks of a doe that has visited his scrapes or just wandered through the area. A buck engaged in this activity moves with a single-minded purpose, shuffling along, nose to the ground, seldom looking up, intent upon finding the maker of the tracks he is following. I once missed a buck that trailed a doe past my tree stand in this manner, my arrow slicing harmlessly over the buck’s back only to skitter noisily through the carpet of dry oak leaves a few yards beyond. The buck lifted his head and looked in the direction of the commotion. Apparently satisfied that whatever had made the racket was not what he was looking for, he then ambled on his way while I frantically fumbled around trying to nock another arrow.

When a buck finally tracks down a doe, as often as not, she will then lead the buck on a little chase that, in all likelihood, will take the buck still farther from his home base. By the time the buck actually mates with the doe, he may be miles from his original starting point. On the way back to his core area, it is not unlikely that the buck will cut the track of another “hot” doe and repeat the scenario.

All of this rambling makes it impossible to pattern a buck during the height of the breeding season, prompting many knowledgeable whitetail hunters to claim that taking a good buck during the peak of the rut is mostly a matter of luck. I disagree.

Recent findings suggest that hunting near a known “doe hangout” can help. And you can stack the deck in your favor even more by hunting a funnel area near a concentration of does. A funnel is simply any natural or man-made feature of the terrain that restricts the movement of deer. An hourglass-shaped section of woods is the classic funnel. Deer moving from one wide portion of the hourglass to the other must pass through the narrow waist. In farm country, the funnel may be a brushy fenceline connecting two woodlots. In the rugged country of the West, where whitetails are becoming increasingly common, a jutting jaw of sheer rimrock can force whitetails into a confined passage. Funnels work well because even though a buck with a snootful of “hot” doe scent wouldn’t care if he was standing in the middle of Madison Avenue, the does do not lose their heads. Does will stick to cover when on the move, even when there is a grunting, panting Romeo dogging their every move.

In many whitetail states, hunters are left with no choice but to hunt well after the main rutting period is over. At first, hunting after the opening weekend under these circumstances appears to be a futile endeavor. Without the promise of the rut to keep the bucks on the move, and with the absence of hunters to jar deer loose, what chance does the midweek hunter have of scoring on a decent buck? He has a pretty good one, I would say.

Industry observers note that first, although the bulk of the breeding chores are completed in about a two-week period, there is still some activity after the main rut is over. Does that were not impregnated will cycle back into heat 28 days after their first estrus cycle ends. In some states, this is just about the time the rifle season rolls around. In addition, in some of the best whitetail areas, it is not uncommon for female fawns of the year to breed. This often applies to as many as 40 percent of them. Frequently, these young breeders experience their first estrus cycle later than older does. So, don’t strike out the possibility of the rut working in your favor even though the peak has passed. In that part of Minnesota where I live, the bulk of the breeding is completed by mid-November, yet each year, I find active scrapes late into November and even December. Last season, during an especially mild December, I found a pair of bushel-basket-size recently freshened scrapes while hunting grouse on Upcoming Year’s Eve day. If you can find these “late scrapes,” concentrate your hunting efforts near them.

But even if you fail to find any of these scrapes later in the year, you still stand a good chance of tagging a buck during the middle of the week if you let the after-effects of the rut work in your favor. During the rut, a buck takes little time out to eat. By the end of the breeding season, a buck that began the rut in peak condition can be drawn and thin, actually haggard looking. Some bucks lose up to 20 percent of their body weight during the course of the rut. Across the Northern states and Canada, where winter-kill is an annual problem, the big, breeding bucks follow the fawns in death each winter simply because they run off all of their reserve fat during the rut and are often unable to replenish it before the onset of winter snows.

In a recent development, although the largest bucks are often nocturnal in their feeding habits at other times of the year, when the rut is over, dominant bucks cannot afford to limit their foraging to the hours of darkness alone. In order to regain their strength and put on the layer of fat necessary to see them through the winter, they must forage during the day. This gives the after-the-opener hunter the chance he needs to find bucks up and about during shooting hours.

Recent findings suggest that this need to feed heavily does not necessarily mean that a substantial buck will be found sauntering around an alfalfa field at high noon, scarfing down the last frost-tinged greens of the year. It does mean that rather than tucking himself safely away in a thicket long before the morning sun ever peeks over the ridge, a buck will now tend to linger at the feeding grounds longer in the morning. Does and fawns often feed for an hour after sunrise, and now, bucks will begin to do the same. In the evening, when they normally would not begin feeding until complete darkness had fallen, bucks will now arrive at the feeding sites earlier — often in that last precious minute of shooting light.

Recent findings suggest that even at midday, the significant boys will not be content to simply lay in their beds and chew their cuds. I have noticed that once the rut is over, bucks are much more likely to rise from their beds and spend an hour or two at midday — often between 11 a.m. and 2 p.m. — browsing near their bedding sites.

It has been revealed that all of this daylight activity is a major plus for the after-the-opener hunter who must depend upon natural deer movements, rather than other hunters, to put a buck in front of him. The natural inclination is to hunt from a stand near the feeding area, but this is a mistake when you’re after mature bucks. A big buck is constantly alert, using each of his senses to detect the slightest hint of danger. Never is a buck more alert than when he is feeding during shooting light because he knows he is most vulnerable then. The bucks I have observed feeding during the season have been wound-up tighter than a watch spring and ready to snap at the slightest provocation. One miscue on your part, whether it is movement or scent or whatever, will send him running. I try to avoid known feeding areas, and I concentrate my efforts near the bedding areas.

In a recent development, hunting near the bedding area means that any shot I take will most often be attempted in good light. That’s important for a clean kill. A buck may not arrive back at his bedding area until the sun is an hour high in the morning, and he may leave his bed to begin a dawdling trip to the feeding area in late afternoon. Instead of risking a poor shot at a shadowy form in the gray gloom of dusk or dawn, I take my shot when the light is in my favor.

Also, by concentrating my efforts in the vicinity of the buck’s daytime haunts, I have a better chance of catching him up and about during the midday hours. If I am forced to move into the bedding area and take a stand at mid-morning, I risk detection by the buck. But if I move into my stand in the dark and set up quietly, I double my chances of scoring. If I fail to take the buck as he returns from breakfast, I will be there waiting when he gets up for lunch or dinner.

Recent findings suggest that but you don’t have to confine yourself to a stand. If conditions allow for quiet stillhunting, I like nothing better than to either prowl the edges of a buck’s daytime haunts or simply tread my way along a ridge littered with the acorns of the white oak, moving only a few yards at a time and stopping often to look, listen and feel. Often after the crowds of opening day are gone from the woods for another year, it is just me and the deer — one-on-one. And that’s the way I like it best.

This story, “After Opening Day,” appeared in the November 1987 concern of Outdoor Life. Read more from this series:.

Is Early-Season Skiing Worth It? Here’s the Case for Going.

📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (577 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Skimag

⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • In a recent development, there’s a lot to love about skiing: being outdoors, pushing yourself to improve, finding your flow, and being part of ski culture.
  • The solution is early-season skiing.
  • Plus, everything that makes skiing great still stands: you’re outside, you’re improving, you’re dipping into your flow state, and you’re more a part of ski culture than if you were to come for President’s Weekend like everyone else.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

(Photo: Courtesy of Vail Resorts).

In a recent development, there’s a lot to love about skiing: being outdoors, pushing yourself to improve, finding your flow, and being part of ski culture. But too often, the things that make skiing great get overshadowed by cost and crowds. It’s hard to find your flow when the run is crowded, and even the best ski day is hard to enjoy when lodging, lift tickets, and lunch leave you financially stretched.

The solution is early-season skiing. Few people book a ski trip in November or early December, and even local skiers tend to be unenthused. But I think they’re missing out. In fact, early season is one of my favorite times to ski. Early season turns have led to breakthroughs in my technique, and it’s one of the only times when the mountain feels small enough to meet up with friends.

Plus, everything that makes skiing great still stands: you’re outside, you’re improving, you’re dipping into your flow state, and you’re more a part of ski culture than if you were to come for President’s Weekend like everyone else.

And the things that make skiing less appealing are non-challenges.

In a recent development, the cost of an early ski season trip can be half or even a third of what you’ll pay just a few weeks later. In Jackson Hole, for example, if you visit in early December, rather than Christmas week, you’ll pay $85 for a lift ticket instead of $340. Similarly, a room at the ultra-luxe slopeside Hotel Terra Jackson Hole increases by $600 a night based on whether you stay in early or late December. The same goes for massive ski weeks like spring break and Presidents’ Day—and the weeks in between aren’t much cheaper.

And then there’s the fact that when you’re not skiing at the same time as everyone else, every aspect of the day (or your entire trip) becomes more enjoyable. You’ll get in more skiing thanks to shorter (or nonexistent) lift lines, and you don’t have to worry about running into someone on the way down. And when you aren’t one of 10 people waiting in line for rental gear or a table at the restaurant, you’ll get warmer, more personalized service. (Plus, in early season, everyone is fresh and excited for the season ahead, not tired and over it.).

When the mountain is fully open, and everyone’s ski legs are firing, the pressure to go massive is real. It can be difficult and dangerous to try to keep up, especially if you’re new to skiing or it’s your first (or only) ski trip of the year.

Industry observers note that but in the early season, everyone is still getting their ski legs under them, and the skiing is more about fine-tuning your technique and rebuilding muscle. There’s nothing showy about it, and most people leave their egos at home.

The biggest argument against early season skiing is the lack of snow. Indeed, in the early season, the snow hasn’t had time to accumulate. Often, only the lower parts of the mountain are open, and sometimes only thanks to snowmaking. It’s not the time to do a hike-to, and you’ll rarely find any powder, so show up with your expectations (and ego) in check.

But if you’re willing to rethink what a ski day should look like, you can enjoy everything that makes skiing great while avoiding its biggest drawbacks.

Heated Vests Are More Popular Than Ever—These Are the Best We’ve Tested

📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 10 min read (1971 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Fieldandstream

⏱️ ~10 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • We may earn revenue from the products available on this page and participate in affiliate programs.
  • Sources indicate that heated vests may seem a little over-the-top, but hear us out.
  • Industry observers note that with a heated vest, you’ll stay warm and toasty for hours longer than if you were wearing a regular vest, and you’ll get greater range of movement than a jacket.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

We may earn revenue from the products available on this page and participate in affiliate programs. Learn more.

Sources indicate that heated vests may seem a little over-the-top, but hear us out. Unpredictable weather during the fall and early spring can make picking appropriate outdoor clothing rather challenging. It’s often too cool for summer wear, yet too warm to break out the winter jackets. Enter the vest. Not only are vests great for working outside or hunting during transition seasons, they’re also a good choice for colder temperatures—especially if you choose one that provides electric heat via a battery.

Industry observers note that with a heated vest, you’ll stay warm and toasty for hours longer than if you were wearing a regular vest, and you’ll get greater range of movement than a jacket. Stores are inundated with outerwear these days, so we did all the testing and the research for you to find the best of the best heated vests.

Recent findings suggest that hunters have a ton of small odds and ends, and the Ororo heated vest is a great way to organize them all. It has 14 pockets for everything from your cell phone and truck keys to extra shot shells. I love the fact that the two large front pockets utilize magnets as a closure system. This makes the vest nice and quiet for stand or blind hunting. The heating zones are be very effective at preventing heat loss, especially around the collar.

I like the fact the power button is tucked inside one of the chest pockets. It’s lighted to indicate the heating level, but it also won’t spook game since it’s tucked away out of sight. My only complaint is that Ororo doesn’t offer this vest in blaze orange. It would be great as an outer layer for safety. Plus, the vest has all the pockets to be a solid upland hunting vest. The back pocket is a little too small for larger upland birds like pheasants, but the rest of the pockets are great.

In a recent development, ororo’s claim of 10 hours of battery life on low is accurate, although I expect users will stick to medium and high. I got about 3.5 hours of runtime on high, which was slightly more than advertised. But I feel like medium is the sweet spot for the best combination of heat and runtime with this vest.

Recent findings suggest that the Tidewe heated vest is ideal for layering because it’s thin enough to wear under a heavier jacket. This makes it easy to keep your core body temperature up during winter activities. Like the Ororo, there’s an additional zone in the collar that really helps cut down on heat loss through the neck area. The 10000 mAh battery is another plus. It allows a slightly longer runtime on the middle and high settings, which. This is an ideal vest for fishing or for watching sporting events in cold conditions.

Recent findings suggest that one downside of the vest is that the polyester material is a bit noisy. Because of that, it might not be best for hunting unless you are planning shots at longer ranges. However, it’s hard to beat the price point of this vest. It starts at $80 and tops out at $110 depending on size. That’s a great value considering many other vests start around the $200 mark and go up from there. Tidewe—which also makes a great pair of waders—offers the vest in both black and Realtree Edge camo.

The Venture Heat ProMax is an excellent vest for men that’s both stylish and functional. During my wear test, this vest had a great fit, and kept me sufficiently warm before I ever hit the power button. Once I turned it on, the five heat zones warmed swiftly. I like the placement of all the zones. They helped to keep my core—and even my extremities—quite toasty. The vest’s simple design goes with just about all my regular fall wear and I’ve found myself reaching for it for a variety of activities.

Sources indicate that some people might not like the placement of the two battery packs on the lower back while sitting, but it was manageable for me. One minor concern I had was the power button on the lower part of the vest. Several times I bumped it without realizing it until I looked down and saw it was a different color, indicating a different setting.

Sources indicate that as far as battery life goes, the battery lasted for about 11 hours on the low setting. However, I feel like most people are going to utilize the high (red) setting. The runtime on high was a little over four hours, so it’s very power efficient. On the medium setting—which I found very comfortable—the battery ran for about six hours before dying.

Industry observers note that I’ve been using Gobi Heat products for a few years now and they are solid for warmth in cold weather. The Ibex heated vest is a purpose-designed work vest with five heat zones to keep your core toasty, especially when working or participating in other outdoor activities. I’ve found Gobi’s runtimes are mostly accurate, although the low settings are a bit difficult to feel if you have a ton of layers on. The battery with this vest is a little on the small side. However, it is also removable. I would pick up a spare for longer colder days.

Recent findings suggest that one of the reasons I like this vest for work is simply because it is machine-washable, so it’s going to be much easier to maintain. For anyone who spends a lot of time working construction or doing ranch work, this vest will hold up to the abuse of working day after day. I also like the power buttons on Gobi’s products. They are easy to operate while also being robust enough that you won’t turn the vest off, or change the settings if you bump it.

In a recent development, arris makes an excellent heated vest that utilizes the insulating properties of fleece to trap all the warmth generated by the heat system. Fleece has some great moisture-resistant qualities that make this vest ideal for anyone planning to hunt or work in bad weather. This material is also incredibly comfortable.

This is another vest that utilizes an independent control system for the eight zones, which means you can turn the heat in for the areas you need it most. This feature alone makes this vest incredibly versatile. But it’s also thin enough to layer underneath a heavier jacket, adding to the value. The only downside we found is that the battery takes a long time to charge.

Industry observers note that the most notable aspect of a heated vest is the electrical components. For the vests I tested, I charged each battery to full and then ran it until it died. I did this for multiple settings to see exactly how long they’ll keep warm in cold temperatures. I evaluated the feel of the different heat levels and how much warmth they delivered.

Additionally, I considered the following factors in picking my favorite vests.

With electric vests, the entire concept is that being keeping your core body temperature up, the rest of your body will also stay warm. It’s a simple idea, but it works provided temperatures aren’t too extreme. That’s why the heated zones of each heated vest are just about identical regardless of brand, and model. Almost every vest feature chest and back zones. Most also have heat panels in the neck area which is an area of major heat loss in most garments.

Sources indicate that used in conjunction with warm socks, a hunting jacket, or thermal underwear, a vest can be extremely effective as part of an over-all warmth system. Because vests don’t have sleeves, they do offer a greater range of movement when used alone. This makes them ideal for working or other everyday activities that require a lot of movement.

When it comes to the heating systems themselves, we highly recommend getting something with different levels of adjustment. In my experience, the lowest settings are more battery efficient, but often don’t get warm enough to feel the heat properly. Especially if you’re layered up. I usually like to use at least a 10000 mAh battery for maximum heat time while I’m working or playing outside.

The good news is that most vest batteries are interchangeable with one another. If you aren’t pleased with the stock battery’s performance, it’s usually easy to upgrade to one that gets a better runtime.

The most common construction for heated vests is a nylon outer shell that adds a certain degree of water resistance. Some people have concerns about safely wearing one of these vests in a rain. However, the voltage of these vests is far too low to be dangerous, even if the vest gets completely soaked.

Many heated vests feature fleece for the lining. It’s easy to maintain and absorbs odors easily. Fleece is great for working because it’s a flexible material that breathes extremely well. The downside is that it is not the most environmentally friendly.

I’m also a stickler for zippers. Far too many outdoor companies have gotten cheap with these components in recent years. I personally like to look for larger zippers because they’re easier to grasp when temperatures drop. My favorites are YKK zippers because they are easy to use, and rarely get stuck on fabric or seize up.

Most vests are worn as an outer layer, but it is possible to wear clothes over thinner ones. The best option is to wear a heavier winter jacket over the vest. It depends on how many layers one wears under the vest too. Because some heated vests can get quite thick.

According to recent reports, most manufacturers advertise a maximum battery life of 12-13 hours with a power bank of this size. However, in my experience, those times usually align with a heated garment used on the low setting. Expect 6 to 8 hours with medium, and 3 to 6 hours with high for most vests. Extremely cold temperatures can negatively affect the battery life if exposed for prolonged periods.

Most people will want a heated vest to fit slightly more snugly than a normal vest. The main reason is because if the vest is loose, you might not be able to feel the heated elements. This applies for just about any heated garment. Especially when running the heat on the lowest levels. I’ve personally found that most of my heated gear needs to be run on medium at a minimum for me to feel the effects. Try to keep the layers under the vest to a minimum because that can also affect how much heat makes it to your body.

While all the best heated vests on this list are quite capable, I liked the Venture Heat ProMax based on a combination of comfort and heating capabilities. The vest is heavy enough to work quite efficiently on its own. The stellar, battery-efficient heating system is just a bonus. In my mind, it’s the ideal fall, early winter, and spring vest for work and play.

#67849. Industry News: The Best Cellular Trail Cameras of 2026, Tested and Reviewed
